News.title: PC Andrew Harper’s colleague says Government is ‘spitting in the face of police’ over killers’ early release
News.content:
ONE of the first cops on the scene after PC Andrew Harper was dragged to his death has accused the Government of “spitting in the faces of police officers”.

Retired dog-handler Chris Bushnell spoke out as Downing Street ruled out an exemption that would stop PC Harper’s killers getting early release.



No 10’s rejection means that two of the officer’s three smirking killers, Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, will be free within months — despite one of the biggest-ever public petitions demanding they be kept locked up.

Chris, 59, drove after the cold-blooded burglary gang that dragged 28-year-old newlywed Andrew to his death in August 2019.



He told the Old Bailey how the gang tried to ram his car with their Seat Toledo before fleeing the scene to their homes on traveller sites.

Chris spoke of the pain he still endures over his colleague’s death — and his anger that two of the killers are due to be freed.



He said: “When I first heard they could be let out early, I was shaking. It’s absolutely outrageous.

“I am angry with them, but I’m also angry with the Government. They’re spitting in the face of police officers.”

Chris said the prospect of early release will impact and demoralise many officers traumatised by losing a colleague in such a violent way.

He said: “This belittles them. It makes them feel worthless.”



Chris, who retired from Thames Valley Police in 2022, said he will “never forgive” Andrew’s killers for what they did.

He added: “To think these people could be out within weeks is appalling. The Government has to understand that this was the death of a police officer.

“Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show respect.”

Chris was working on a West Berkshire dog unit when Andrew was killed, and recalled having a cup of tea with him earlier in the day.



He said: “He was so friendly and always asked about the dog. He was an animal-lover, a nice lad.”

Late that night Chris was alerted on his police radio about a burglary gang that stole a £10,000 Honda quad bike from a house near Sulhamstead, Berkshire.

Unbeknown to Chris, Andrew had been lassoed round his ankles by a trailing rope from the teenage traveller gang’s car.

Andrew — due to go on honeymoon with wife Lissie after he finished his shift — was dragged more than a mile down a country lane.



Chris was waiting in a lay-by for the suspects’ vehicle when he saw it emerge from the darkness without its lights on.

He later fought back tears as he told the Old Bailey how he initially believed Andrew’s body was a deer carcass — before realising it was human as it accelerated away.

Chris pursued the vehicle and came to a fork in the road, telling jurors when he looked to the right he saw the Seat driving at him.

He said: “Without warning it was coming straight towards me.

“I then reared to the left. I took the view that they had deliberately chosen to drive straight at me.”



Chris gave chase after the vehicle until an inspector instructed him over the radio to stop.

In the meantime, Andrew’s patrol partner radioed: “My crewmate is gone. I don’t know where he is.”

Minutes later Chris received the devastating news that his colleague had been killed.

He said: “I’ve seen people die before. I’ve seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.”

Chris was left “numb and in disbelief”.



He received counselling and support from the Police Federation, and revisits the scene of Andrew’s death every year.

He said: “I will never get over it.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A petition organised by PC Harper’s Police Federation branch — demanding his killers are kept behind bars — was set to hit 900,000 signatures on Monday evening.

Aileen O’Connor, chair of the branch, said: “The public are speaking loudly and clearly. The silence from the Government is deafening. What they’re doing is indefensible.”

News.title: Special Concorde flights, 500k flocking to Cornwall & biggest ever power surge… How UK stopped for 1999 total eclipse
News.content:
CROWDED on to rooftops, ships, hillsides and bridges, millions of us were awestruck as we witnessed 1999’s total solar eclipse.

The date was August 11, and it was the first time this country had experienced the celestial spectacle for 72 years.



No one wanted to miss it. Like the audience at a 3D movie, they wore special glasses to protect their eyes so they could gaze to the heavens as the moon covered the sun.

Factories closed, roads were clogged by traffic jams and trials at the Old Bailey in London were even briefly paused so that judges, lawyers, and jurors could watch day turn to night in the first full eclipse visible in the UK since June 29, 1927.



Tomorrow, the nation will once again have the chance to witness this incredible phenomenon when 90 to 95 per cent of the sun is hidden from view in a dramatic partial eclipse.

These cosmic coincidences happen because the sun is about 400 times larger than the moon, and about 400 times further away from Earth, making them appear almost the same size in our sky.

This allows us to witness wonders such as a breathtaking total solar eclipse, where the moon can perfectly cover the sun.​

So be sure you do not miss out on tomorrow’s marvel because the next full one is not due until September 23, 2090.

Dr Cyrielle Opitom, a member of the Royal Astronomical Society council, tells The Sun: “If the moon had been just a little bit further away from us there would never be a total eclipse.”

The moon passes just above or below the sun every month.



Normally, when this happens, the moon is not visible because it is obscured by the solar glare.

But during an eclipse, the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun.

In another stroke of random good fortune, Cornwall should again be the best place to view the phenomena.



In 1999, the “path of totality” — meaning the point at which there is a 100 per cent eclipse — passed between Penzance and Falmouth on the peninsula of England.

This time, around 95 per cent of the sun will be blotted out above Cornwall just after 7pm tomorrow.

Edinburgh and London will both see a 91 per cent eclipse, while it will be 93 per cent in Belfast and 92 per cent in Newcastle.

Anyone wishing to enjoy a “totality” tomorrow needs to head elsewhere in Europe.

The most western point of Iceland, a tiny part of Portugal and a large chunk of northern Spain are in its path.



To celebrate, Bjork is headlining a rave near Iceland’s capital, Reykjavik, and there are seven festivals in Spain.

Other fanatics will be out in the Atlantic on specially chartered ships to catch the historic moment.

A solar eclipse does happen once every 18 months somewhere on Earth and there are obsessives who try to witness as many as possible, though not all are as dramatic as tomorrow’s.



Dr Opitom, who saw a full one on the horizon from an observatory in Chile in 2019, says: “It is absolutely spectacular.”

Back in 1999, two Concordes were sent up by British Airways so that 200 passengers paying £1,500 per seat had the best chance of getting a clear view of the event from the air.

On the ground, a total eclipse lasts for around two minutes, but due to the supersonic craft travelling at twice the speed of sound, they got to enjoy it for some six minutes.

The number of people on the tiny Channel island of Alderney swelled fivefold, from 2,000 to 10,000, because it was one of the best spots to see the incredible sight.

Around 250,000 extra tourists headed for Devon and Cornwall 27 years ago, and there were traffic jams on the way to Land’s End, one of the first places in Europe to go fully dark at 11.11am.



As the eclipse started, the birds went quiet and ducks tucked their heads in their wing feathers, believing it was night-time.

Once it was over, the air was filled with a “dawn chorus” as they woke up again.

The temperature also dropped, but the South West was largely cloudy so onlookers only caught glimpses of the total eclipse.

There were some parts of the British Isles where the skies were clear enough to fully enjoy the eerie moment, particularly the North East of England.



Tomorrow, there is far more chance of the clouds parting as the heatwave continues.

Most of Britain should be sunny until the moon begins to obscure the rays just after 6pm.

Whether it is cloudy or not, one rule always applies — never look at the sun with the naked eye.

Even with the moon covering most of the giant fireball, it can still blind onlookers.



Wearing regular sunglasses is no protection at all and only eclipse glasses bearing the ISO 12312-2 safety standard should be used.

Make sure they are bought from a trusted retailer because fake ones are being sold online.

Despite repeated warnings about the risk in 1999, hospitals across the country received hundreds of calls from people complaining about eye problems in the aftermath of the eclipse.

If you want to keep the party going this year, then there is a good reason to stay out beyond 6pm.



That is because there is the added bonus of the Perseid meteor shower.

With the moon in its new moon phase, and its light diminished, during the Perseid’s peak it should be much more visible over the UK.

Keep your eyes peeled between midnight tomorrow and 5.30am on Thursday.

The eclipse will also be a far more relaxing occasion this time around.



In 1999, with the turn of the millennium just over four months away, there were a lot of predictions that the darkened skies heralded the end of the world.

Verses from the 16th century French astrologer Nostradamus had been interpreted to predict “fire from heaven” in that year.

Fashion designer Paco Rabanne had even warned that the MIR space station would plummet to Earth and that Paris would be destroyed.

As with all the millennium scare stories, no disasters befell anyone.

In fact, after the eclipse passed Britain on its way towards the Middle East and India, everyone returned to their desks to switch back on their computers and make themselves a cup of tea.



The power surge was the biggest the UK had ever experienced.

With a peak demand of 36,150 megawatts, it was even higher than when the nation tuned in to watch Prince Charles marry Lady Diana Spencer in 1981.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And as the skies lightened there was one other lesson we learned from 1999.

Nothing can ever truly eclipse The Sun.

News.title: Residents of tiny Welsh community left ‘blindsided’ after migrant families are secretly moved into former village hall
News.content:
RESIDENTS of a tiny ­community say they have been blindsided by plans to house asylum seekers in their old village hall.

Locals were expecting the new homes to be put up for rent on the market but were shocked to discover the Home Office had already moved migrant families in.



Earlier this year, the Government promised to stop housing ­asylum seekers in newbuilds after The Sun revealed an entire street had been designated as migrant housing.

But out of the 15 new units in the North Wales ­village, 13 have been taken over by Clearsprings, the Government contractor run by asylum billionaire Graham King.



Gronant in Flintshire has a population of just 1,600, with residents fearing new arrivals will put pressure on stretched resources.

Kerrie Cox, 39, lives near the new asylum accommodation and said: “No-one was notified whatsoever.

“I was washing my car and a blacked out minibus arrived and seven people got out, five males and two females.

“We had been told the properties were to be leased out or sold with a promise of them going as social housing.

“Everyone is in shock. We have had the police here all day and night.

“We don’t normally have a police presence around here.



“I feel betrayed by the Government as a taxpayer.”

Julie Tuson, 65, said: “We want to know who is coming and vetted.

“If we want a better Britain, we all have to be involved. We were not told about it. I feel absolutely betrayed by the Government.”



Her partner Robert Bagshaw, 64, said: “They wouldn’t have a ­consultation beforehand because they would know the outcome. It’s definitely the wrong area.”

Laurie Gilmour, 29, said: “The feeling in the village is one of anger and uncertainty.

“It’s about not knowing who will be there. Who would want a load of random people moving into a village?

“It’s the wrong area. There’s nothing here.”

Keith Williams, 57, commented: “Our homeless people should get priority. You see ex-soldiers like myself on the street.”



Councillor Glyn Banks is seeking a meeting between the area’s Labour MP Becky Gittins, police and representatives of worried residents.

He told The Sun: “It’s just too big for a small village.”

Resident Joanne Gilmore has started a petition urging the council to reconsider.



She pointed to problems such as “limited access to healthcare, education and employment opportunities”.

Flintshire council said: “They are not illegal immigrants.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They are individuals exercising their legal right to claim asylum and deserve to be treated with compassion and respect.”

A ­Government spokesman said: “The concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms.”

News.title: How mega-dinghy that holds more migrants than an EasyJet flight will cost Brits £25MILLION in tax from single crossing
News.content:
A RECORD 230 illegal immigrants cram on to a single dinghy heading for Britain — landing taxpayers with an estimated £25million bill.

The 49ft craft carried more passengers on Sunday afternoon than an average EasyJet flight, with the migrants’ arrival slammed as “beyond a joke”.



It smashes the record for the most migrants on one boat — beating the 165 total set just last month.

Reform UK boss Nigel Farage said: “It’s yet more proof that this illegal invasion is a national security emergency.”



The crammed craft collected its passengers along the French coast, with some needing to be rescued when it started “buckling” off the resort of Berck-sur-Mer.

But it arrived here in the early hours of Monday with mainly young men straddling the sides, many not even wearing life jackets.

It had more passengers than the average EasyJet flight from France.

Each is estimated to cost taxpayers around £106,000 in immediate pressures, so the one boat could mean close to a £25million burden.

They were among 423 migrants arriving on Sunday in five dinghies as French cops again failed to thwart launches from their shores.



Home Office sources insist that smuggling gangs are packing more people into each boat as interceptions are improving.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham claimed Labour’s crackdown plan “is working”, and said this year’s total of 15,242 is 42 per cent down on 2025.

But Mr Farage hit back: “Yes, the overall numbers are down this year but they’re still horrendous.

“If I had told the British people a few years ago that tens of thousands of young men, some of whom are going to be terrorists, would come into Britain, you wouldn’t have believed me.



“So whether we have fewer bad people this year than last year, the situation is desperate.

“It should be declared a national security emergency. And yes, we have managed to stop some of the dinghies, but it doesn’t stop the problem. It is still something that is completely out of control.”

More than £1billion has now been handed to France to help stopping Channel crossings.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has also signed a “performance-related” extension where cash is withheld for poor results — and critics are demanding a refund.

Tory Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “This is now beyond a joke. The French authorities could easily have stopped a vessel this size from embarking in shallow waters.”



The mega-dinghy was carrying about 50 people when monitored by rescue vessel Abeille Normandie just after 5pm on Sunday.

Lifeboat crews at the SNSM, the French equivalent of the RNLI, were then called to an area between Berck and Merlimont, where a large group was waiting.

When rescuers arrived, they saw people near the water, before around 150 people, including women and children, suddenly emerged from the dunes.



Witnesses said they rushed to the inflatable like a “human tide”, and began climbing aboard.

The SNSM says the boat became so overloaded that about 30 people ended up in the water, even as the boat continued on its journey.

The rising tide also left part of the group isolated on the French coast, prompting gendarmes and firefighters to intervene.

Rescuers said the boarding operation was a “major risk”, with many occupants unable to swim.

Meanwhile, the Abeille Normandie deployed its smaller boats as crews attempted to prevent a mass- casualty incident.



French rescuers remained in contact with it until around 7.45pm, at one point reporting the vessel was “taking on waves”.

By the time the overloaded boat headed out to the Channel, 230 people had been counted aboard, including more than 20 children.

The SNSM described that figure as a “new and sad record”.

But it claimed the coordination between the different emergency services had helped “avoid a tragedy”.

The dinghy then continued across the Channel overnight, before being brought into Dover at around 2.30am on Monday.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Government source said: “While this boat is larger, the number of crossings is down significantly, and we just had the lowest figures for a July since 2020.”

A Home Office spokesman added: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people on to unseaworthy vessels.”

News.title: Urgent search for missing mum, 31, who vanished with her three kids two days ago
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIND THEM Urgent search for missing mum, 31, who vanished with her three kids two days ago

AN urgent search is underway to find a missing mum who disappeared with her three kids two days ago.

Alimat, 31, from Wolverhampton, was last seen with her children on Saturday in the Digbeth area of central Birmingham.

A CCTV image shows Alimat and her three children walking with at least two suitcases.



The mum also appears to be pushing a pram laden with coats and other clothing.



West Midlands Police said in a social media post: “Have you seen Alimat?

“The 31-year-old from Wolverhampton is missing along with her three children.

“They have been missing since 8 August and were last seen in the area of Digbeth in Birmingham.



“If you see Alimat please call 999 quoting RID 1160387.”

News.title: Moment massive WW2 bomb weighing 79 STONE is blown to smithereens at UK quarry in dramatic explosion
News.content:
THIS is the dramatic moment a huge WW2 bomb discovered at a sand and quarry was blown up in a controlled explosion.

The seven-foot-long, 79 stone device was found by workers at a site in Barton-under-Needwood, Staffordshire.



Emergency services rushed to the scene on August 6, including cops and military teams to tackle the huge ordnance.

Dramatic footage has now emerged showing enormous plumes of smoke billowing into the air as the 1,100lb device was blown to smithereens.



Ahead of the war relic being destroyed by bomb disposal experts, seven residents living nearby were evacuated.

It was blown to bits after experts determined the device was too dangerous to move.



Specialist teams used sand from the quarry to build protective cages around the device before it was pulverised.

A 900m (2,953ft) cordon was initially put in place in the area before this was reduced to 200m.



It was later fully removed so people could return to their homes.

A Heidelberg Materials UK spokesperson said: “Well thankfully that’s not something we have to deal with every day.

“Earlier this week we uncovered an historic WWII bomb at our Barton sand and gravel quarry in Staffordshire.

“After its discovery within the excavation area at the southern end of the quarry near to the River Trent, our emergency procedures came into play and the police and military were soon on site.

“After establishing that the device was unsafe to move, bomb disposal experts used sand from the site to create cages to contain the bomb and subsequently carried out a safe, controlled explosion.



“Well done to our Barton quarry team for their calm and efficient handling of this unexpected event and huge thanks to the teams from East Staffordshire Police and the Ministry of Defence for their professionalism and diligence.”

The unexploded bomb was initially found on Tuesday, August 4.

Cops worked with specialist colleagues from Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) to dispose of the ordnance safely.

All railway lines running between Tamworth and Burton-on-Trent were blocked on August 6.

Some trains were cancelled or delayed by up to an hour prior to the explosion, National Rail said.



The A38 and other roads that were closed were also reopened to traffic following the detonation.

News.title: Plagiarism prof is just a thinking man’s Lee Andrews – beggars belief that woke Cambridge & BBC made him a poster boy
News.content:
JASON ARDAY: Cambridge University’s widely publicised youngest black professor.

Now its youngest black ex-professor after he resigned last week.





On some level, it is hard not to have some sympathy with a sweet-looking chap whose lies have not so much caught up with him, more snowballed over him completely and absolutely.

But those who really deserve our sympathy are the hard-working Cambridge students, whose degrees may forever now be called into question.

And the cerebral candidates whose dream job he snatched by virtue of what appears to be a largely fabricated CV.

And the bleeding-heart liberals who slammed the right-wing Press for trying to bring down a trailblazer.

They have just taken back their collective DEI cause 30 years. Because Arday is little more than a thinking man’s Lee Andrews: A smiling assassin who has single-handedly almost brought down an academic institution.

Make no bones about it, this is Cambridge’s Ratner moment.

His departmental boss, Hilary Cremin, came out to laud his anorexically thin body of “work” as the “best in the world”. Which, as one commentator observed, might not sit well with students of, say, Harvard’s Lawrence D Bobo, Stanford’s Thomas Sowell or the profound insights on race of Britain’s luminary, Heidi Safia Mirza of UCL.

How those Dark Blues must be chuckling to themselves across the River Thames.





At the time of writing, publishers at Simon & Schuster still plan to go ahead with Arday’s memoir, Great And Unfortunate Things.

Presumably, then, it will sit in the fantasy section of Waterstones, near Harry Potter.

Not even JK Rowling in her pomp could have come up with such a tale, though.

Wild claims of running 600 miles in six days and 30 marathons in 35 days, completing the latter feat with a broken leg, one that had ballooned to twice its normal width.

Alas, a photo of him crossing the finish line of said run showed a normal-looking appendage.

And here lies Mr Arday’s biggest problem. As a millennial, he grew up in an age of receipts.

That is to say, anything anyone under-45 has ever done is plastered all over the internet.

Every spit and cough documented for all to see. I mean, there is a literal photo of me spitting on Facebook circa 2007, which is lovely.

Yet very few photos appear to exist of any of this fantasist’s spurious claims.

You’d think Cambridge — who came out on the veritable rampage when the first allegations of plagiarism surfaced — might have done even a cursory background/social media check when they first actively championed this fall guy.



Likewise the BBC, who pompously declare themselves the world’s “most trusted broadcaster”, might have done some due diligence before breathlessly highlighting interviewing him.

The clues about Mr Arday, who denies being a liar, were all there.

After all, a man who scraped two GCSEs in textiles and PE might not be our next Great Mind. But no.

So desperate to find a poster boy were these two veritable institutions, all basic common sense went out the window.

Now, it emerges, Cambridge’s own newspaper is refusing to cover the story. Which is, at best, an embarrassing oversight for what is rapidly becoming the most talked-about news story of 2026, and, at worst, pernicious censorship.

Elevating a man so ill-equipped to deal with the inevitable fallout is cruel. Although if it’s any consolation to Jason, his story makes for a Bafta-winning documentary.

The Tinder Swindler for the internet age: The Professor Who Never Was, perhaps.

Naturally, TikTok and Instagram are going wild with their own hot takes.

One meme showed an AI Jason overtaking Sir Mo Farah to win Olympic gold in 2012, another showed him landing on the moon before Neil Armstrong (not unreasonable given Jason claimed to have been in the series Seven- Up, which first aired decades before his birth) and others are questioning whether he also managed to survive the Titanic.

One meme showed an AI Jason overtaking Sir Mo Farah to win Olympic gold in 2012, another showed him landing on the moon before Neil Armstrong (not unreasonable given Jason claimed to have been in the series Seven-Up, which first aired decades before his birth) and others are questioning whether he also managed to survive the Titanic.



It would all be funny if it wasn’t so unavoidably sad.

SMACKS OF FILM FIONA

PRINCESS Fiona is alive and well.

Ahead of the fifth instalment of Shrek, due for release next summer, up popped this X-rated preview.

Is it just me, or does this dominatrix have a touch of the green ogre about her? Maybe it’s just unfortunate lighting.

Whatever, Melanie Bull, who receives more than £1,000 a month in benefits including disability, is selling sexual services on adult websites as a side hustle.

But hey, whatever floats your boat.

POLITICIAN Jo Galer took a live zoom straight from the toilet. The utterly unbothered New Zealand councillor joined a live-stream meeting from her bathroom, with drying undergarments and laundry on full display.



Thus sharing precisely what she thinks of antipodean politics.

MR BIG BUCKS

ANOTHER fine mess by Thames Water chiefs this weekend.

Six weeks after implementing a hosepipe ban in my West London borough – where environmentalist Sir David Attenborough lives – a water main burst, causing millions of litres of flooding.

Naturally, barely a peep from Thames Water.

And no sign of boots on the ground, despite the fact countless homes have been left without running water.

Oh that’s right. They’re too busy paying Steve Buck, their new chief financial officer, a £1million signing-on fee.

Grrr.

OLD JOKE, RICHARD

AND so, gerbils the world over exhaled a collective sigh of relief*.



Because here’s Richard Gere spotted “getting close” to his latest, much younger co-star Diana Silvers on the set of their new romantic drama, Asymmetry.

Quite how producers and script writers, in this day and age, think it’s OK to cast a 76-year-old opposite a 28-year-old female love interest baffles.

*Only funny if you’re familiar with the notorious urban myth about the Hollywood actor.

SPEED ZONE RUSE

CAN we all stop pretending, please, and admit that 20mph speed limits are little more than money-making ruses.

Lynda La Plante, she of Prime Suspect fame, is the latest to fall foul of such endlessly opportunist cameras.

The 83-year-old, who drives her dog to the park and uses the car to “meet criminals for research”, was done for by confusing signs, and one camera only ten seconds beyond the 20mph sign.

She has now been handed a six-month ban, something she fears might end her writing career.

These cameras aren’t catching Premier League footballers in souped-up Lamborghinis or 17-year-old boy racers.

They’re crippling hard-working, otherwise law-abiding citizens.

News.title: Savile Row tailors in clash with The Beatles over plans for new museum at Fab Four’s old HQ where they played iconic gig
News.content:
PLANS for a Beatles museum have received a dressing-down from tailors.

The Fab Four’s old HQ in London’s Savile Row is set to be a visitor attraction featuring the rooftop where they played their final gig in 1969.



But Mark Henderson, of the Savile Row Bespoke Association, said it could cause “dangerous congestion” and have a “negative impact” on businesses.

He told council planners: “The pavements on the street are narrow — already frequently clogged with visitors.”



The association represents brands including Edward Sexton, who made suits for The Beatles.

Apple Corps, the Fab Four’s record label, plans to open The Beatles at 3 Savile Row next year.



The seven-floor museum would open the roof where John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr played in public for the last time before cops called a halt due to noise complaints.

There’s also a re-creation of the basement studio where Let It Be was recorded.

Reps told Westminster City Council it will be a “local cultural asset (not just a tourist destination)” and an “education platform rooted in music, creativity, and social history”.

The council will decide in due course.



But the plan is backed by surviving Beatles Paul and Ringo.

Paul said previously: “There are so many special memories within the walls, not to mention the rooftop.”

News.title: Colombia earthquake - live: President confirms 111 killed in devastating 7.4 magnitude quake
News.content:
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake has struck San Jose del Palmar in Colombia, with the impact also causing major damage in the capital Bogota - at least 111 people have been killed

The Colombian government has declared a national disaster after dozens of people have been killed by a devasting 7.4 magnitude earthquake that has struck the region, knocking down buildings and leaving scores trapped beneath rubble.

President President Abelardo de la Espriella told a press conference that 111 people have died so far, with at least 87 people injured by the disaster.

Around 1,575 homes have been damaged and 37 have been destroyed, with a further 61 buildings affected.

Hundreds have died after the devastating quake struck Colombia today, impacting the capital of Bogota and other nearby cities.

Witnesses felt the tremor, which had its epicentre in San Jose del Palmar, some 300 miles away on the border with Venezuela. The quake also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.

The earthquake occurred at a depth of around 115km, with several parts of the country impacted, including Medellín - the capital of Colombia's mountainous Antioquia province. Flights have been grounded at several key airports.

News.title: Coffee CEO drowned daughter, 9, in swamp to get 'revenge' on ex-wife, court hears
News.content:
Coffee CEO drowned daughter, 9, in swamp to get 'revenge' on ex-wife, court hears

Luciano Frattolin, the founder of organic coffee brand Gambella, has been convicted of murdering and hiding the body of his daughter Melina's death last year

View Image Luciano Frattolin with his daughter (Image: Instagram)

A coffee magnate has been found guilty of drowning his nine-year-old daughter in a shallow swamp to get revenge on his ex-wife.

‌



Luciano Frattolin, the founder of organic coffee brand Gambella, has been convicted of murdering and hiding the body of his daughter Melina's death last year.

‌



The 45-year-old from Montreal, Canada, had taken Melina on a trip across the north east of the US in the summer of 2025 in what prosecutors claimed was a ploy to kill his daughter so that he would no longer have to pay child support.

‌



He then lied to police officers that his daughter had been kidnapped, sparking a massive county-wide manhunt.

The young girl's remains were then found on July 19, 2025 hidden under a log in a remote pond in the town of Ticonderoga, New York. Frattolin now faces life in prison after being convicted of second-degree murder and concealment of a body.

Melina’s mum, Kali Galanis, had full custody over her after she ended a long distance relationship with Frattolin in 2019.

‌



Frattolin initially called police and told authorities his daughter had been abducted from a parking lot near Lake George, a resort town in the Adirondack region, authorities said. That led officials to issue an Amber Alert to enlist the public’s help in finding her.

But authorities said there were inconsistencies in the father’s account, and that they concluded there was no evidence she had been taken.

Frattolin initially said he could not find his child after he stepped out of a wooded area at a parking lot near Lake George.

‌



“During a subsequent interview, he then reports two unknown males forced her into a white van,” New York State Police Capt. Robert McConnell said last year. “That lead was thoroughly investigated and disproven.”

Surveillance video shows the father and daughter in another nearby resort town, Saratoga Springs. The girl spoke on the phone with her mother about an hour later and did not indicate she was under duress, police said.

Police believe Frattolin killed the girl after the phone call and before he contacted emergency services. Forest rangers found the girl’s body in the shallows of a pond about 30 miles north of Lake George, in Ticonderoga, authorities said.

News.title: Andy Burnham vows to give locals bigger say over shops in 'hollowed-out' high streets
News.content:
Andy Burnham vows to give locals bigger say over shops in 'hollowed-out' high streets

Kicking off a nationwide summer tour on Tuesday, PM Andy Burnham will promise to hand new powers to councils and people as he highlights the decline of town centres

View 2 Images 'We want more butchers, bakers and bookshops - the businesses that make a high street feel like home,' Andy Burnham says (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/POOL PA via AP)

Andy Burnham has vowed to give locals a greater say over new shops that can open as he attempts to revitalise Britain's hollowed-out high streets.

‌



Kicking off a nationwide summer tour on Tuesday, the Prime Minister will promise to hand new powers to councils and people as he highlights the decline of town centres.

‌



He will launch a crackdown on vape shops, new bookies and "rouge businesses" - building on ex-PM Keir Starmer's efforts to boost neglected high streets. Writing for The Mirror, Mr Burnham said: "These changes are about giving local people something they lost a while back: the power to say no.

‌



"They're about wrestling back the control taken from our communities decades ago and finally giving them a proper say on what happens to the places they call home. But they're also just the beginning. Because saying no is only half the job. We don't just want fewer vape and betting shops. We want more butchers, bakers and bookshops - the businesses that make a high street feel like home."

Downing Street said the government will revoke the Blair-era "Aim to Permit" rule, which they said restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting and 24-hour slot machine shops on the high street. They said local people and authorities will also get a say over whether vape shops open - and to stop them opening near schools.

Officials added the formal definition of a vape shop will be tightened to stop businesses side-stepping the new rules by claiming to be a "convenience store or a retailer".

‌



Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnahm will launch a crackdown on vape shops, new bookies and 'rouge businesses' (Image: In Pictures via Getty Images)

Under proposals first announced by Mr Starmer's government, police will also be able to shut down "dodgy" barbers, vape shops and nail salons for up to a year.

In a statement, Mr Burnham added: "For many people, the high streets they grew up with have been hollowed out and become unrecognisable over decades of decline.

‌



"The rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for. That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do.

"We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street. Local councils will be given the powers they need to rein in unwanted shops and bring town centres back to life."

Housing and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner added: "People know when their high street isn't working for them. Whether it's the vape shop or betting shops that's opened with no say from locals, the shopfront that's seen better days, or the sense that nobody's in control."

‌



She added: "These problems have built up over years, but this government won't leave councils and communities powerless to crackdown on everyday eyesores that blight our high streets. That's why we're giving local leaders the power to say no to what doesn't belong on their high street, and the tools to fix it themselves."

Last year, The Mirror reported on how UK high streets were becoming "ghost towns" with banks, libraries, pharmacies and public toilets replaced by vaping shops, bookies and takeaways.

Downing Street also highlighted analysis from the Centre for Social Justice think tank, which found that Britain has lost nearly 1,800 pubs and bars while vape and tobacco shops have increased in number to almost 2,200 since 2016.

‌



Joshua Nicholson - the head of housing and communities at the CSJ - said: "Britain's high streets have been hijacked by a growing number of dodgy vape shops, mini marts, and barbers, many of which are linked to organised crime.

"The Government is right to give councils new powers to say no to these dodgy shops. High street renewal is vital to restoring security within our communities."

But the Betting and Gaming Council disputed any suggestion that betting shops were spreading unchecked and insisted the real threat to high streets was "more empty units and fewer local jobs, not businesses rooted in the communities they serve".

Article continues below

A spokesperson for the industry body said: "We support tough action against criminal operators and agree local people should have a proper say over their high streets. But the suggestion that betting shops are spreading unchecked is simply wrong. Betting shop numbers have fallen by over a third since 2019. Around 3,000 shops have closed and over 15,000 jobs have already been lost.

"It is wrong to lump highly regulated, licensed betting shops together with rogue or criminal businesses. Betting shops still support 37,500 jobs, bring vital footfall to neighbouring businesses and, for many customers, are valued community hubs."

News.title: Amber heat health alerts issued across almost ALL of England as mercury forecast to hit 36C this week
News.content:
Amber heat health alerts issued across almost ALL of England as mercury forecast to hit 36C this week

The Met Office has issued amber heat health alerts for most of England as temperatures are forecast to soar into the mid-30Cs this week, with the heat expected to peak at 36C on Thursday amid ongoing England drought conditions

View 9 Images People enjoy the warm weather on the beach in Folkestone, Kent (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Amber heat health alerts have been issued across almost all of England, as the mercury was forecast to reach the mid-30Cs again this week.

‌



The UKHSA heat health warnings came as almost three-quarters of England was officially declared in a drought, after a record-breaking hot summer. Amber heat health alerts were issued for the East Midlands, East of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, London, North West, South East, South West, and West Midlands. A single yellow heat health alert was issued for the North East. All of the warnings were in effect from Tuesday August 11 at 9am until Friday August 14 at 9pm.

‌



The Met Office confirmed it was forecasting temperatures to reach the mid-30Cs later in the week, following a relatively cool Monday. The mercury was expected to peak at 36C in some areas on Thursday.

‌



Drought declared in 11 key areas of England as 45 MILLION people urged to save water by any means necessary READ MORE :

Ancient village pond dries up in killer heatwave leaving more than 100 dead fish READ MORE :

View 9 Images Sunseekers at Brockwell Lido in south London (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: "Heat will gradually build this week, with temperatures reaching into the mid-30s Celsius in what will be a fairly widespread heatwave for England and Wales. The driver for this week's heat is high pressure, this becoming dominant over the next day or so, bringing plenty of sunshine and allowing temperatures to build day-by-day.

"Southerly or southeasterly winds will also tap into the hot conditions over Europe, meaning we're looking at further notable heat for many this week, likely peaking on Thursday."

‌



View 9 Images Parts of the UK are set to see their fifth heatwave of the summer (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

The Met Office added that cooler air would sweep in from the north west over the weekend, with weakening high pressure potentially allowing showers or prolonged spells of rain to move across parts of the UK for a period. But forecasters warned that any rainfall would fall far short of compensating for the significant shortfall seen in recent weeks and months.

England and Wales have endured their driest July in records stretching back to 1836, with provisional figures revealing that 19 counties in England saw absolutely no rainfall throughout the entire month. Southern England also recorded its hottest July on record, while Wales experienced its joint hottest July on record, and both the UK and England sweltered through their second hottest July, according to Met Office figures.

‌



View 9 Images Brockwell Park in south London has turned brown during the drought (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Devastating wildfires have torn through areas including the Pennines, the Cairngorms in Scotland, Llanwonno in the Rhondda Valleys, South Wales, and Dunwich Heath in Suffolk. More than 120 firefighters were battling on Monday to contain the latest blaze, which is engulfing a square kilometre of heathland in the New Forest, Hampshire, forcing the closure of the A31 following a vehicle fire.

The sweltering dry conditions this summer have combined with several heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures for the time of year in May and June, which led to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

‌



View 9 Images The pitch at Radnage Recreation Ground, Buckinghamshire (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

An 18-year-old died after getting into difficulty in the sea at Camber Sands beach, East Sussex on Sunday, bringing the total number of fatalities in open-water incidents throughout the scorching, dry summer to more than 40. On inland waterways, the Canal and River Trust announced it has temporarily lifted the requirement for boats without a permanent mooring to relocate at least every 14 days, as part of measures to conserve water supplies.

‌



Britain is increasingly battling the effects of more extreme weather events such as drought, heatwaves and wildfires driven by climate change, which is predominantly caused by burning fossil fuels in power stations, vehicles, homes and industry.

View 9 Images Cricket pitches at Marlow Cricket Club, Marlow, Buckinghamshire (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Downing Street insisted it remained committed to both the immediate response and building long-term resilience against escalating extreme weather events.

‌



The Prime Minister's official spokesman said: "We know these conditions are having a significant impact on communities, farmers and businesses across the country. Our climate is changing. Droughts are becoming more common, which is why we're focused on both the immediate response and long-term resilience.

View 9 Images Air Ambulance Charity Kent Surrey Sussex (KSS) captured a 'dust devil,' caused by the hot weather over Kent (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

"That includes working through the national drought group with the Environment Agency, water companies, farmers, and environmental organisations to protect water supplies and minimise environmental damage. And we're also backing major investment in water infrastructure, including new reservoirs, whilst making clear that water companies must do more to cut leaks and improve resilience."

‌



As amber heat health alerts were put in place, Polly Ashmore, acting consultant in public health at the UK Health Security Agency, called on people to take straightforward precautions to remain safe, such as drinking plenty of fluids, keeping homes cool and steering clear of the sun during the hottest part of the day.

View 9 Images The mercury could hit 36C again this week (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

"For vulnerable groups including older adults and those with existing health conditions, warmer weather can result in serious health outcomes.

Article continues below

View 9 Images The country continues to bake in an unprecedented period of dry, hot weather (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

"We urge health and social care services to ensure they are prepared and encourage people to check on vulnerable friends and family to make sure everyone is aware of the forecast, follows the necessary advice and stays safe in this period of hot weather," she said.

News.title: Police officer 'followed colleague everywhere' during 'spiteful' and 'vindictive' stalking spree
News.content:
Police officer 'followed colleague everywhere' during 'spiteful' and 'vindictive' stalking spree

Detective Constable Timothy Fory was convicted of stalking a former romantic partner and colleague during a 'spiteful' and 'vindictive' eight-week campaign, a court has heard

View 2 Images Metropolitan Police detective Timothy Fory departs Westminster Magistrates' Court following his stalking trial (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

A 'vindictive' police officer sent an ex-partner a string of inappropriate messages and followed her "everywhere she went" during an eight-week stalking campaign, a court has heard.

‌



Detective Constable Timothy Fory, of the Metropolitan Police’s directorate of professional standards, was convicted of stalking a fellow detective from July to September 2024.

‌



The pair had briefly been romantically involved, but broke up after she accused Fory of not respecting her boundaries, Westminster Magistrates’ Court heard on Monday.

‌



Fory, 34, who had been serving in the force for four years, then “persistently” sent her messages on WhatsApp, before he was blocked and he turned to Instagram and Facebook.

In one message, Fory sent his victim a link to Ann Summers lingerie, the court heard.

She replied to the message saying: “I’m starting to think you’ve not registered that we’re not seeing each other anymore.”

‌



Fory replied that he was still “going to imagine you in stockings”.

In another message, Fory asked her “Why are you looking so sexy?”, and added: “I want to put my arms around you.”

View 2 Images Fory was handed a five-year restraining order banning him from contacting his victim (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

‌



The court also heard how Fory followed the woman to a social event in which “everywhere she went he followed”, prosecutor George Crivelli said.

After she blocked him on social media, the defendant tracked down a former partner of hers on Instagram and sent him a message about him being in a relationship with her “out of pure spitefulness and perhaps desperation,” the court heard.

Reading a victim impact statement to the court, the victim said that Fory was “spiteful” and “vindictive” and his actions left her “anxious, nervous and on edge”.

‌



She said she has struggled sleeping, has lost weight and now constantly looks over her shoulder.

Trainee cop arrested on rape and kidnap charges after 'dangerous' car chase READ MORE :

She also said the stalking has “affected” her work, especially when cases “similar” to her own come up.

Fory had denied stalking without fear, alarm or distress in March of last year, but was convicted of the offence after a trial last month.

‌



The defendant was spared jail and handed a 12-month community order and must carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of a rehabilitation requirement.

A five-year restraining order was put in place, meaning he cannot contact his victim either directly or indirectly.

District Judge Caroline Jackson said Fory was in a “position of trust”, saying: “You of all people ought to be fully aware and appreciate the impact your actions have on people”.

‌



The judge told the defendant: “I am saddened that you still don’t appreciate and understand the impact of your conduct.”

She also said a pre-sentence report showed he still believed that she sent him “mixed messages”.

The judge added that his “worrying” behaviour only stopped because he was blocked on the platforms.

‌



Following the incident, Fory was suspended from duty on full pay and will now seek employment in the construction industry, the court heard.

The Met said Fory was suspended from duty when he was charged in February 2025, and now faces an accelerated misconduct hearing as soon as possible.

Detective Chief Superintendent Iain Keating of professional standards said: “DC Fory’s behaviour is a discredit to the thousands of Met officers who are committed to tackling offences against women and girls in London.

Article continues below

“His actions are even more concerning given he is attached to the Met’s directorate of professional standards, a unit directly responsible for investigating misconduct and upholding high standards across the Met.

“This court result, off the back of a swift investigation by officers, is a welcome one that I hope reassures women and girls, including the victim in this case, that the kind of conduct shown by DC Fory will not be tolerated.”

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of £430m undersea cable to avoid desecrating 'Dobby's Grave'
News.content:
Harry Potter fans force diversion of £430m undersea cable to avoid desecrating 'Dobby's Grave'

A £430m power cable between the UK and Ireland has been diverted from Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire due to a backlash from Harry Potter fans as it would desecrate the "grave" of Dobby

View 3 Images Dobby is an elf in Harry Potter (Image: Mirror Screen Grab)

Harry Potter fans have forced a £430m power cable between the UK and Ireland to be diverted from a Welsh beach after claiming it desecrated the "grave" of the fictional elf, Dobby.

‌



The elf died in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - Part One and the scene in which he was laid to rest was filmed on the popular Freshwater West beach in Pembrokeshire.

‌



And since then the location has been treated as a shrine for Harry Potter fans with many leaving tributes including painted stones at the beach reading “Here Lies Dobby” - despite being asked not to by the National Trust as it is an ecologically sensitive site.

‌



But now the importance of the site for fans of Dobby has led to the diversion of a major energy project.

View 3 Images The fictional elf was laid to rest on Freshwater West beach in filming (Image: John Hodge)

The £430m Greenlink interconnector links the National Grid to Ireland via 125-mile cable and it was set to run between County Wexford and Freshwater West.

‌



However, fans became aware of the plans after project manager Simon Ludlam pointed out where the cable would go during a BBC interview.

He told the Energy Revolution podcast: “We did the shot, we finished, I went back to London, and they then aired it a couple of weeks later. And we got hundreds of calls, I mean, hundreds of calls.”

View 3 Images Many fans leave painted stones at the beach (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Mr Ludlam went on to say he did not know who Dobby was or why there was so much fuss, with a colleague then telling him: “Apparently we’re going to go straight through Dobby’s grave”.

He continued: “I said: ‘Dobby, who’s Dobby? I don’t know Dobby?’ I said: ‘He’s a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?’.” And his colleague explained: “No it’s very, very serious.”

At this point the company was forced to look at different routes which would avoid the beach and the grave. “A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby’s happy,” he said while adding: “We went quite close to some real Bronze Age remains, but we avoided Dobby’s grave”.

Article continues below

It is understood the Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in a Pembrokeshire council planning documents reported the BBC. It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

News.title: Family pay tribute to 'happy and outgoing' girl, 11, found dead in Scottish park
News.content:
Family pay tribute to 'happy and outgoing' girl, 11, found dead in Scottish park

Faith Curran was found dead in the water in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, Midlothian following an intense search and rescue operation

View Image Faith Curran, 11, died following an incident in a country park in Scotland. (Image: Police Scotland/PA Wire)

The family of an 11-year-old girl who died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Scotland have paid tribute to their “happy, adventurous and outgoing" daughter.

‌



Faith Curran was found dead in the water in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, Midlothian, at around 4.25pm on Thursday, after her family reported her missing several hours prior.

‌



Following an intense search and rescue operation, her body was later found in Gore Water, near to Shank Bridge.

‌



In a statement issued through Police Scotland, Faith’s family described her as a “happy, adventurous and outgoing girl who enjoyed life”.

They also thanked those who assisted them with their search, and paid tribute to their support and kindness.

Police confirmed Faith’s death is being treated as unexplained, but there are not believed to be suspicious circumstances.

‌



On Friday, police maintained a cordon around paths which pass underneath Shank Bridge, with police tape blocking access along the walking route.

The bridge carries the A7 road over the Gore Water.

On the bridge above the river, a single bunch of flowers had been left tucked in the railings at the side of the road.

‌



A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We were made aware of concern for an 11-year-old girl in the Gore Glen area, near Gorebridge, around 12.40pm on Thursday August 6.

“The body of the girl was found in the Gore Water near to Shank Bridge around 4.25pm.

“She was pronounced dead at the scene and her family are aware.

‌



“Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances.”

The Gore Water river runs through the park, which is a beauty spot with views of the Pentland Hills to the south of Edinburgh.

A spokesperson for the Scottish Ambulance Service said: “We received a call at 2.33pm on Thursday to attend an incident in Gorebridge and dispatched two ambulances, our special operations team and a critical care paramedic to the scene.”

‌



Colin Beattie, the MSP for Midlothian North, said: “I was deeply saddened to hear of the tragic death of a young girl at Gore Glen Woodland Park.

“My thoughts are with her family, friends and all those affected by this heartbreaking loss.

“This is a deeply distressing incident for the local community, and I know many people will be shocked and saddened by the news.

Article continues below

“However, with a Police Scotland investigation ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on the circumstances surrounding the incident.

“I would urge people to respect the privacy of the family and their loved ones at this extremely difficult time, and to allow the police the space they need to carry out their inquiries.”

News.title: New Forest fire - live: Wildlife haven could take 'decades' to recover as 120 firefighters tackle blaze
News.content:
A massive wildfire has scorched the New Forest after a lorry caught fire with the flames spreading to heathland as drivers ran for their lives with children in their arms

New Forest fire - live: Wildlife haven could take 'decades' to recover as 120 firefighters tackle blaze

A devastating wildfire has scorched the New Forest forcing the closure of a busy road and damaging precious heathland that could take decades to recover.

Firefighters are continuing to tackle a blaze by the A31 and are expected to remain in the area for some time. The road remains closed with no estimated time for reopening.

A spokesperson for the New Forest National Park Authority said the destruction of heathland would mean a tragic loss of rare species and biodiversity.

Drivers were forced to run for their lives with children in their arms as flames tore towards them on Sunday night with police telling them to abandon their cars if they "want to live".

One driver, Robert Green said: "People abandoned cars, running away on the opposite carriageway carrying kids. Our side was trying to turn around and move back through the middle of the cars but it was chaos."

News.title: More than two-thirds of England now in drought
News.content:
Chair of the National Drought Group, Tony Grayling, said that drought conditions will continue to worsen until "significant and sustained rainfall".

The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, as the fifth heatwave of the year intensifies, although there are signs of some rain coming into the UK on Sunday.

"We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment," Grayling said in a statement, adding that "we need everyone's help in using a little less water to make sure our current water reserves last".

The National Drought Group said most of England is now experiencing a flash drought, which "develops very quickly" and is "brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures."

Yorkshire and north-east England have been moved to "prolonged dry weather" status, which is the stage before drought.

Nowhere in England is now under a "normal" status.

Hot weather is continuing, with the UK Health Security Agency issuing amber heat health alerts for all of England apart from the North East from Tuesday at 09:00 BST until Friday at 21:00 BST.

An amber alert means significant impacts "are likely" across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

The continued hot and dry conditions increase the risk of wildfires. Dozens of firefighters are currently battling a fire in the New Forest, which earlier on Monday was estimated to be the size of 140 football pitches (247 acres).

Scotland and Northern Ireland have not been experiencing drought conditions and are expected to see spells of heavy rain over the week ahead.

Scotland does not declare drought, but monitors "water scarcity".

While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

News.title: New Forest firefighting to continue overnight as cars abandoned
News.content:
A firefighting operation will continue into the night to quell a blaze which began on Sunday and has affected one square kilometre (250 acres) of the New Forest national park in Hampshire.

It began when a van caught fire on the A31 near Bratley Wood, forcing motorists to abandon more than 20 vehicles.

Lindsey Legg was with her husband and three children when they were forced to stop by police and leave their car. She said "women and children were walking with buggies" on the road and it had been "pretty scary".

National Highways said the A31 dual carriageway through the New Forest would remain closed in both directions until further notice.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service said more than 120 firefighters had been working "in challenging conditions" to contain the blaze.

Forestry England said the blaze was under control, but it expected the firefighting operation to continue for several days.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and "for many people, the high streets they grew up with have become unrecognisable".

BBC News has exposed organised crime on high streets across the country, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes and vapes, selling cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham said "the rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for".

He added: "That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do.

"We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street."

News.title: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
News.content:
A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France.

They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said.

The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added.

News.title: GB's Hunt wins European 100m gold
News.content:
Amy Hunt claimed her first senior international title by storming to 100m glory and delivering Great Britain's first gold medal at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham.

Hunt announced herself on the sport's global stage last year by claiming world 200m silver in Tokyo, where she secured the first individual international medal of her senior career.

Having backed that up with Commonwealth 100m silver two weeks ago, the 24-year-old would not be denied gold this time on home soil at Alexander Stadium.

"It feel so sweet. I have had such a string of silvers and I was starting to get a bit fed up with it, so I thought it was time for gold," Hunt told BBC Sport.

"My parents gifted me these gold earrings to finally level up, because I wear all-silver jewellery. They said it was time for gold - they left me that note two nights ago - so it made me quite emotional.

"It was definitely time for me to come of age here and win the gold."

Hunt, full of confidence after this season breaking the 11-second barrier for the first time, raised her arms in celebration after producing a trademark strong finish which delivered her from fifth to first over the second half of the race.

Finishing in 11.00 seconds, she could have as many as three further opportunities to add to that tally on home soil, in the 200m and both the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later this week.

British defending champion Dina Asher-Smith, bidding to win her seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships, finished fifth in 11.10 as Poland's Ewa Swoboda (11.02) and Belgian Delphine Nkansa (11.06) completed the podium.

It was Great Britain's second medal on the opening day of action, after the hosts took silver in the mixed 4x400m relay.

Yemi Mary John held off Dutch athlete Myrte van der Schoot in the home straight to bring a British quartet also featuring Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich and Toby Harries home in three minutes 10.47 seconds, behind winners Norway (3:09.62).

News.title: New weight-loss pill approved for use in UK
News.content:
A daily weight-loss pill made by the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab has been approved for use in the UK - the first country in Europe to do so.

Foundayo, made by Eli Lilly, is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.

But while people will be able to buy it privately with a prescription, the approval by the Medicines and Healthcare productors Regulatory Agency does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.

Foundayo is a form of GLP-1 medication that blunts appetite, and comes after the MHRA approved a pill version of a similar weight-loss drug, Wegovy, in June.

Eli Lilly said while it could immediately be used by the NHS for type 2 diabetes, it would be making an application to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England for it to be recommended as a weight loss treatment as well.

Dr Simon Cork, from Anglia Ruskin University, said while the weight-loss benefits of Foundayo were less than other treatments, patients could still expect to see "significant, clinically meaningful changes to their weight".

And he said a key advantage was that it was likely to be cheaper than other weight-loss treatments, which have tended to be tightly restricted by the NHS.

University of Glasgow expert Prof Naveed Sattar agreed it was "good news".

He said another benefit was its convenience, pointing out that unlike the Wegovy pill, which has to be taken on an empty stomach, this pill could be taken at any time of the day.

"The arrival of another effective oral option is a positive development and should help more people access treatment that best suits their needs and preferences," he added.

Experts believe it could help people coming off weight-loss jabs remain slim.

Trials found that patients who had used weight loss jabs and then been given the tablet, also called orforglipron, every day for a year avoided regaining much of the weight they had lost - a known risk when coming off GLP-1 injections.

People on weight loss medication are also advised to eat a healthy diet and get enough exercise.

And, like any medication, there can be side effects to using Foundayo, including nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting.

News.title: Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears
News.content:
The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an inquest has heard.

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Surrey Coroner's Court heard the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy which would have made clear that if the allegations were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said it was "considering the findings carefully".

In a statement to the press, Moffat's family said they believed the Treasury failed in its duty of care.

"When she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced her career and reputation had been destroyed," they added.

The inquest, in which a conclusion of suicide was recorded, heard that on 19 May Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

She was told of allegations she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job.

Moffat, from London, denied this.

News.title: From Dubai to a Dublin court - how alleged cartel boss Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland
News.content:
Armed police took up positions at the entrances to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin, as the plane carrying Daniel Kinahan approached the city.

On the steps of the building, journalists from Irish and international media tracked the flight online.

The Irish government had sent its jet to Dubai.

It is usually used to transport ministers, but it left the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with a suspected crime boss on board.

The doors of the court opened around half an hour after the aircraft landed at a military airfield nine miles (14km) away.

As reporters went through security, we heard the sound of sirens outside - indicating the arrival of the accused.

The courtroom filled up over the next 45 minutes - as detectives, prosecutors, and some members of the public took up seats along with the media.

From the moment Kinahan entered the dock, until he was led out 13 minutes later, almost everyone was looking towards him - and the proceedings were accompanied by constant typing from the press benches.

Complex international investigations, and diplomacy, had led to this moment.

Kinahan was charged with a single offence - directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.

He did not have to enter a plea at this stage of the court process.

But his lawyers have previously told the BBC that the allegations he is a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

They also said he had no criminal record or convictions.

News.title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
News.content:
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.

It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.

At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."

News.title: Cocaine worth £232m found in banana shipment
News.content:
Cocaine with a street value of Â£232m was discovered hidden in a large shipment of bananas from South America.

The 2.9-tonne (2,900kg) haul was smuggled into London Gateway Port in Thurrock, Essex, on Thursday.

The drugs were removed from the container and then delivered to an address near Buntingford, Hertfordshire, where Border Force officers swooped in.

They arrested nine men allegedly connected to the bust, who were later released on bail.

Border Force had been tipped off about the illegal consignment by the National Crime Agency.

News.title: Antiques stolen in 16th Century manor house raid
News.content:
More than 20 antiques were stolen from a National Trust (NT) property during a break-in last month, it has been revealed.

The silver, pewter and brass items were taken from the 16th Century manor house at Baddesley Clinton in Warwickshire, on 30 July.

The most notable piece of the 25 taken was a Georgian silver salver engraved with the coat of arms of the Ferrers, the family who resided at the house for about five centuries, the NT said.

"We very much hope the objects will be returned, so they can be enjoyed by everyone," a spokesperson added.

News.title: Six arrested after woman found dead in north London
News.content:
Six people have been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a 23-year-old woman in north London.

Police were called at 09:33 BST on Thursday, following concerns for the welfare of a woman at a residential address on Bollinder Place, Clerkenwell.

Officers attended alongside the London Ambulance Service and found an unresponsive woman, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

Four women, aged 20, 21, 23, and 26, and two men, aged 21 and 24 were arrested at the scene. All six have since been released on bail while enquiries continue.

Work is ongoing to trace the woman's next-of-kin, who will be supported by specially trained officers once identified.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young woman who has lost her life.

"We understand that news of an incident like this will cause concern within the local community."

News.title: Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
News.content:
An asylum seeker who raped a 13-year-old girl after pretending to be a teenager on Snapchat has been jailed.

Abdul Khan attacked the girl in a nature reserve in Clifton, Nottingham, on 14 May last year.

Khan arrived in the UK in the back of a lorry in 2015, Nottingham Crown Court heard, and faces automatic deportation to Afghanistan after he has served two thirds of his sentence.

He was jailed for nine and a half years on Monday after he was convicted of two counts of rape, one count of sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child, meeting a child following grooming and perverting the course of justice.

A four-day trial was told Khan, who is believed to be 28 and already serving a 23-month sentence for sexual communication with a different child in Derbyshire, arranged to meet his victim in woodland after telling her on the Snapchat messaging app he was a 14-year-old boy.

When they met in person and it was clear he was not 14, he tried to appease her by claiming to be 16, the court heard.

After activity that jurors found had been consensual, Khan, of HMP Nottingham, twice raped the girl.

Judge Mark Watson said the victim told her father what had happened and he contacted police.

Khan was then linked to the rapes by a mobile phone seized during his arrest over his contact with the child in Derbyshire.

Yet despite DNA evidence subsequently linking him to the attack, Nottinghamshire Police said he continued to deny having met the victim.

Addressing Khan, the judge said: "You deliberately concealed your true identity. She thought she was communicating with a child of her own age.

"It was a lie you have persisted with throughout these proceedings."

News.title: MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
News.content:
A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.

Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.

In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.

The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast , externalrecorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.

News.title: Owner of 250-year-old Grade II-listed windmill gave it colourful makeover without permission
News.content:
Dr Eiddwen Jones, 85, is the great-great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Jones, who she said was the first miller at Llynon mill in 1776.

He managed the property in the village of Llanddeusant, Anglesey, until he died in his nineties.

She said the windmill should be repainted in whitewash as it is a historical building, and traditionally "that's how the mills were".

The author, whose family moved from Anglesey to Flintshire 150 years ago, said she did not agree that the windmill was painted in the first place to celebrate the Eisteddfod.

She has visited the windmill several times throughout her life where Thomas Jones' name is painted inside, and said he "would have turned in his grave, I believe," if he had known about its new appearance.

Jones added that it looked "very impressive in its original colour" when driving towards it.

"It's been made fun of now rather than kept the fact that it was a historical building and that people have been working there for a couple of centuries," she said.

Holt said the mill can be hard to find for visitors, as it is not close to the A55 road.

But the new colours have sparked a lot of interest.

With winters especially proving difficult with fewer people coming, he added: "I have a duty to ensure the future of the mill for the next generation."

He apologised to the local authority, saying he "realises that they [the council] are only doing their job and I know that I have broken the rules".
