Venezuela oil exports to the United States hit a seven-year high in July 2026. Shipments averaged about 786,000 barrels a day, second only to Canada among US crude suppliers.

Venezuela Oil and the US

Venezuela oil flows to the US reached 786,000 barrels per day in July 2026. That’s the highest level since early 2019, according to Reuters vessel-tracking data.

That volume made the US Venezuela’s largest customer for crude. Earlier in 2026, Kpler and EIA data showed Venezuela as the second-largest US crude supplier.

Canada held the top spot. So the picture is clear: Venezuela is a major supplier, but not the biggest.

Date-specific claims matter here.

The Numbers Behind It

The 786,000 bpd figure comes from Reuters tracking of tanker movements. It reflects a sharp rebound in Venezuelan exports.

Chevron’s joint ventures with PDVSA contribute roughly 250,000–280,000 bpd of that total. That makes Chevron a critical player.

The US was Venezuela’s top destination for crude in July 2026. But the overall US import mix still favors Canada.

For July 2026, it’s not accurate.

An Appeal to Trump

Delcy Rodríguez, described as acting president in 2026 sources, has urged the Trump administration to lift sanctions. But no direct quote from her was verified in the provided research.

Her appeals are part of a broader push by Caracas to ease restrictions. The exact wording of her statements remains unconfirmed.

Rodríguez’s role itself is a point of contention. Some sources call her ‘presidenta encargada,’ not an elected president.

That distinction matters for how her appeals are received in Washington. The White House hasn’t publicly responded to her requests.

The Sanctions Question

US sanctions on Venezuela‘s energy sector were eased in 2026, not fully removed. That’s a key nuance.

Limited authorizations allowed Chevron and others to expand operations. But a broader sanctions framework remains in place.

This partial easing is why exports could rise to 786,000 bpd. Full removal would likely push volumes even higher.

For now, the sanctions regime is a work in progress. Any further easing depends on political and economic factors.

Chevron’s Role

Chevron is the only major US oil company still active in Venezuela in early 2026. Its joint ventures with PDVSA are central to output.

Those ventures produce about 250,000–280,000 bpd, a substantial share of Venezuela’s total. That makes Chevron a linchpin.

The company’s license to operate is tied to the sanctions framework. Any policy shift directly affects its production.

So Chevron’s future in Venezuela is intertwined with US policy. That’s a key factor for investors to watch.

What Comes Next

Venezuela’s oil exports to the US will likely stay elevated if sanctions remain eased. Watch for updates from Kpler and EIA on monthly rankings.

Those will clarify Venezuela’s position relative to Canada. Also monitor Chevron’s license renewals and any new sanctions waivers.

Those decisions will shape production levels. For now, the data shows a strong rebound, not a top ranking.

Keep that distinction in mind.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Venezuela the largest oil supplier to the US?

No, not as of early 2026.

How much oil does Venezuela export to the US?

Venezuela exported an average of 786,000 barrels per day to the US in July 2026. The highest since early 2019, per Reuters vessel-tracking data.

What is Chevron’s role in Venezuela?

Chevron operates through joint ventures with PDVSA, producing about 250,000–280,000 bpd. It’s the only major US oil company still active in Venezuela in early 2026.

Are US sanctions on Venezuela fully lifted?

No. Sanctions were eased or partially lifted for the energy sector. Allowing expanded oil activity, but a broader sanctions framework remains in place.

Sources: US Energy Information Administration; Venezuelan government; wire reports.

World.title: Panama Economy Targets 4.9% Growth in 2026
World.content:
Panama · Economy

Key Facts — Panama’s MEF projects 4.9% economic growth for 2026, per Minister Felipe Chapman.

— The 2027 budget is built on 4.0% growth and a fiscal deficit of 2.97% of GDP.

— January–June 2026 SPNF revenue $7,328.2M, spending $9,209.4M, deficit $1,881.2M (1.98% of GDP).

— Central government H1 2026 revenue $4,400M, deficit $2,683M, with negative current saving.

— Panama Canal 10,726 transits in first nine months of FY2026, up 5.2% year-over-year.

— Canal cargo volume 389.96 million PC/UMS tons, up 7.2%; transit revenues $4.802B, profits $3.614B.

— Unemployment is a major challenge, with one report citing 10.4% (unverified in provided sources).

Minister Felipe Chapman projects 4.9% GDP growth for 2026, while the 2027 budget assumes 4.0% growth and a 2.97% deficit.

A container ship at the Panama Canal. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Panama economy is on course to grow about 4.9% in 2026. Panama’s economy is set to grow 4.9% in 2026, according to Minister of Economy and Finance Felipe Chapman.

The government’s 2027 budget assumes a slower 4.0% expansion with a fiscal deficit of 2.97% of GDP.

What the Panama Economy Forecast Says

Panama’s Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) projects 4.9% economic growth for 2026. This figure comes from Minister Felipe Chapman, as reported in August 2026.

The projection reflects optimism despite global headwinds. It aligns with the government’s push to boost investment and canal activity.

Chapman’s statement highlights confidence in Panama’s recovery. The 4.9% target is higher than the 2027 budget assumption of 4.0%.

This growth call is central to fiscal planning. It underpins revenue estimates and spending priorities for the coming years.

The 4.9% Forecast

The 4.9% figure appears in August 2026 reporting around the MEF budget discussion. It is attributed directly to Minister Chapman.

No standalone MEF press release with the exact wording was found in the provided results. The figure is supported indirectly by official coverage.

For 2027, the budget assumes 4.0% growth, a more conservative estimate. This suggests policymakers expect a gradual normalization.

The fiscal deficit target for 2027 is 2.97% of GDP. That is a slight improvement from the 2026 mid-year deficit of 1.98% of GDP.

The Jobs Gap

Unemployment remains a major challenge for Panama’s economy. One report cites a rate of 10.4%, while another says it is ‘higher’ without a specific figure.

No official labor-force release was included in the research. High unemployment contrasts with strong GDP growth.

This gap suggests growth is not yet translating into broad job creation. Policymakers face pressure to address joblessness.

The 2027 budget may need to prioritize labor-intensive sectors.

What Is Driving Growth

The Panama Canal is a key growth driver. In the first nine months of FY2026, transits rose 5.2% to 10,726, and cargo volume increased 7.2% to 389.96 million PC/UMS tons.

Canal revenues reached $4.802 billion, with profits of $3.614 billion in the same period. This strong performance boosts government coffers.

Public finances show mixed signals. The SPNF deficit for January–June 2026 was $1,881.2 million, or 1.98% of GDP.

Central government data shows a larger deficit of $2,683 million, with negative current saving. This indicates spending pressures beyond canal income.

Risks Ahead

Global economic uncertainty could dampen Panama’s growth. Trade disruptions or lower commodity prices might hit canal revenues.

Fiscal discipline is a concern, given the central government’s negative current saving. This could limit future spending flexibility.

The 4.9% forecast may be optimistic if external conditions worsen. The 2027 budget’s 4.0% assumption reflects some caution.

Unemployment, if not addressed, could fuel social unrest. That would threaten the investment climate and growth outlook.

What It Means for You

For businesses, 4.9% growth signals opportunities in logistics and construction. The canal’s expansion supports related industries.

For workers, the jobs gap means wage growth may lag. High unemployment could keep labor markets competitive.

For investors, the fiscal deficit and negative saving are red flags. Watch for policy adjustments in the 2027 budget.

For residents, economic growth may not immediately improve living standards. Job creation and inflation will be key indicators to monitor.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Panama’s projected GDP growth for 2026?

Panama’s MEF projects 4.9% economic growth for 2026, according to Minister Felipe Chapman, as reported in August 2026.

What is the 2027 budget growth assumption?

The 2027 budget is built on 4.0% growth and a fiscal deficit of 2.97% of GDP.

What are Panama’s mid-year fiscal figures for 2026?

For January–June 2026, the SPNF had revenue of $7,328.2 million. Spending of $9,209.4 million, and a deficit of $1,881.2 million (1.98% of GDP).

Is the unemployment rate verified?

One report cites 10.4%, but this needs official confirmation.

Sources: Panama’s Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF); Panamanian press.

World.title: Peru Economy Growth Forecast Raised to 3.5%
World.content:
Peru · Economy

Key Facts — Peru’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 was raised to 3.5% from 3.2%.

— Economy Minister Elmer Cuba said growth could reach ‘3.5% or perhaps 4%’.

— The revision came amid concerns over El Niño Costero’s impact.

— Minimum wage will rise to S/ 1,300 from S/ 1,130, a S/ 170 increase.

— The wage hike comes in two tranches: S/ 100 in November 2026 and S/ 70 in April 2027.

— Annual inflation hit 4.1% in July 2026, above the central bank’s 1%-3% target.

— The exchange rate implied by the reporting is roughly S/ 3.33-3.37 per US$1.

The MEF lifts its 2026 GDP outlook to 3.5%, with the minister hinting at up to 4%. While the minimum wage is set to rise in two steps.

Lima’s business district. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Peru economy growth forecast for 2026 has been raised to 3.5% from 3.2%, according to the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF).

What the MEF Now Expects

The MEF updated its April 2026 macro projections, lifting the GDP growth forecast for this year. The new official figure stands at 3.5%, up from the previous 3.2%.

Minister Elmer Cuba went further, saying the economy could grow ‘3.5% or perhaps 4%’ in 2026. He made the statement while discussing the potential impact of El Niño Costero.

The April projection of 3.2% was part of the MEF’s medium-term outlook. That same report saw annual growth averaging 3.2% from 2027 to 2029.

The revised forecast reflects stronger-than-expected momentum in key sectors. However, the minister’s upper-end estimate of 4% remains a possibility, not a formal target.

The Peru Economy Growth Upgrade

The Peru economy growth upgrade to 3.5% marks a clear improvement over the April forecast. It signals renewed confidence in the country’s economic resilience.

Market surveys still place 2026 GDP growth around 3.1% to 3.3%, lower than the MEF’s new figure. The gap highlights differing views on the recovery’s strength.

The central bank’s inflation expectations for 12 months stood at 3.01% in July 2026. That is within the target band but close to the upper limit.

The exchange rate forecast for end-2026 is S/ 3.35 to S/ 3.40 per US$1. This stability supports the government’s growth narrative.

The Minimum Wage Rises

The government announced a minimum wage increase to S/ 1,300 from S/ 1,130, a rise of S/ 170. That is roughly US$50.33 at the implied exchange rate.

The hike will be phased in two tranches. The first S/ 100 (about US$30) comes in November 2026, and the second S/ 70 (about US$21) follows in April 2027.

This proposal aims to support low-income workers amid rising inflation. Annual inflation hit 4.1% in July, above the central bank’s 1%-3% target band.

The increase is still a proposal, not yet a finalized rule. Workers and businesses will watch for the official decree.

Why the Outlook Improved

The MEF’s upgrade stems from stronger domestic demand and resilient exports. Minister Cuba’s comments suggest the economy is weathering climate risks better than expected.

El Niño Costero posed a threat to agriculture and infrastructure. Yet the growth revision implies the impact may be manageable.

Private consumption and investment have shown steady gains. These factors offset external headwinds, supporting the higher forecast.

The government’s fiscal policy, under President Keiko Fujimori, aims to sustain this momentum. The wage hike is part of that broader stimulus package.

Risks Still on the Table

Inflation remains a key risk, running above the target band for five straight months. The central bank expects it to ease, but the path is uncertain.

El Niño Costero could still disrupt supply chains and push prices up. The minister’s 4% scenario depends on these risks not materializing.

Market expectations for growth are more conservative than the MEF’s. This gap suggests investors remain cautious about the recovery’s durability.

The exchange rate forecast of S/ 3.35-3.40 per US$1 implies relative stability. But any external shock could alter that outlook.

What It Means for You

If you earn the minimum wage, your pay will rise by S/ 170 over the next year. That extra income could help offset higher living costs.

For businesses, the phased wage hike allows time to adjust budgets. The first increase in November is small, easing the transition.

Investors might see the growth upgrade as a positive signal. A stronger economy often boosts corporate earnings and market confidence.

Keep an eye on inflation and the exchange rate. They will shape your purchasing power in the coming months.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new GDP growth forecast for Peru in 2026?

The MEF raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 3.5% from 3.2%. Minister Elmer Cuba also mentioned growth could reach up to 4%.

When will the minimum wage increase take effect?

The minimum wage will rise in two steps: S/ 100 in November 2026 and S/ 70 in April 2027. Bringing the total to S/ 1,300.

Why did the MEF revise its growth forecast?

The revision reflects stronger domestic demand and resilience against El Niño Costero. The minister’s comments suggest the economy is performing better than initially expected.

What is the current inflation rate in Peru?

Annual inflation reached 4.1% in July 2026, up from 4.0% in June. It remains above the central bank’s target band of 1%-3%.

Sources: Peru’s Economy Ministry (MEF); Peruvian press reports.

World.title: Peabody Argentina Stops Production, Shifts to Imports
World.content:
Argentina · Business

Key Facts — Peabody, controlled by Goldmund S.A., stopped manufacturing in Argentina.

— The La Tablada plant was dismantled and machinery stored elsewhere.

— Part of production moved to Paraguay under maquila regime.

— The company will import finished goods from Asia.

— Jobs fell from 158 to 111 during the bankruptcy proceeding.

— Peabody had about 350 workers in 2023, a much larger reduction.

— Producing in Paraguay is 30%–35% cheaper than in Argentina.

The appliance brand Peabody, controlled by Goldmund S.A., has ceased manufacturing in Argentina and moved production to Paraguay and Asia.

Home appliances; Peabody is shifting to imports and Paraguay. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)

Peabody Argentina, the home-appliance brand under Goldmund S.A., has stopped manufacturing locally. The company dismantled its La Tablada plant and now operates as a commercial importer.

What Peabody Argentina Is Closing

Peabody, the historic Argentine appliance brand, has ceased local manufacturing. The company dismantled its La Tablada plant and removed the machinery.

The equipment is now stored elsewhere, according to reports. Goldmund S.A., the controlling firm, confirmed the shift in operations.

Peabody now operates as a commercial and importing business. It remains under a concurso preventivo, a bankruptcy protection proceeding.

The company’s production lines, especially for climatization, have been relocated. This marks the end of an era for the brand’s local manufacturing.

Where Production Is Going

Part of Peabody’s production has already moved to Paraguay under a maquila regime. This allows for lower-cost manufacturing with tax benefits.

The company also plans to import finished goods from Asia. This shift is part of a broader strategy to reduce costs.

Paraguay offers significantly cheaper production, about 30% to 35% lower. This makes it an attractive alternative to Argentina.

The climatization line, which includes air conditioners, is a key focus. It will be produced in Paraguay and imported from Asia.

Why It Is Leaving

Peabody said producing in Argentina had become uncompetitive. Higher labor costs, taxes, and a heavier cost structure are the main reasons.

The company’s cost structure in Argentina was too high. This made local manufacturing unsustainable in the current economic climate.

Imported competition and rising costs pressured the brand. The shift to imports and regional production is a response to these challenges.

The move reflects a broader trend in Argentina’s appliance sector. Many companies are moving to lower-cost production bases.

Argentina’s Industrial Squeeze

Argentina’s appliance industry is facing a significant squeeze. Local manufacturing is giving way to imports and regional production.

High costs and economic instability are driving this change. Companies like Peabody are adapting to survive.

The government’s policies have not been able to reverse this trend. Imported goods are often cheaper than locally produced ones.

This shift is reshaping the industrial landscape. More companies are becoming commercial importers rather than manufacturers.

The Jobs at Stake

Peabody ended June with 111 employees, down from 158 at the start of the bankruptcy proceeding. That means 47 jobs were lost during that period.

The longer-run reduction is much larger. The company had about 350 workers in 2023.

This represents a significant loss of employment in the sector. Many workers have been affected by the production shift.

The move to Paraguay and Asia will not bring these jobs back. Local employment in the appliance industry continues to decline.

What to Watch

Observers will watch how Peabody’s import strategy performs. The company’s survival depends on its ability to compete with imports.

The bankruptcy proceeding will be closely monitored. Creditors and workers are awaiting the outcome.

Other appliance makers may follow Peabody’s lead. The industry is likely to see more shifts to lower-cost production.

Government policy responses could affect the trend. Any changes in trade or tax policy might impact these decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Peabody Argentina the same as Peabody Energy?

No, Peabody Argentina is the home-appliance brand controlled by Goldmund S.A. It is not related to Peabody Energy. Which is a mining company.

Where will Peabody now produce its appliances?

Peabody has moved part of its production to Paraguay under a maquila regime. It will also import finished goods from Asia.

How many jobs were lost at Peabody?

Peabody’s workforce fell from 158 to 111 during the bankruptcy proceeding, a loss of 47 jobs. The company had about 350 workers in 2023.

Why did Peabody stop manufacturing in Argentina?

Peabody said production in Argentina was uncompetitive due to higher labor costs, taxes, and a heavier cost structure. Producing in Paraguay is 30%–35% cheaper.

Sources: Company statements; Argentine press reports.

World.title: Lula Courts Congress Allies as Milei Feud Deepens
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts — Lula met Republicanos and Podemos leaders in Brasília on August 4.

— Those parties announced neutrality in the national race after the talks.

— Lula has 26 state-level electoral platforms versus 16 for Flávio Bolsonaro’s side.

— Senate President Davi Alcolumbre is helping Lula push for neutrality in key states.

— Milei called Lula a ‘thief,’ ‘corrupt,’ and ‘ex-convict’ in recent interviews.

— Brazil downgraded diplomatic ties with Argentina to chargé d’affaires level.

— Ambassador Julio Bitelli remains away from Buenos Aires while attacks continue.

Brazil’s president rebuilds legislative support while diplomatic ties with Argentina hit a new low.

Brazil’s Congress in Brasilia. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)

Lula is working to break his political isolation in Brazil. President Lula is rebuilding support among congressional party leaders while facing an escalating diplomatic clash with Argentina’s Javier Milei.

Lula’s New Outreach

Lula met with leaders of the Republicanos and Podemos party caucuses in Brasília on August 4. Those meetings came just before both parties announced neutrality in the national race.

This outreach signals a shift toward legislative allies rather than governors. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre is helping Lula push for neutrality in key states.

The strategy aims to secure a stable base for the upcoming election. Lula’s team counts 26 state-level platforms aligned with him.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s side has organized only 16 such platforms. That gap gives Lula a structural advantage in the campaign.

Breaking the Isolation

The meetings mark a deliberate effort to break political isolation. Lula has struggled to rally broad support amid the diplomatic crisis.

By courting party leaders, he hopes to lock in neutral stances that reduce opposition momentum. Alcolumbre’s involvement adds Senate weight to the effort.

Neutrality from Republicanos and Podemos prevents them from backing the Bolsonaro ticket. That keeps Lula’s path to reelection clearer.

The state-level palanques further strengthen his ground game. Each platform represents a coordinated local campaign structure.

The Milei Factor

Javier Milei has repeatedly insulted Lula, calling him a ‘thief,’ ‘corrupt,’ and ‘ex-convict. ‘ These remarks came in an LN+ interview and at a São Paulo event backing Flávio Bolsonaro.

Brazil responded by downgrading diplomatic relations to the chargé d’affaires level. Ambassador Julio Bitelli has not returned to Buenos Aires while the attacks continue.

The two presidents have not held an official bilateral meeting since Milei took office. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira called the remarks ‘agressivas, descabidas e grosseiras.

Vieira stressed that ‘education and respect are fundamental, without this there can be no dialogue. ‘ He added that ‘the ideological question is totally secondary.

A Warning to Argentina

Vieira said Milei ‘must immediately stop the aggressions’ against Brazilian institutions. He framed the attacks as four statements in one week, calling them ‘very crude, very direct and very aggressive.

The foreign minister demanded a gesture to ‘stop the aggressions’ and return to normality. Argentina’s Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said his country would not retaliate diplomatically.

That restraint leaves the ball in Milei’s court. Brazil’s position is clear: respect must precede any dialogue.

The downgrade is a strong signal of displeasure. It also serves as a warning to other leaders who might insult Brazil’s sovereignty.

The Domestic Calculus

Lula’s diplomatic stance plays well with his domestic base. It frames him as a defender of national dignity against foreign insults.

The political outreach to party leaders complements this narrative. It shows a president focused on governance despite external noise.

The 26 versus 16 platform count gives Lula a talking point on organization. It also reassures allies that his campaign machinery is superior.

Alcolumbre’s role bridges the Senate and the presidential campaign. That connection could prove vital in close states.

What to Watch

Watch whether Milei escalates or softens his rhetoric in the coming weeks. Any new insult could trigger further diplomatic measures from Brazil.

Monitor whether Republicanos and Podemos maintain their neutrality. A shift could alter the legislative balance ahead of the vote.

Track Lula’s state-level platform rollout for signs of friction. Success there would cement his electoral advantage.

Finally, see if Vieira and Quirno open any backchannel. A quiet meeting could defuse tensions without a public summit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Lula meet with Republicanos and Podemos leaders?

Lula met those party leaders to secure neutrality in the national race. This helps him avoid opposition endorsements and strengthens his legislative base.

What triggered the diplomatic downgrade with Argentina?

Milei’s repeated insults, including calling Lula a ‘thief’ and ‘corrupt,’ triggered the downgrade. Brazil reduced ties to chargé d’affaires level in response.

Who is Davi Alcolumbre and what is his role?

Davi Alcolumbre is the President of the Brazilian Senate. He is helping Lula push for neutrality in key states as part of the political outreach.

Has Lula and Milei met officially?

No, the two presidents have not held an official bilateral meeting since Milei took office. The ongoing insults have prevented any such encounter.

Sources: Brazilian government; Brazil’s Foreign Ministry; Brazilian press.

World.title: Chile Unemployment Steady at 9.4% in April–June 2026
World.content:
Chile · Economy

Key Facts — INE unemployment rate hit 9.4% in the April–June 2026 moving quarter.

— Informal employment stood at 27.0% for the same period, per INE.

— President José Antonio Kast leads Chile amid these labor figures.

— The moving quarter averages three months of data for stability.

— Informal jobs lack contracts and social security protections.

— High informality often signals weak job quality, not just quantity.

— Kast’s government faces scrutiny over labor market conditions.

INE reports 9.4% jobless rate and 27% informal work as President Kast faces economic pressure.

A Chilean urban area; informal work is widespread. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)

Chile unemployment held at 9.4% in the April–June 2026 moving quarter, per INE data.

Where Chile Unemployment Stands

Chile unemployment remains a hot topic for workers and policymakers alike. The latest INE report shows a 9.4% rate for the moving quarter.

This figure covers April through June 2026, giving a three-month average. INE, or the National Statistics Institute, tracks these numbers monthly.

A moving quarter smooths out short-term ups and downs in hiring. It compares the latest three months with the previous three-month period.

For everyday Chileans, this rate means nearly one in ten workers is jobless. That pressure shapes household budgets and national confidence.

The 9.4% Jobs Rate

The 9.4% rate is the official benchmark for Chile unemployment right now. INE calculates it from a national household survey each quarter.

This rate includes people actively seeking work but not finding it. It excludes students, retirees, and those not looking for jobs.

Compared to recent years, 9.4% sits at a moderate level for Chile. Yet it still signals a tight labor market for many families.

The rate also reflects broader economic trends like investment and consumption. Slow growth often pushes this number higher over time.

Informality’s Grip

INE also reports a 27.0% informal employment rate for the same quarter. This means over a quarter of workers lack formal contracts.

Informal jobs often come without health benefits or pension savings. Workers in these roles face higher financial vulnerability daily.

This informality rate is a key measure of job quality, not just quantity. It shows many people work but without legal protections.

High informality can weigh on tax revenues and social safety nets. It also limits workers’ ability to plan for the future.

Why Chileans Feel the Squeeze

Even with a 9.4% unemployment rate, many Chileans worry about job security. Informal work adds anxiety since it offers little stability.

Rising living costs can make any job loss feel catastrophic for families. A single missed paycheck can push households into debt.

The combination of moderate unemployment and high informality creates stress. People feel the economy is not working for them.

This sentiment drives public pressure on leaders to create better jobs. It also fuels debates about labor reforms and social policies.

The Political Stakes for Kast

President José Antonio Kast faces tough questions on Chile unemployment. His administration must address both job numbers and quality.

Kast’s conservative agenda promises economic growth and private investment. Yet the current figures show room for improvement.

Voters will judge his government on whether jobs improve over time. High informality could become a political liability for him.

Kast needs to balance reform with stability to keep public trust. His policies on labor and business will face close scrutiny.

What to Watch

Watch for INE’s next quarterly reports to see if unemployment moves. Any shift above or below 9.4% will grab attention.

Also track informality trends, as a drop below 27% would be positive. Persistent high informality signals deeper structural issues.

Monitor government policy announcements on job creation and training. Kast’s team may roll out new initiatives to boost formal work.

Finally, watch consumer confidence and business hiring plans. These early indicators often predict future unemployment changes.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does INE stand for?

INE is Chile’s National Statistics Institute. It collects and publishes official economic data, including unemployment rates.

What is a moving quarter?

A moving quarter averages data from three consecutive months. It smooths out monthly fluctuations to show a clearer trend.

What is informal employment?

Informal employment means working without a formal contract or social security. These jobs often lack benefits and legal protections.

How does 9.4% unemployment affect Chileans?

It means nearly one in ten workers cannot find a job. This creates financial stress and reduces household spending power.

Sources: Chile’s INE statistics agency; Chilean press reports.

World.title: Argentina RIGI: BCRA Eases FX Access for Insurers
World.content:
Argentina · Markets

Key Facts — BCRA Communication A 1064 took effect on 10 August 2026.

— The rule applies to all RIGI projects meeting funding-source conditions.

— Insurers must use funds from the project’s Single Project Vehicle bank account.

— Covered sectors include mining, energy, oil and gas, infrastructure, and technology.

— A mid-2026 estimate counted 16 approved projects worth about US$30 billion.

— A late-July report said 21 approved projects totaled US$46.7 billion.

— Minimum RIGI investment is US$200 million, with higher thresholds for oil and gas.

New central bank rules let local insurers buy dollars for reinsurance payments tied to RIGI projects. But only with funds from approved foreign financing.

Buenos Aires; the BCRA eased FX access for RIGI insurers. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)

Argentina RIGI projects just got a new boost: the central bank now lets local insurers access foreign exchange for reinsurance payments. But only under strict conditions.

The rule, Communication A 1064, took effect on 10 August 2026 and targets projects under the country’s large-investment incentive regime.

What the BCRA Changed

The central bank published Communication A 1064 as Circular CAMEX 1-1064. It eases foreign-exchange access for insurers paying premiums and auxiliary services for reinsurance linked to RIGI projects.

This access is conditional, not blanket. Funds must come from the project’s local Single Project Vehicle bank account and be tied to permitted foreign-financing inflows.

Eligible inflows include foreign debt settlements or issuances allowed under existing rules. The central bank had already eased financing and FX treatment for RIGI projects in April 2026.

That earlier move let direct investment contributions, financial borrowings, and capital-goods import financings count as SPV inflows. The new rule extends similar logic to insurance payments.

How Argentina RIGI Works

RIGI stands for Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones, designed to attract large, long-horizon investment. It combines tax, customs, and foreign-exchange benefits with 30 years of legal and regulatory stability.

A standard entry condition is a minimum investment of US$200 million, with higher thresholds for oil and gas upstream projects. Projects must use a dedicated Single Project Vehicle.

They also commit at least 40% of the agreed amount within the first two years. The application window reportedly runs until July 8, 2027, after an extension.

The regime covers mining, energy, oil and gas, infrastructure, technology, steel, industrial forestry, and tourism. A later expansion, called Súper RIGI, added AI data centers, lithium batteries, green hydrogen, and more.

Why Insurers Matter

Large infrastructure and energy projects need substantial reinsurance coverage. Local insurers previously struggled to buy dollars for those payments, creating a bottleneck.

The new rule removes that hurdle for RIGI-backed projects. It lets insurers convert pesos to foreign currency specifically for reinsurance linked to approved investments.

This matters because reinsurance is typically priced and settled in dollars. Without FX access, projects could face delays or higher costs.

The central bank’s move signals a practical step to keep RIGI projects on track. It addresses a real operational need rather than just offering headline incentives.

The Dollar Access Question

Argentina has long restricted dollar purchases to protect reserves. This rule creates a narrow, controlled exception for RIGI-related insurance payments.

The exception only works when funds trace back to foreign financing inflows. That ensures the central bank isn’t dipping into its own reserves for these payments.

Insurers must document the source of funds from the SPV bank account. The central bank can verify that the dollars match permitted inflows.

This design keeps the capital account stable while supporting the investment regime. It’s a targeted fix, not a broad liberalization of the FX market.

Who Benefits

The primary beneficiaries are RIGI-approved projects in mining, energy, and infrastructure. These sectors dominate the regime, accounting for more than 95% of projects and committed amounts.

Local insurers also benefit by gaining a clear path to settle reinsurance obligations. That reduces their currency risk and operational uncertainty.

Foreign reinsurers benefit indirectly through smoother payment flows. The rule makes Argentina more predictable for international partners.

The government benefits by keeping the RIGI pipeline moving. As of late July 2026, officials counted 21 approved projects worth US$46.7 billion, with more approvals expected.

What to Watch

Watch whether the central bank extends this FX access beyond reinsurance. Other RIGI-related payments could face similar bottlenecks.

Monitor the project pipeline: early August reports suggested two more approvals would push totals to 23 projects and about US$49.768 billion. Track whether insurers actually use the new mechanism.

If uptake is low, the rule may need adjustment to be more practical. Finally, watch the broader RIGI application window, which runs until July 8, 2027.

More projects could mean more demand for this FX channel.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does BCRA Communication A 1064 do?

It lets local insurers access the FX market to pay reinsurance premiums and auxiliary services for RIGI projects. But only using funds from the project’s Single Project Vehicle bank account tied to permitted foreign-financing inflows.

Which projects are covered by this new rule?

The rule applies to all projects under the RIGI regime that meet the funding-source conditions. It is not limited to a single named project or sector.

What is the minimum investment for RIGI?

The standard minimum is US$200 million, with higher thresholds for oil and gas upstream projects. Projects must also commit at least 40% of the agreed amount within the first two years.

How many RIGI projects have been approved so far?

Estimates vary by date: one mid-2026 count said 16 projects worth about US$30 billion. While a late-July report said 21 projects worth US$46.7 billion, with more approvals expected.

Sources: Argentina’s central bank (BCRA); Argentine press.

World.title: Venezuela Oil: Key Facts on US Supply, Sanctions, and Chevron
World.content:
Venezuela · Energy

Key Facts — Venezuela shipped 786,000 barrels per day to the US in July 2026, the highest since early 2019.

— Venezuela was the second-largest US crude supplier after Canada earlier in 2026, per Kpler/EIA data.

— Chevron operates through joint ventures with PDVSA, producing about 250,000–280,000 bpd.

— US sanctions on Venezuela’s energy sector were eased, not fully removed, in 2026.

— Delcy Rodríguez is described as acting president in 2026 sources, not elected president.

— The US was Venezuela’s largest oil customer in July 2026, per Reuters vessel-tracking data.

— Chevron is the only major US oil company still active in Venezuela in early 2026.

Venezuela’s crude exports to the US hit a seven-year high in July 2026, but claims of top supplier status need nuance. Here’s what the data shows.

Venezuela oil exports to the US hit a seven-year high in July 2026. But the claim of top supplier status needs careful reading.

Here’s what the data shows.

Venezuela Oil and the US

Venezuela oil flows to the US reached 786,000 barrels per day in July 2026. That’s the highest level since early 2019, according to Reuters vessel-tracking data.

That volume made the US Venezuela’s largest customer for crude. But it doesn’t automatically make Venezuela the top supplier to the US.

Earlier in 2026, Kpler and EIA data showed Venezuela as the second-largest US crude supplier. Canada held the top spot.

So the picture is clear: Venezuela is a major supplier, but not the biggest. Date-specific claims matter here.

The Numbers Behind It

The 786,000 bpd figure comes from Reuters tracking of tanker movements. It reflects a sharp rebound in Venezuelan exports.

Chevron’s joint ventures with PDVSA contribute roughly 250,000–280,000 bpd of that total. That makes Chevron a critical player.

The US was Venezuela’s top destination for crude in July 2026. But the overall US import mix still favors Canada.

So when you hear ‘largest supplier,’ check the date. For July 2026, it’s not accurate.

An Appeal to Trump

Delcy Rodríguez, described as acting president in 2026 sources, has urged the Trump administration to lift sanctions. But no direct quote from her was verified in the provided research.

Her appeals are part of a broader push by Caracas to ease restrictions. The exact wording of her statements remains unconfirmed.

Rodríguez’s role itself is a point of contention. Some sources call her ‘presidenta encargada,’ not an elected president.

That distinction matters for how her appeals are received in Washington. The White House hasn’t publicly responded to her requests.

The Sanctions Question

US sanctions on Venezuela‘s energy sector were eased in 2026, not fully removed. That’s a key nuance.

Limited authorizations allowed Chevron and others to expand operations. But a broader sanctions framework remains in place.

This partial easing is why exports could rise to 786,000 bpd. Full removal would likely push volumes even higher.

For now, the sanctions regime is a work in progress. Any further easing depends on political and economic factors.

Chevron’s Role

Chevron is the only major US oil company still active in Venezuela in early 2026. Its joint ventures with PDVSA are central to output.

Those ventures produce about 250,000–280,000 bpd, a substantial share of Venezuela’s total. That makes Chevron a linchpin.

The company’s license to operate is tied to the sanctions framework. Any policy shift directly affects its production.

So Chevron’s future in Venezuela is intertwined with US policy. That’s a key factor for investors to watch.

What Comes Next

Venezuela’s oil exports to the US will likely stay elevated if sanctions remain eased. But the ‘largest supplier’ claim needs a date-specific check.

Watch for updates from Kpler and EIA on monthly rankings. Those will clarify Venezuela’s position relative to Canada.

Also monitor Chevron’s license renewals and any new sanctions waivers. Those decisions will shape production levels.

For now, the data shows a strong rebound, not a top ranking. Keep that distinction in mind.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Venezuela the largest oil supplier to the US?

No, not as of early 2026. Kpler and EIA data show Venezuela as the second-largest supplier after Canada.

How much oil does Venezuela export to the US?

Venezuela exported an average of 786,000 barrels per day to the US in July 2026. The highest since early 2019, per Reuters vessel-tracking data.

What is Chevron’s role in Venezuela?

Chevron operates through joint ventures with PDVSA, producing about 250,000–280,000 bpd. It’s the only major US oil company still active in Venezuela in early 2026.

Are US sanctions on Venezuela fully lifted?

No. Sanctions were eased or partially lifted for the energy sector. Allowing expanded oil activity, but a broader sanctions framework remains in place.

Sources: US Energy Information Administration; Venezuelan government; wire reports.

World.title: American Detained in Costa Rica Over $3.6 Million Investment Fraud Case
World.content:
Agents from the INTERPOL San José office of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) detained a 46-year-old United States citizen on a public street in Pavas, San José, on the afternoon of Tuesday, August 4, acting on an active international arrest warrant. The OIJ identified the man only by the surname Dunning and said he was sought by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation as a suspect in fraud and money laundering.

The agency said judicial investigators conducted a series of inquiries to establish that the man was inside Costa Rican territory before moving to detain him. He was placed at the disposal of the competent judicial authority to begin extradition proceedings and will remain subject to whatever precautionary measures that authority imposes while the United States formalizes its request. The OIJ released no further detail about the FBI investigation behind the warrant.

Separately, U.S. federal court records describe a fraud case with the same surname, age profile and Costa Rican connection. In August 2023, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a civil enforcement action in the Northern District of Texas against Walter Dunning Larrick III, a Corpus Christi resident, and his company, Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC. The complaint stated that Larrick was believed to be living in Costa Rica at the time of filing. Costa Rican and U.S. authorities have not publicly confirmed that the man detained in Pavas is the defendant in that case.

According to the CFTC complaint, Larrick and Cambridge collected at least $3,644,817.52 from approximately 70 investors between November 2020 and January 2023, on the stated premise of trading futures and options contracts in natural gas, oil and gold. Of that sum, the complaint alleges $2,831,748 was wired to bank accounts in Costa Rica, and that none of those accounts ever returned funds to Cambridge’s U.S. accounts.

Investigators traced roughly $116,615 in cash withdrawals and another $34,805 spent on food and entertainment, Uber rides, airline travel, Airbnb rentals, hotels and video games, the filing states. A further $388,942 went to payments to earlier investors in what the CFTC characterized as a Ponzi-like structure — money that also represents the only funds, about 10 percent of the total collected, ever returned to participants.

The solicitation ran largely by telephone. The complaint alleges that some calls, including unsolicited cold calls, were placed by people working for call centers operated by unidentified co-conspirators in Costa Rica. Callers represented that Cambridge had been in business for more than 20 years, that client money would stay in a U.S. bank account, and that the firm used a hedging strategy guaranteeing profits regardless of which way commodity prices moved.

Marketing materials cited by the CFTC claimed Cambridge had posted positive revenue on roughly 85 percent of trading days in 2019. Larrick registered Cambridge Financial Advisors LLC with the Texas Secretary of State on September 10, 2020. The company was never registered with the CFTC in any capacity.

Investors who deposited money received login credentials for an online portal showing account statements with dates, strike prices, contract expirations and commissions. The complaint states those statements were fabricated and reflected trading that never occurred. One participant who deposited $60,000 was shown earnings of $569,508; another who deposited $141,000 was shown a figure of $1,619,096.

When participants asked to withdraw, the complaint alleges, they were urged to reinvest in new “blocks” of contracts, given excuses, or simply not called back. On at least one occasion, someone contacted a prospective investor while posing as a representative of the Securities and Exchange Commission to provide what was described as independent verification that Cambridge was not committing fraud. Around the summer of 2022, Cambridge stopped communicating altogether, its phone lines were disconnected, and the website and customer portal went dark.

The CFTC action is civil and carries no criminal penalty on its own. The agency is seeking restitution for investors, disgorgement of unlawfully obtained funds, civil monetary penalties and permanent trading and registration bans. Any criminal exposure would come through the separate federal matter underlying the FBI’s warrant, details of which have not been made public.

Costa Rica has surfaced repeatedly in U.S. investment fraud enforcement. In September 2021, the CFTC charged Texas resident Rudy Avila and six companies — three of them registered in Costa Rica — over two schemes totaling roughly $6 million; a federal judge entered judgment of more than $10.5 million against them in August 2024, and Avila received a 210-month prison sentence after pleading guilty to wire fraud.

In a separate case, U.S. citizen David Butler was detained in Costa Rica in April 2022, extradited that July, and later pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy in a binary options scheme. Older residents will recall the 2002 collapse of the Villalobos brothers’ operation, which drew in thousands of foreign depositors.

In the Cambridge filing, the CFTC credited Costa Rica’s securities regulator, the Superintendencia General de Valores (SUGEVAL), for its assistance — the same agency it thanked in the Avila case. That cooperation has become a routine feature of these prosecutions, even as the country’s banking system and history as an offshore financial services hub continue to make it a recurring destination for money taken from American investors.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens Consular Line in Colombia as Earthquake Toll Climbs Past 70
World.content:
If you have family or friends in Colombia, or you are booked to fly there this week, here is what changed since this morning. Costa Rica’s embassy in Colombia has opened direct lines for nationals affected by this morning’s magnitude 7.4 earthquake. You can reach consular staff at concr-co@rree.go.cr or on +57 313 841 3850. The Foreign Ministry has also expressed its solidarity with Colombia, saying Costa Rica stands with the Colombian people and hopes for a swift recovery.

The scale of the disaster grew sharply through the morning. Colombia’s government has declared a national disaster, a move that unlocks emergency funding and speeds the deployment of resources to affected regions. Authorities have confirmed 21 deaths, though a tally compiled from preliminary reports by governors and mayors puts the number at at least 74.

More than 100 people are reported missing. Officials have cautioned that these figures will shift quickly as search, rescue and building inspections advance. The coffee region took the worst of it. Pereira Mayor Mauricio Salazar reported 18 deaths in his city and a very high number of collapsed buildings. In Manizales, Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo said between 20 and 30 homes collapsed along with several churches, and one of the towers of the city’s cathedral partially came down.

Around 20 buildings were badly damaged in Cali, which hosted the new president’s inauguration three days earlier. The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. with its epicenter in Chocó, on Colombia’s Pacific side. For anyone flying, the practical picture is this. Seven airports are shut while inspectors check them — Matecaña in Pereira, La Nubia in Manizales, El Edén in Armenia, El Caraño in Quibdó, Santa Ana in Cartago, Gerardo Tovar López in Buenaventura, and Alfonso Bonilla Aragón in Cali. More than ten airports in total are reporting some form of damage or operating restriction as inspections continue.

The closures are precautionary. Runways, control towers and terminal structures all have to be cleared before aircraft can move again, and inspectors will not sign off until they are certain — which is why a terminal with visible damage stays shut even when the damage looks cosmetic. At least 46 flights were scheduled Monday across Armenia, Buenaventura, Manizales, Pereira and Quibdó alone.

Bogotá is the important exception for anyone traveling from Costa Rica. El Dorado reported no damage and kept operating. That matters because it is the airport Avianca’s direct San José service uses. Your flight to Bogotá is probably fine — but if your itinerary continues onward to Cali, Pereira or Armenia, that leg is the problem, and you should sort it out before you leave home rather than at the connection.

Both major carriers have opened the door to changes. Avianca is letting passengers with confirmed domestic tickets for today rebook up to 15 days later, switch destination, or get a refund, all without penalty or fare difference — though if you change destination you cover your own onward transport. LATAM is offering a free date change, a free refund or a route change for anyone flying to or from Pereira, Cali or Armenia between Monday and Sunday.

Aviation authorities are asking travelers to check with their airline and watch official channels before heading to any airport. Two other things worth knowing. The maritime authority has ruled out any tsunami threat to Colombia’s Pacific coast. Aftershocks have already followed, including a magnitude 4.8 in Chocó within the first hour and a 3.8 later in the morning — normal after a rupture this size, and a reason damaged buildings are being kept empty.

President Abelardo De La Espriella, three days into his term, has convened a unified command post at the national disaster agency and said he will travel to Pereira. Offers of rescue teams and medical help have come in from El Salvador, Ecuador and Chile.

The numbers attached to this earthquake will keep moving for days. Confirmed tolls in a disaster of this size tend to lag the real figure by a wide margin in the first 24 hours, then jump as crews reach places that were cut off — which is the stage Colombia is entering now.

World.title: Minister of Foreign Affairs meet with Senior Advisor of United Nations Development Coordination Office
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs meet with Senior Advisor of United Nations Development Coordination Office

By Zoila Palma: Today, Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca met with Charles Abani, Senior Advisor, United Nations Development Coordination Office (DCO), Rodolpho Valente, Senior Programme Management Officer, United Nations DCO; Raul Salazar, United Nations Resident Coordinator, Belize.

Discussions focused on the operations and engagement of the United Nations system in Belize, with particular emphasis on UN support towards Belize’s national development priorities and sustainable development goals.

Minister Fonseca was accompanied by Ambassador Ayesha Borland, Director of International Affairs (Multilateral), and Cindy Novelo, Foreign Service Officer.

World.title: Who decides who Is qualified to build Belize?
World.content:
Who decides who Is qualified to build Belize?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

Perhaps We’ve Been Asking the Wrong Question About Government Contracts.

By Lennox Lamb: Some ideas refuse to leave you alone.

Some begin as a passing thought. Others become questions that stay with you for years, quietly demanding an answer. This is one of those ideas.

When I accepted a position as Manager of the City of St. Louis’ Minority and Women Business Enterprise (M/WBE) Certification Program, I believed I was simply taking the next step in my professional career. My responsibility was to oversee the certification process that determines whether businesses qualify to participate in the City’s M/WBE contracting program, an important part of the broader public procurement ecosystem. I expected to learn about contractor certification, compliance, and economic opportunity. I did not expect the experience to fundamentally change the way I think about public administration in Belize.

Every day I watched businesses come through a structured certification process. They were required to demonstrate who owned the company, who actually controlled it, whether it possessed the operational capacity to perform, and whether it met established standards before becoming eligible to participate in contracting opportunities under the program.

It was a professional system built on published rules, evidence, accountability, and due process.

As I worked within that system, there was one question that kept returning to my mind.

Before government spends the people’s money, how do we determine whether a company is truly qualified to do the work?

That question followed me long after I left the office each day.

It followed me when I travelled to Barbados and examined aspects of its procurement reforms.

It followed me as I studied Jamaica’s contractor registration and classification system.

It followed me through my research into procurement systems across the Caribbean and the wider Commonwealth, including Trinidad and Tobago, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Singapore.

The more I studied, the more I realized something important.

This wasn’t an American idea.

It wasn’t a Jamaican idea.

It wasn’t a Barbadian idea.

It was a principle that had been adopted, in different ways, by many successful procurement systems.

Eventually I stopped asking how other countries approached contractor qualification.

I started asking a different question.

Why hasn’t Belize built its own version?

Let me say something that I believe is important before going any further.

This article is not a criticism of Belize.

Nor is it a criticism of the Government.

Nor is it a criticism of the dedicated public officers who work every day to administer our procurement system.

In fact, I believe Belize has made tremendous progress.

Over the years, our country has strengthened public financial management, modernized procurement procedures, established a Procurement Unit within the Ministry of Finance, empowered the Office of the Contractor-General, maintained constitutional oversight through the Auditor General, and continued improving transparency and accountability within government.

Those reforms deserve recognition.

They represent years of hard work by public servants, policymakers, legislators, and professionals committed to strengthening governance.

Yet after working in contractor certification and studying procurement systems throughout the Caribbean, I have become convinced that Belize is still missing one institutional piece that could strengthen everything we have already built.

For years, Belize has debated government contracts.

Every controversy follows a familiar pattern.

Who received the contract?

Was the process fair?

Was the price reasonable?

Were the specifications appropriate?

Was politics involved?

Did taxpayers receive value for money?

Those are legitimate questions.

But they all come after the contract has already become public.

Perhaps we have been asking the wrong question.

Perhaps the first question should be much simpler.

Who independently determined that the contractor was qualified before the contract was ever awarded?

That single question changes the entire conversation.

Today, every ministry, department, and public body performs some level of contractor evaluation when reviewing bids.

Tender committees review documents.

Procurement officers verify compliance.

Oversight bodies monitor processes.

Public officers work diligently to protect public resources.

But there is currently no single national institution whose primary responsibility is to certify, classify, and continuously monitor contractors across the whole of Government.

The result is that much of the same work is repeated over and over again.

Businesses submit similar documents to different procuring entities.

Different agencies may apply different qualification standards.

Institutional knowledge often remains within one ministry instead of benefiting the entire public service.

Most importantly, there is no single national record that tells Government or the public how a contractor has performed across multiple public projects.

Imagine a different approach instead.

Imagine that every contractor wishing to undertake significant public work first becomes certified through an independent national system.

Imagine that certification is based on published standards.

Not relationships.

Not familiarity.

Not perception.

Standards.

Imagine that businesses are classified according to their actual capabilities.

A company qualified to construct a village community center should not automatically qualify to build a major highway.

A contractor capable of completing a two-hundred-thousand-dollar project should not necessarily be expected to undertake a twenty-million-dollar national infrastructure project without demonstrating the required capacity.

Likewise, a young Belizean entrepreneur with the ability, determination, and professionalism to grow should have a clear pathway for doing exactly that.

Certification should not become a barrier to opportunity.

It should become a ladder.

A young contractor in Punta Gorda should know exactly what is required to move from small community projects to district-level work and eventually to national projects.

A company in Corozal should be able to build its reputation through successful performance.

Businesses in Orange Walk, Cayo, Stann Creek, Belize District, and Toledo should compete based on demonstrated capability, integrity, and performance, not uncertainty.

That is one of the greatest strengths of a professional certification system.

It creates opportunity.

It rewards investment.

It encourages training.

It encourages professionalism.

Most importantly, it gives small businesses a transparent roadmap for growth.

Instead of asking, “Who do I know?” entrepreneurs begin asking a far better question:

“What do I need to do to qualify?”

That single shift changes the culture.

Companies invest in better accounting systems.

They invest in better equipment.

They hire qualified professionals.

They improve safety.

They strengthen management.

Why?

Because professionalism becomes the pathway to opportunity.

The benefits do not stop with Government.

Banks gain greater confidence when assessing certified businesses seeking financing.

Insurance companies gain additional confidence when evaluating operational risk.

Private-sector companies looking for subcontractors have access to verified information.

Non-governmental organizations implementing development projects can identify qualified local firms.

Training institutions gain a clearer understanding of the skills employers need.

Professional associations help establish higher industry standards.

Everyone benefits.

But perhaps the greatest beneficiary is the Belizean taxpayer.

Every citizen deserves confidence that public contracts are awarded to businesses that have demonstrated the ability to deliver quality work before public money is committed.

That is not merely good procurement.

That is good governance. One of the questions I expect some readers will ask is whether Belize really needs another public institution.

It is a fair question.

My answer is equally straightforward.

This proposal is not about creating another layer of bureaucracy.

It is about strengthening the institutions we already have by giving them one missing tool they currently do not possess.

The Procurement Unit should continue doing what it was created to do.

Tender Committees should continue evaluating bids.

The Office of the Contractor-General should continue providing independent oversight.

The Auditor General should continue safeguarding public finances.

Each institution has an important and distinct responsibility.

The proposal I am putting forward does not replace any of them.

Instead, it complements them.

It fills the institutional gap that exists before a contractor is awarded a contract and continues throughout the life of that contractor’s performance.

It creates one trusted national source of information regarding contractor qualifications, classifications, compliance history, and performance.

To me, that is not duplication.

It is coordination.

There is another feature of this proposal that I believe is equally important.

Certification should never become the decision of one politician.

Nor should it rest solely in the hands of one public officer.

The credibility of any certification system depends upon public confidence that decisions are based on professional judgment rather than individual discretion.

That is why I believe Belize should consider a multidisciplinary certification panel made up of professionals from across society.

Imagine engineers assessing engineering capability.

Architects evaluating architectural competence.

Accountants reviewing financial strength.

Procurement specialists ensuring compliance with published standards.

Legal professionals safeguarding due process.

Representatives of the private sector contributing practical business experience.

Appropriate government officials ensuring public accountability.

No one profession would dominate.

No single political office would control certification.

No one individual would decide who succeeds or fails.

Instead, recommendations developed through professional review would be considered collectively, against published standards, with written reasons supporting every decision and a fair right of appeal available to every applicant.

That approach protects both Government and the contractor.

It also strengthens public confidence.

Equally important, certification should not simply determine who is eligible.

It should become part of a contractor’s journey.

A company should not remain in the same category forever.

Businesses that consistently perform well should be able to move upward into larger classifications as they gain experience, employ more Belizeans, strengthen their management systems, and complete increasingly complex projects.

Likewise, businesses that repeatedly fail to perform should be required to improve before undertaking larger public responsibilities.

This is not punishment.

It is professional development.

One of the greatest benefits of such a system is that it creates a transparent pathway for growth.

Young entrepreneurs often ask what they must do to compete for government work.

Today, the answer is not always clear.

Under a national certification framework, every requirement would be published.

Every standard would be known.

Every contractor would understand what is expected.

That creates fairness.

It rewards preparation rather than perception.

It encourages investment rather than speculation.

It motivates businesses to improve because improvement creates opportunity.

The benefits would extend beyond public procurement.

Commercial banks could gain greater confidence when financing certified businesses.

Private developers could identify qualified contractors more easily.

Non-governmental organizations implementing community projects could access a trusted national registry.

Training institutions could align programmes with industry needs.

Professional associations could contribute to raising technical standards across entire industries.

In other words, the value of certification would extend well beyond government contracts.

It would become part of Belize’s broader economic development infrastructure.

Perhaps that is the point I hope readers will remember most.

This proposal is not really about procurement.

It is about nation building.

Strong countries are not built only by passing better laws.

They are built by creating institutions that continue serving the public long after individual governments have changed.

Institutions create consistency.

Institutions create confidence.

Institutions preserve professional standards.

Institutions protect public trust.

Throughout my career, I have believed that Belize possesses extraordinary talent.

Our engineers are capable.

Our architects are capable.

Our accountants are capable.

Our contractors are capable.

Our public servants are capable.

The challenge has never been a lack of talent.

The challenge has often been creating systems that allow that talent to flourish fairly, transparently, and consistently.

That is why this proposal excites me.

It is not because I believe I have discovered something new.

Many countries have developed institutions that strengthen contractor qualification and compliance.

The real opportunity lies in learning from those experiences and designing something that reflects Belize’s own legal framework, administrative culture, economic realities, and national aspirations.

It would not be an American model.

It would not be a Jamaican model.

It would not be a Barbadian model.

It would not be a British model.

It would be a Belizean model developed by Belizeans, for Belizeans.

One of the greatest privileges of studying and working abroad is that you eventually stop asking what another country does better.

You begin asking how the lessons you have learned can strengthen your own country.

That is what this article represents.

For several years, I have carried this idea with me.

I have studied it.

I have compared systems.

I have made notes.

I have asked questions.

I have challenged my own assumptions.

Today, I simply believe the time has come to place the idea before the Belizean people.

Not because I believe it is perfect.

Not because I expect universal agreement.

But because I believe Belize benefits when good ideas are openly discussed, professionally challenged, and collectively improved.

If this proposal encourages engineers to think differently, if it causes contractors to imagine new opportunities, if it inspires public officers to consider new approaches, if it encourages our universities to discuss procurement reform, or if it simply starts a thoughtful national conversation about how we strengthen public contracting, then it will already have achieved something worthwhile.

The best public policies are rarely born from politics alone.

They emerge from dialogue.

From evidence.

From professional experience.

From listening.

From improving.

And from a shared commitment to building stronger institutions for future generations.

Belize has already taken important steps toward strengthening public procurement.

Perhaps the next chapter is not about writing more rules.

Perhaps it is about building one institution that helps every other institution work better.

That is the conversation I hope this article begins.

Because in the end, the question is not simply who receives government contracts.

The question is whether Belize is prepared to build a system that gives every qualified Belizean business a fair opportunity to grow, ensures that every public dollar is spent with greater confidence, and leaves behind institutions that our children will one day take for granted as part of a stronger, fairer, and more prosperous Belize.

I believe we can.

Now I invite the country to tell me what it thinks.

World.title: Applications open for UK Government’s Chevening scholarships
World.content:
Applications open for UK Government’s Chevening scholarships

By Zoila Palma: Applications for the UK Government’s prestigious Chevening Scholarships are now open, offering Belizeans and other eligible applicants the opportunity to pursue fully funded master’s degrees at universities across the United Kingdom.

Applications opened on August 4, 2026, and will remain open until October 6, 2026.

The scholarship programme seeks individuals who can demonstrate strong leadership, influence and networking skills, along with a commitment to creating positive and lasting change in their communities.

Successful scholars become part of a global network of future leaders and gain access to UK education, professional connections and experiences aimed at helping address global challenges and support sustainable development.

British High Commissioner to Belize Alistair White encouraged talented Belizeans from all backgrounds to apply, noting that Belize’s Chevening alumni have made valuable contributions across various sectors.

White said the programme represents “one of the UK’s most enduring investments in future leaders” and encouraged applicants to share their vision for how a UK education and global network could contribute to Belize’s future development and prosperity.

Since its establishment in 1983, more than 60,000 professionals have advanced their careers through Chevening.

Prospective applicants can submit their applications here.

World.title: International News: Western Europe records hottest summer start as heatwaves and wildfires intensify
World.content:
International News: Western Europe records hottest summer start as heatwaves and wildfires intensify

By Zoila Palma: Western Europe has recorded its hottest first two months of summer on record, with the region facing devastating wildfires, severe drought and another heatwave expected this week. The European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said the average temperature for June and July reached 21.62 degrees Celsius, about 2.79 degrees above the average and surpassing the previous record set in 2022.

July was also the hottest month ever recorded for the world’s non-polar oceans, with record temperatures reported across the Atlantic and western Mediterranean, CNN reports.

Scientists warned that unusually warm seas are putting marine life and coastal communities at risk, while Europe’s extreme heat has been intensified by persistent drought.

Climate experts said dry soils lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing temperatures to rise further.

The extreme conditions have also fueled Europe’s worst wildfire season on record, with more than 1.23 million acres burned, mainly across Spain, France and Italy, according to an EU report.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, while smoke from the fires has worsened air quality across wider areas. Soil moisture levels in western Europe were significantly lower in July than during the severe drought of 2022, with France, Spain and parts of Germany and the United Kingdom recording exceptional or record rainfall and soil moisture deficits.

World.title: International News: Strong El Niño could bring greater weather impacts and improve seasonal forecasting
World.content:
International News: Strong El Niño could bring greater weather impacts and improve seasonal forecasting

By Zoila Palma: An unusually strong El Niño is rapidly developing in the tropical Pacific and could become the strongest recorded since at least 1950, according to computer model projections.

The climate pattern is already beginning to influence weather around the world, giving forecasters increased confidence in predicting potential conditions over the next one to two years, CNN reports.

El Niño occurs when ocean temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific become warmer than average, releasing large amounts of heat into the atmosphere and altering weather patterns far beyond the Pacific.

Scientists caution, however, that a record-strength El Niño does not necessarily mean every region will experience more extreme weather. Instead, a stronger event increases the likelihood that typical El Niño-related effects, known as “teleconnections,” will occur.

Potential impacts include drought in Indonesia and Australia, a drier-than-normal summer monsoon in India and varying risks of drought and heavy rainfall across parts of Africa.

Experts say the unusually strong and persistent signal could make seasonal weather patterns more predictable and provide governments with valuable time to prepare for potential heat waves, droughts, floods and disruptions to food supplies.

World.title: International News: Almost three-quarters of England declared in drought
World.content:
International News: Almost three-quarters of England declared in drought

By Zoila Palma: Nearly three-quarters of England has now been officially declared in drought as the country continues to experience historically dry and hot weather.

The National Drought Group said 71.3 percent of England is experiencing flash drought, with severe pressure on water resources affecting public supplies, agriculture, navigation and the environment.

The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs were the latest regions placed under drought status. The North East and Yorkshire have been moved to prolonged dry weather status, the stage before drought, leaving no region in England classified as having normal water conditions.

The worsening water crisis follows provisional figures showing that England and Wales experienced their driest July since records began in 1836, with 19 English counties recording no rainfall during the entire month.

World.title: Taiwan, Belize strengthen Climate Resilience through Disaster Risk project
World.content:
Taiwan, Belize strengthen Climate Resilience through Disaster Risk project

By Zoila Palma: Taiwan and Belize are strengthening their partnership on climate resilience and disaster preparedness through initiatives aimed at improving flood monitoring and early warning systems.

In recent years, the Taiwan Technical Mission has partnered with the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change to establish nine flood monitoring stations and an early warning system covering flood-prone areas along Belize’s river basins.

Building on this mechanism, Taiwan and Belize officially launched the “Belize Multi-Hazard Risk Management Capacity Building Project” in February 2026.

The project seeks to expand Belize’s existing disaster prevention mechanisms to cover at least 70 percent of disaster-prone areas across the country.

Taiwan said it remains committed to working with Belize to strengthen the country’s capacity for disaster mitigation while reducing climate-related risks and vulnerabilities.

World.title: National Hurricane Center monitoring 3 disturbances in Atlantic
World.content:
National Hurricane Center monitoring 3 disturbances in Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) is monitoring three weather disturbances across the Atlantic, with one system having a 60 percent chance of developing into a tropical depression over the next seven days.

The first disturbance is located a few hundred miles south of the Cabo Verde Islands and is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. The system is expected to move westward and merge with a tropical wave currently over West Africa. The NHC gives it a 20 percent chance of formation within 48 hours and a 60 percent chance within seven days.

A second disturbance, associated with a tropical wave in the central tropical Atlantic, is located roughly midway between West Africa and the Lesser Antilles. Some gradual development is possible through midweek as it moves westward, but unfavorable upper-level winds are expected to limit development later in the week. It has a 10 percent chance of formation over both the next 48 hours and seven days.

The third disturbance is a trough of low pressure located several hundred miles northwest of Bermuda. It is expected to move eastward north of Bermuda, with a 10 percent chance of development over the next 48 hours and seven days.

The NHC said the system is expected to reach cooler waters later this week, ending its chances of development after Wednesday.

World.title: BWE organisers respond to viral fight video, reaffirms commitment to patron safety
World.content:
Videograb showing a brawl at a Best Weekend Ever beach event on Sunday, August 10, 2026.

ST ANN, Jamaica – The directors of party series Best Weekend Ever (BWE) has expressed disappointment and regret over a physical altercation involving patrons at its beach event on Sunday.

Videos of the incident have been widely circulated on social media, showing a group of men engaged in a brawl.

In a media release Monday, the party organisers said, “Best Weekend Ever has never condoned, and we abhor the proliferation of violence of any kind at our events.

“We are extremely disappointed and sincerely regret that this unfortunate and isolated situation has occurred,” the release continued. “We have contacted the family of those affected and the individuals involved in the altercation have been clearly identified, and the relevant actions will be pursued by the designated authority.”

According to the directors, over the years, BWE has established a strong track record of providing safe, well-managed entertainment experiences for thousands of patrons.

“The safety and security of our guests remain a priority, and this incident is not reflective of the culture of Best Weekend Ever or the experience we work diligently to provide,” they said.

The directors also sought to clarify that, contrary to some narratives circulating, the MC at the event “brought attention to the incident to allow the appropriate intervention to take place and we have made our team available to the relevant authorities to assist in the process of ensuring this does not reoccur.”

According to the release, throughout the staging of Best Weekend Ever 2026, the events have been enjoyed safely by thousands of patrons with improved traffic management and movement between events.

“We are also grateful for the positive feedback from patrons which is an indication of the high level of satisfaction with the production of the event series,” the organisers said.

“Additional security measures have been put in place for the final event being staged today,” they added. “We thank our patrons, partners, security teams and stakeholders for their support as we continue to remain committed to delivering an environment where everyone can celebrate responsibly and safely.”

World.title: Tropical depression could form in Atlantic by the end of the week
World.content:
