World.title: Chilling details emerge about how Japanese mother Megumi was brutally murdered by foreigner ex-husband
World.content:
Megumi, a Japanese mother of two, was brutally killed by her former Irish husband – but police initially believed his account of what had happened. The Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office has charged a 45-year-old Irishman with premeditated murder and is seeking a lengthy prison sentence after he allegedly disguised the killing of his former wife as a domestic fire, prosecutors told Hungary’s MTI news agency on Monday. The tragedy provoked widespread outrage over the police’s victim-blaming statements and serious failures, which led to disciplinary consequences for several officers.

Prosecutors say murder was carefully planned

Prosecutors said they would seek a 17-year prison sentence if the defendant made a full confession. They are also seeking a custodial sentence followed by his expulsion from Hungary, and asking the court to rule that he should not be eligible for parole, MTI wrote.

According to the indictment, the Irishman, who lived in the Netherlands, decided to kill his Japanese former wife the next time he travelled to Hungary to see their children. He allegedly planned to make her death appear to have been caused by a household fire. The crime was committed on 29 January in 2025.

The case arose after the victim applied to the guardianship authority in March 2024 for permission for the children to settle in Japan, as well as seeking arrangements concerning their choice of school and parental custody. Prosecutors say the man decided to kill his former wife in order to avoid a protracted administrative process – and any subsequent court proceedings – and to prevent a decision that might have gone against him.

Japanese mother Megumi had no chance of survival – yet police believed the Irishman’s story

The defendant travelled to Hungary on 27 January 2025, and stayed at the former family flat in Budapest’s fifth district. On 29 January, after their son had left for school, he took their daughter to a swimming pool, leaving his former wife alone at home.

He took a change of clothes with him, changed, and began making his way back to the flat. On the way, he also put on a hood and a helmet. When he returned to the flat, he allegedly attacked and killed his former wife. He then placed her body on the sofa and arranged a wine bottle, tea lights, cigarettes and cigarette ends nearby.

The suspect, David A., returning to the building his ex-wife lived in – moments before the brutal murder took place. PrtScr: YouTube/PoliceHungary

In an attempt to destroy evidence of the crime, he set fire to the furniture and left the flat. While walking around the area, he discarded the clothes he had changed into and put his original outfit back on. He then went to a wellness centre before returning to the flat in the early afternoon. When he opened the door, the influx of fresh oxygen caused the fire he had lit earlier to flare up more fiercely. Ten minutes later, he reported the blaze.

Police arrested the man on 3 February 2025. He has been held in pre-trial detention since 6 February. At the request of the Chief Prosecutor’s Office, the court extended the detention after charges were brought.

Murder sparked widespread outrage

Megumi’s killing caused widespread outrage at the beginning of 2025, with several civil liberties and women’s rights organisations examining the police’s role in the case.

If you missed – Ex-husband charged with Japanese woman’s murder in Budapest: Arson, death list, and a chilling history of threats

In 2022, Megumi had reportedly complained about her former husband, saying that he had kept her in fear and had even threatened to kill her, warning that she would “die in agony”.

A small area of the city centre of Budapest. Photo: Karácsony Gergely/Facebook

Police failed to act on the complaint. They also carried out a cursory investigation following her death and for days accepted the Irishman’s version that the fire had been caused by smoking in bed.

Megumi’s friends said on social media that she did not smoke. In response, they received patronising and mocking replies from the member of staff running the police’s official social media account.

The case led to an internal investigation. Several officers were removed from their posts, the employee responsible for social media was dismissed, and even the chief of police in Budapest’s fifth district was replaced.

A march was organised for the murdered Japanese woman in Budapest

World.title: Have Orbán’s former allies abandoned him? He may be seeking international posts that offer protection
World.content:
By this time next year, former prime minister Viktor Orbán could hold a senior international position after Tisza’s two-thirds election victory closed off his prospects in Hungarian politics – at least for now. One post would allow him to pursue his childhood passion; another could provide diplomatic immunity in the event of criminal proceedings in Hungary.

Is Viktor Orbán’s political career over?

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán turned 63 this year. If we take the comparison literally, he has two years left before reaching Hungary’s official retirement age. He spent virtually his entire active life as a member of parliament, from 1990 to 2026, including 20 years as prime minister – from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010 to 2026. During four parliamentary terms, he governed with what was effectively a two-thirds majority.

But Tisza secured a two-thirds majority in the 2026 election. Following the shock defeat, Orbán also resigned his parliamentary mandate – despite the fact that it would have taken him neatly to retirement age – because he did not want to face his challengers in the National Assembly. Péter Magyar’s government has also passed a constitutional amendment preventing him from serving as prime minister again.

The age of Péter Magyar has dawned after Orbán’s crushing April defeat. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes oldala

The only exception would be a fresh two-thirds victory for Fidesz. At present, however, that appears highly unlikely: support for the former governing parties has fallen below 20 per cent among most reputable polling organisations.

He committed himself for a year

Orbán is currently leader of Fidesz, the largest opposition party, but he has given no indication that he intends to withdraw from public life. Although there is resistance to him within the party and rumours of a possible breakaway civic party, he was nevertheless re-elected as leader with 97 per cent of the vote at July’s leadership congress.

He agreed to serve for one year, saying that he wanted to put the party back in order, rejuvenate it and transform it. That period would also be long enough for him to assemble an international portfolio of his own.

Orbán could launch an international career – and pursue his passion

During the year available to him, Orbán could use his extensive international contacts – and powerful supporters – to begin a new international career, if the information obtained by investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi is accurate.

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán with Fidesz MP Zsolt Németh during the 35th Bálványos Summer University and Students’ Camp. Photo: MTI/Veres Nándor

One possible destination is Fifa. According to Panyi, Orbán held talks with the leadership of football’s world governing body in the United States during the 2026 World Cup about a possible position. The exact role is unknown, but the post of Fifa vice-president may have been discussed.

Orbán was subjected to a barrage of attacks in Hungarian domestic politics because he was not in the country when, in his view, the new government dismantled the foundations of the rule of law – namely by removing the president of the republic elected by Fidesz.

To secure the position, however, he would need allies. One of the European vice-presidencies at Fifa is currently held by Sándor Csányi, president of the Hungarian Football Association and OTP Bank. His mandate expires during the 2027 election cycle.

There are plenty of obstacles

Orbán would nevertheless face several hurdles. If he wanted to join the Fifa Council as Hungary’s candidate, he would first have to secure the presidency or a vice-presidency of the Hungarian Football Association. He would then need to win the backing of UEFA’s member associations.

It was no coincidence that Orbán and Csányi appeared at the same American football event during the World Cup. Orbán watched the semi-final between Spain and France in Dallas with members of his family, while Sándor Csányi was seated close to Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

Will Fidesz split soon? A poll suggests the breakaway faction would have a strong chance

The UN could offer an easier route

The other possible route is the United Nations – specifically, according to Panyi, a position as a deputy secretary-general. An analysis by Portfolio.hu noted that Orbán would “merely” need to cultivate a good relationship with the future secretary-general and secure the support of figures such as President Trump and Argentina’s President Javier Milei.

Trump and the former prime minister last November in Washington. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The latter could prove important because one of the leading contenders to become the UN’s next secretary-general is Rafael Grossi, the Argentine head of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The greatest attraction of the deputy secretary-general scenario, according to Mr Panyi, would be diplomatic immunity. We have reported that Orbán could find himself in serious trouble if János Hajdu, former head of Hungary’s Counter-Terrorism Centre and Fidesz’s current security chief, refuses to accept responsibility for ordering the raid on the Ukrainian “gold convoy” and the unlawful assault on the money couriers, instead pointing the finger higher up in his testimony.

Questions have also been raised over the castle built on the Hatvanpuszta estate, as well as the enrichment of Orbán’s father, the elder Győző Orbán.

Viktor Orbán filmed in Serbia with MOL executive and controversial Hatvanpuszta estate architect

The claims were firmly denied by Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s director of communications, who dismissed the reports as “fake news”. A separate report has likewise described the proposed UN appointment as a possible route to diplomatic immunity for Orbán.

Viktor Orbán shares his plans after politics: family, football, teaching

World.title: Alert: A WWII bomb may have been stolen from the Danube in Budapest
World.content:
Budapest police have asked for help from the public in locating an object, thought to be a Second World War explosive device, that resurfaced in the Danube but disappeared before officers arrived.

Bomb disappears from drying out Danube in Budapest

A man reported finding a rusted object resembling a shell in the Danube in Budapest’s 22nd district on Monday, during historically low water levels which had revealed several objects in the riverbed. However, police only found the empty site upon arrival, the statement of the city’s police headquarters said.

Based on photographs taken by the finder, officials cannot rule out that the device is a Second World War artillery grenade, the statement said.

Authorities warned the public against moving, disassembling or transporting the object. Even decades-old devices embedded in soil or water can remain dangerous and should only be handled by bomb disposal experts, the statement said.

The police have launched an investigation on suspicion of misuse of explosives, the statement added.

World.title: Why Hungary’s cheapest shop may have closed – and shoppers are already furious
World.content:
Hungary’s cheapest shop has refused to explain why it has been closed for several days, citing “technical reasons” – an explanation that few people believe. Most suspiciously, all of the company’s European shops have reportedly shut, with “technical issues” cited in each case. Some commentators already believe the Budapest outlet will not be closed for merely a few days – which might be understandable in the event of a technical problem – but for much longer. Its staff have reportedly already been dismissed.

Hungary’s cheapest shop – with compromises

Until 1 August, Basket Plusz, the Mere group’s only Hungarian shop, regularly posted videos advertising a range of cheap products. The Russian-backed group’s Budapest outlet, located in the city’s 18th district, opened at the beginning of December last year, just in time for Christmas, and marketed itself as Hungary’s cheapest shop – a claim that, judging by customers’ experiences, appeared to be justified.

That came with serious compromises. The store relied on B- and C-tier brands, contracts that favoured suppliers – who were paid only for goods that had actually been sold – and a stark, warehouse-like appearance. The premises, crammed with pallets and resembling a Metro-style warehouse more than a conventional supermarket, offered a poor shopping experience but undoubtedly helped to keep prices down.

Some customers, however, complained that the products they bought were not as good as comparable items sold by other retailers.

Another explanation for the closures

The sole Hungarian outlet closed last week, citing technical problems. Its Facebook page has not been updated since, and reports suggest that the small number of employees working in the quasi-warehouse-style shop have already been sacked.

The technical explanation appears particularly suspicious when viewed alongside similar reports from Slovakia and the Czech Republic.

The Russian MERE discount chain. Photo: mere.ws

Világgazdaság reported that Mere’s Slovak shops – where the chain also arrived last December – as well as its Baltic and Czech outlets, had also ceased trading. Technical reasons were cited in those cases, too. The real explanation, however, may be the EU’s sanctions package adopted at the end of July, which placed Sergei Schneider, one of the owners of the group behind the Mere, Svetofor and MyPrice chains, on a sanctions list.

The Czech Republic even froze the family’s shares after the sanctions came into force. As a result, they cannot sell their holdings or receive dividends.

Is the group withdrawing or merely going dormant?

In Lithuania, the authorities are investigating whether the newly opened Ola shops are linked to the Russian group and whether they represent an attempt to evade sanctions. Previously, 30 shops closed in the country and 250 people were sacked.

According to Világgazdaság, the central question is whether the closures signal the group’s withdrawal from Central Europe or are merely temporary measures.

The Russian MERE discount chain. Photo: mere.ws

Hungarian customers have expressed their anger over the closure in Mere-related Facebook groups, while hoping that the shop will reopen soon. Although some accept that the closure may be the result of sanctions, many believe that neither the EU nor the government led by Péter Magyar should drive out what they regard as a promising initiative.

If you missed: Is shopping abroad really cheaper? Why are Romanians and Bulgarians outspending Hungarians? New study provides answers

Why was the owner of a food company sanctioned?

The sanctions against Sergei Schneider came into force on July 23 and include an asset freeze, a ban on financing and the suspension of the company’s operations.

The stated reason is that the Russian businessman’s corporate empire plays a significant role in sustaining Russia’s domestic economy and therefore contributes indirectly to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

World.title: Real Hungarian summer starts this week after record heatwave – latest weather forecast
World.content:
Sunny, hot weather is expected throughout next week, with a brief spell of cooler conditions in the middle of the week. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in isolated spots at the beginning and end of the week, according to a forecast by HungaroMet Zrt sent to the Hungarian news agency MTI on Sunday.

Real Hungarian summer weather – forecast

Monday will be largely clear and dry, although cloud cover may increase from the west during the afternoon. There is a small chance of an isolated shower or thunderstorm moving in from the direction of the Alps. Southerly winds will occasionally freshen across the north-western Transdanubian region and the Northern Hungarian Mountains, while remaining mostly moderate elsewhere. Temperatures will rise to between 31 and 37C.

Tuesday will be mostly sunny, with some high and cumulus cloud. Showers and thunderstorms are likely only in a few places, chiefly in the west, south-west and north-east of the country. North-westerly winds will freshen across an increasing number of areas and may become strong in places. Morning temperatures will generally range from 16 to 22C, although it will be warmer near the water, in elevated areas, city centres and the Kisalföld region. Afternoon highs will reach 32 to 38C, with the hottest conditions expected in the Great Plain.

It will be hot this week, but not as scorchingly hot as last week. Source: Anadolu

Wednesday will bring predominantly clear or sunny skies and dry conditions. Northerly and north-easterly winds will freshen in several areas and may become strong at times, particularly east of the River Tisza. Morning temperatures will generally be between 17 and 24C, while afternoon highs are expected to range from 27 to 34C, with the lowest readings in the north-east.

Warming starts in the second half of the week

Thursday will be clear or sunny and dry. North-easterly winds will freshen mainly in the eastern half of the country. Temperatures will range from 9 to 19C in the early hours and from 28 to 33C in the afternoon.

Friday will remain clear or sunny, with no rain expected. North-easterly winds may freshen in places across the eastern and north-eastern parts of the country. Overnight lows will range from 8 to 19C, while daytime temperatures will reach 30 to 35C.

Rare solar eclipse to grace Hungarian skies this week – here is where you can see the most!

Saturday will continue to be largely clear, sunny and dry. Winds will be light or moderate and variable in direction. Temperatures will fall to between 8 and 20C overnight before rising to 31 to 36C during the day.

Sunday is expected to be mostly clear or lightly clouded and sunny. There is a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms in the north-west. Southerly winds will freshen, with temperatures rising from 10 to 22C at dawn to between 32 and 38C in the afternoon.

World.title: Romania comes in fourth at International Olympiad in AI with 8 medals
World.content:
Romania ranked fourth in the world at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI), held between 2 and 8 August in Astana, Kazakhstan, after all eight students in its delegation managed to win medals.

In total, the Romanian team won three gold, two silver, and three bronze medals in a competition that brought together contestants from 108 countries and territories, according to one of the coordinators of the Romanian team, Robert Mihai Colca.

The three gold medals were won by David Georgescu from the “Constantin Diaconovici Loga” National College in Timișoara, Alexandru Thury-Burileanu from the “Mircea cel Bătrân” National College in Constanța, and Roland Petrean from the “Silvania” National College in Zalău.

The silver medals were obtained by Mihnea-Teodor Stoica from the International Theoretical High School of Informatics in Bucharest and Darius-Adrian Dobre from the “Matei Basarab” National College of Informatics in Râmnicu Vâlcea.

Three other students won bronze medals: Iulian Nistor from the “Tiberiu Popoviciu” Informatics High School in Cluj-Napoca, Daniel-Antoniu Bence-Muk from the “George Barițiu” National College in Cluj-Napoca, and Matei-Tudor Pop from the “Avram Iancu” Theoretical High School in Cluj-Napoca.

According to a press release, the participation of Romania’s team at IOAI 2026 was supported by the Ministry of Education and Research, together with the Union of Informatics Teachers of Romania (UPIR) and the Romanian Artificial Intelligence Hub (HRIA).

Approximately 500 students from more than 100 countries took part in the olympiad. The competition was held over two days, each consisting of six hours of work and three problems, according to Digi24.

The tests assessed both theoretical knowledge and the competitors’ ability to quickly build and improve solutions based on modern artificial intelligence techniques. Among this year’s challenges were reconstructing the correct order of a conversation from mixed audio fragments, predicting the next action of a robot based on environmental information and a natural-language instruction, and identifying the point at which a human-written text began to be continued by an AI-generated sequence.

The preparation of the team was coordinated by Robert Mihai Colca, a doctoral student at the West University of Timișoara, and Mihai Nan, a lecturer at the National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest.

This year’s result surpassed the one achieved at the previous edition, when Romania had also won eight medals, but only one of them had been gold. This year, Romania placed ahead of the United States, United Kingdom, India, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, France, Germany, and others.

During the olympiad, competitors had access to the same infrastructure and worked under comparable technical conditions. The differences between countries became visible during the preparation period, when access to high-performance processors and computing resources allowed students to become familiar with training and optimizing artificial intelligence models.

World.title: Romanian agricultural inputs producer Norofert to build second plant in Brazil
World.content:
Norofert (BVB: NRF), a producer of organic agricultural inputs and biotechnology provider for agriculture in Romania, said in an announcement at the Bucharest Stock Exchange that it was contracting non-repayable funds worth EUR 2 million for the construction of a production facility and biotechnology laboratory in Brazil.

Its subsidiary, Norofert do Brasil LTDA, will develop the new industrial facility in Guatambu, Santa Catarina state.

Located on a 3-hectare plot, the facility is designed for the production of agricultural inputs and for biotechnology research and development, with a high-capacity laboratory.

The land is leased to Norofert do Brasil LTDA for an initial period of ten years, with the possibility of extension and subsequent acquisition.

Last year, the company announced the official launch of the fertilizer production line Norofert Brasil LTDA in Brazil’s Chapecó.

The second Norofert do Brasil factory complements the already operational unit, which will be used exclusively for the production of biological plant protection products. The new factory will integrate production, storage, quality control, and its own laboratory for the production and multiplication of bacteria, reducing dependence on suppliers and giving Norofert do Brasil better control over costs, deadlines, quality, and product development, the company said.

The total estimated investment, cumulating the two contracted financing lines, is approximately 12 million Brazilian reais (EUR 2 million). The financing is provided by Banco Regional de Desenvolvimento do Extremo Sul, BRDE, a public development bank in southern Brazil, through two financing contracts, one of which is under the Inovacred program run by Finep, the Brazilian agency for innovation and research.

The facility, with a planned capacity of approximately 70,000 liters per day, will produce microbiological inoculants, biofungicides, bioinsecticides and bionematicides. The targeted portfolio covers multiple needs in modern agriculture, from plant nutrition and soil health to biological crop protection.

"Through this project, we are building our own production, research, testing and marketing platform in Brazil, not just a local factory. Brazilian agriculture represents a market of approximately 96 million hectares for solutions dedicated to productivity, soil health and regenerative agriculture. With the portfolio maturing, certifications obtained, distribution expanded and penetration increased in the Brazilian market, we see significant scaling potential compared to the initial stage,” Vlad Popescu, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Norofert, explained.

Since 2020, Norofert has been listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange’s AeRO market, and from October 2021, the company's shares have been included in the BETAeRO index.

World.title: Romania under Yellow, Orange heatwave alerts this week
World.content:
Romania’s National Meteorological Administration (ANM) issued a Yellow Code warning for heatwave and particularly high temperatures in seven counties in the west and north of the country, valid from Monday, August 10, to Tuesday, August 11. Afterwards, the same areas will see a 24-hour Orange Code warning for extreme heat.

In the counties of Caraș-Severin, Timiș, Arad, Bihor, Satu Mare, Sălaj and Maramureș, temperatures will be particularly high, with high thermal discomfort. The temperature-humidity index (THI) will reach the critical threshold of 80 units.

Maximum temperatures will range between 33 - 34 degrees in Maramureș and north-western Transylvania and 35 - 36 degrees in Banat and Crișana, while in limited areas the night will be tropical, with minimum temperatures of 21 - 23 degrees in the western parts of the country.

The same counties will see an Orange Code warning for heatwave conditions, which will be in force between Tuesday and Wednesday morning, August 11-12. Maximum temperatures will range between 35 and 38 degrees, with the highest values in the Western Plain, where 39 degrees may be reached in isolated areas. Locally, especially in hilly areas, the night will be tropical, with minimum temperatures of 19 - 21 degrees.

A Yellow Code will also be valid between Tuesday and Wednesday, August 11-12, in Oltenia, Muntenia, the south and locally the center of the Moldova region and most of Transylvania. In these areas, on Tuesday, 11 August, particularly high temperatures will be recorded. There will locally be a heatwave, thermal discomfort will increase, and the temperature-humidity index (THI) will reach the critical threshold of 80 units in limited areas.

Maximum temperatures will range between 33 and 37 degrees, with the highest values in south-western Oltenia. In limited areas, the night will be tropical, with minimum temperatures of 18 - 20 degrees Celsius.

World.title: Lidl Romania introduces Anti-Waste Bag for fruits, veggies
World.content:
Lidl Romania, the operator of one of the largest retail chains in the country, announced on Monday, August 10, the introduction of the Anti-Waste Bag.

The new initiative is aimed at helping reduce food waste by making use of fruits and vegetables that no longer meet the aesthetic standards for shelf presentation, but still retain their quality and remain suitable for consumption.

Available in all Lidl stores across the country at the fixed price of RON 5 (EUR 1), the Anti-Waste Bag contains approximately 2 kg of fruits and/or vegetables in a product mix. For consumer safety, the bags will not include allergenic products such as celery or parsnip.

The Anti-Waste Bag is part of an initiative currently implemented in more than 20 countries where Lidl operates. In the 2025 financial year alone, this concept helped save more than 100,000 tons of fruits and vegetables from being wasted.

“Every product that we manage to save from waste represents an important success – for the value chain, the environment and climate protection. This is not only an operational efficiency measure through which we turn sustainability objectives into concrete actions, but also proof that reducing food waste and conserving resources depend on the choices we make together, day by day,” said Mihai Cazacu, Head of Corporate Communications Lidl Romania.

World.title: Colliers: Retail deliveries in Romania slow in 2026, next year promises recovery
World.content:
Romania’s modern retail market added approximately 80,000 square meters of new retail space in the first half of 2026, compared with around 122,000 square meters in the same period last year, taking the total stock to more than 5.2 million square meters, according to Colliers’ report on the performance of the real estate market during the first six months of the year.

The decline was mainly due to the absence of very large projects, as the extension of Mall Moldova accounted for almost 50% of the total volume delivered in the first half of last year.

However, the pipeline for 2027 remains solid and could support a return to growth, provided the economy stabilizes. Moreover, the geographical distribution of projects confirms continued interest in regional cities and in developments supported by clearly identifiable local demand, at a time when investment decisions are being assessed more carefully.

The largest projects completed during the first part of the year were the extension of Arena Mall in Bacău, comprising approximately 17,000 square meters, and the first phase of Urbano Shopping & Living in Cluj-Napoca, with around 15,000 square meters. Other significant deliveries included Aurora Retail Park in Bacău, the extension of Electroputere Parc in Craiova, and Galeriile Iris in Târgoviște, each providing approximately 10,000-12,000 square meters.

According to Colliers consultants, these deliveries took place against a more challenging economic backdrop, marked by a weaker labour market, higher taxes, domestic uncertainty and price pressures, all of which contributed to a decline in consumer spending. Higher oil prices and rising logistics costs placed further pressure on companies and consumers, while consumer confidence fell close to its lowest level since 2012.

”Confidence remains relatively low, but purchasing power is still well above where it was ten or fifteen years ago, and retail sales remain at a healthy level compared with recent years. In practice, this means consumers are spending almost as much as they did in 2025, but because prices have risen, they are buying less than they did a year ago,” said Simina Niculiță, Director | Partner | Retail Agency, Colliers Romania.

Weaker retail sales are pressuring retailers, although the market remains resilient following several years of growth. Colliers data indicate a slight recovery from the low reached in the first half of the year, even though sales remain marginally below the 2025 level. As real incomes and the labour market are in a stronger position than they were 15-20 years ago, an improvement in the economic environment could support a faster recovery in consumption.

At the same time, Romania continues to attract international brands, and the entry of names such as Lululemon confirms continued interest in the local market’s long-term potential.

Dominant shopping centres and new developments continue to see high occupancy levels, while the best-performing malls in major cities also have waiting lists. Retailer interest remains strong in projects currently in the pre-letting phase, as well as in many of the retail parks developed in recent years.

The turnover-related component of rents came under some pressure in 2026, but the growth recorded in previous years continues to place high-performing schemes in a strong position in their relationships with retailers.

Higher construction costs and a more cautious consumer have led to the postponement of certain projects, as this context has made it more difficult to support increased rents. Against this backdrop, Colliers has revised its estimate for 2026 deliveries to approximately 150,000 square meters, down from around 230,000 square meters that developers were promising at the beginning of the year.

The outlook for 2027 is more positive. The five largest projects alone could add approximately 140,000 square meters, alongside numerous smaller retail parks. As a result, 2027 could become the most active year for retail deliveries in the past decade and a half, provided projects remain on schedule, although this will depend on economic developments during the second half of 2026.

Economic and political uncertainty, external conflicts and domestic imbalances will continue to influence the market during the second half of 2026. Although both the budget deficit and the current account deficit are narrowing, they continue to leave the economy vulnerable to further shocks.

Over the medium term, however, the outlook remains favorable. Actual individual consumption in Romania has reached approximately 86% of the EU average, very close to Poland’s level of 88%. This convergence towards the European average suggests that the market is entering a more mature phase, in which investment will increasingly focus on cities and projects supported by a solid consumer base, according to Colliers.

World.title: Romanian director Radu Jude’s latest film selected for Toronto, New York festivals
World.content:
The Diary of a Chambermaid, the latest feature film by Radu Jude, has been selected for the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) and the New York Film Festival (NYFF).

The film has been selected in TIFF's Wavelengths section, dedicated to auteur cinema, as well as the Main Slate, the official selection of the New York Film Festival.

The film had its world premiere in this year’s Quinzaine des Cinéastes/Directors’ Fortnight, an independent section held alongside the Cannes Film Festival.

“I’m very happy that this film, which has been made with a great deal of effort, is reaching the most important festivals in North America. It is a film shot mostly in France, the first one I have made outside Romania, but it is a Romanian film, primarily because of the issues it addresses. I’m happy to see the work of the lead actress, Ana Dumitrașcu, recognized, and I’m also glad for the Romanian co-producer, Avanpost, which has made tremendous efforts to bring the film to fruition, especially since the project was rejected in the Romanian National Cinematography Centre’s [e.n. funding] competition,” director Radu Jude said.

The Diary of a Chambermaid (Le Journal d'une femme de chambre) is a predominantly French production by SBS Productions, produced by Saïd Ben Saïd, with Avanpost as the Romanian minority co-producer. The Romanian co-producers are Vlad Rădulescu and Carmen Rizac.

Loosely inspired by Octave Mirbeau’s novel of the same name, the film “offers a contemporary reinterpretation of the story, bringing Romania and France, East and West, migration, domestic work, social inequality and power relations in today’s Europe into dialogue.”

The film follows Gianina, who works as a housekeeper for a wealthy family in Bordeaux. She devotes herself entirely to caring for her employers’ son, while her own daughter grows up far away from her in Romania.

The cast includes Ana Dumitrașcu, Sofia Drăgoman, Ilinca Manolache, Liliana Ghiță, Marie Rivière, Mélanie Thierry and Vincent Macaigne. The film was shot by cinematographer Marius Panduru and edited by Cătălin Cristuțiu.

The Diary of a Chambermaid will be released in Romanian cinemas on November 20, distributed by Independența Film.

Radu Jude was born in Bucharest in 1977. He graduated from the Media University’s Film Directing Department in 2003 and worked as an assistant director on films including Amen by Costa-Gavras and The Death of Mr. Lazarescu by Cristi Puiu.

He has directed several short films, including The Tube with a Hat (2006), which received prizes at Sundance, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Rotterdam, Trieste, Cottbus and numerous other festivals.

His feature-film debut, The Happiest Girl in the World (2009), was selected for the ACID program at Cannes and won awards in Berlin, Sofia and IndieLisboa. It was followed by Everybody in Our Family (2012), winner of the Heart of Sarajevo award, and Aferim! (2015), which earned him the Silver Bear for Best Director at the Berlin International Film Festival. In 2021, Bad Luck Banging or Loony Porn won the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival. Last year, he won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay for Kontinental '25 at the Berlinale.

His 2016 Inimi cicatrizate/ Scarred Hearts received two awards at the Locarno International Film Festival and brought him the best director award at the Mar del Plata Film Festival. Jude's 2018 Îmi este indiferent dacă în istorie vom intra ca barbari/ I Do Not Care If We Go Down in History as Barbarians received the Crystal Globe Award at the 53rd edition of the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival.

Previous films by Jude, Dracula and Kontinental ’25, have also been selected at the New York Film Festival.

Also at TIFF, Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord has been selected in the official competition.

World.title: Romania banks 6 medals, first place among nations at U19 World Rowing Championships
World.content:
Romania finished the U19 World Rowing Championships held in Plovdiv, Bulgaria, with 6 medals, among which 3 gold, one silver, and 2 bronze, and first place in the nations' medal ranking.

On Sunday, August 9, the women’s 8+1 crew, made up of Teodora Sandu, Carolina Pănuţă, Elena Bianca Niţu, Maya Renata Bumbac, Elena Denisa Baciu, Mariana Casu, Angela Gabriela Cazacu, Mădălina-Dumitriţa Ursaciuc and Sarra-Maria Vasca, became Under-19 world champions, according to the Romanian Rowing Federation.

The silver medal was won by the mixed 8+1 crew: Anca-Andreea Culidiuc, Denisa Mihaela Vasilica, Răzvan Ioan Marin, Andrei Mihai Bălan, Radu-Andrei Enescu, Dumitru Cristian Pascari, Marina Ariana Balint, Jessica Popescu and Sarra-Maria Vasca.

The other two world titles were won by Radu-Andrei Enescu and Dumitru Cristian Pascari in the men’s coxless pair, and by Ana-Maria Bordanc, Alexandra Daria Crăciun, Anca-Andreea Culidiuc and Denisa Mihaela Vasilica in the women’s coxless four.

The two bronze medals came through Gabriela Costinela Ursu and Andreea Măriuca Dumitraşcu in the women’s double sculls, and through Ioana Gabriela Cristescu, Francesca Iulia Stejar, Sonia Teodora Biţă and Daria-Elena Maximiuc in the women’s quadruple sculls.

In total, 42 athletes represented Romania in the competition in Plovdiv.

World.title: NATO Peacekeepers’ ‘Transition’ at Flashpoint Bridge Alarms Kosovo Serb Party
World.content:
A Kosovo Police patrol car on the Iber bridge in Mitrovica, August 10, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Florinda Kelmendi.

The NATO-led peacekeeping mission in Kosovo, KFOR, said on Monday that it had begun a gradual transition away from its permanent presence on the main bridge in the ethnically divided town of Mitrovica, citing “an improved security situation in Kosovo”.

The town has been split into a northern, Serb-run half and a southern, Kosovo Albanian-run half, since the end of the Kosovo war in 1999, sparking numerous incidents since then.

“In line with the improved security situation in Kosovo, this is part of the process for optimising KFOR’s posture,” KFOR told BIRN on Monday.

“This process will be gradual, conditions based, and is being closely coordinated with all relevant stakeholders, including representatives of the Institutions in Kosovo and of international organisations, as well as with representatives of the Kosovo Police and the EU Rule-of-Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX),” it added.

However, after a Kosovo Police vehicle appeared on Monday on the bridge, Srpska Lista, the Belgrade-backed Kosovo Serb party, said it strongly opposed the withdrawal of KFOR members from the bridge and called for an urgent meeting with KFOR commander Ozkan Ulutas.

“Given the extremely complex political and security situation, as well as the fact that the area around the main bridge has for decades been a site of serious tensions and conflicts, we believe that any decision that could affect security at this sensitive location must be made with the utmost care and with full consideration for the concerns of citizens,” Srpska Lista said.

According to Srpska Lista, Kosovo Police “have failed to build the trust of the Serbian people through their actions.

“Their conduct in numerous situations, including their support for actions that we consider unlawful and directed against the Serbian people and their institutions, has further deepened mistrust and the sense of insecurity among Serbs,” the statement said.

Apart from the main bridge over the Iber/Ibar in Mitrovica, Kosovo’s government has opened two additional bridges connecting the southern and northern, Serb-run, parts of the city.

Earlier on Monday, meanwhile, KFOR announced that it has begun a “gradual integration of Kosovo Police personnel into KFOR’s security architecture” at the Decani Monastery in western Kosovo, an important site for Serbian Orthodox believers. The mission said the move was part of a “broader process to optimise its security posture and will be implemented gradually and based on conditions on the ground”.

KFOR noted that it “remains the first responder responsible for the Monastery site’s protection and will maintain a visible presence in south and north Mitrovica and in northern Kosovo”.

The monastery, a UNESCO World Heritage site, has been under KFOR protection since the end of the war in Kosovo in 1999. The mission said it would maintain close cooperation with the Serbian Orthodox Church, Kosovo institutions, international organisations and the Serbian Armed Forces, in order “to safeguard mutual transparency, cooperation and trust, and to avoid misunderstandings”.

“KFOR’s commitment to the security of the Visoki Decani Monastery and to the safety of all local communities is steadfast,” the mission said.

World.title: Kosovo Protests as Serbia Mulls Changing River’s Course
World.content:
Ujman/Gazivoda lake in northern Kosovo accumulates water from the Iber/Ibar river. Photo: BIRN/Denis Sllovinja.

Kosovo’s Acting President, Albulena Haxhiu, protested on Monday after the Serbian President announced that Belgrade may change the course of the Iber/Ibar river. Deeming the plan a “serious concern”, Haxhiu said the issue should be addressed with the international community.

“As you know, the Iber Lepenc and Ujman [Gazivoda] lake are part of a strategic system for the water supply, energy, agriculture and the lives of hundreds of thousands of citizens of Kosovo,” Haxhiu told the Conference of Ambassadors in Pristina.

“A unilateral intervention in transboundary water flows would have consequences far beyond a technical issue, as it would affect the water, energy, environmental and human security of our republic,” she added.

Haxhiu spoke out the day after President Aleksandar Vucic of Serbia hinted at the initiative in what he described as justified retaliation against the Kosovo government’s policies towards Serbs in Kosovo.

“Since they are harassing our people so much, let’s see, we have various reasons for changing the course of the Ibar, so we’ll see what the Albanians will do and how they will behave,” Vucic said.

On Monday, Vucic doubled down on the statement, adding that he was simply “addressing the waterways within the territory of the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with domestic law”. Serbia regards Kosovo as part of its territory and refuses to recognise its independence.

Vucic insisted that he was not threatening anyone. “We will simply deal with our own problems. We have our own interests, and we are taking care of our own interests,” he said.

This is not the first time Vucic has mentioned the idea of moving the course of the Ibar, which originates in Montenegro, passes through the south-western tip of Serbia and then flows through northern Kosovo and then back into Serbia.

After an explosion on the Ibar-Lepenac canal, which supplies several towns through Lake Ujman/Gazivode, in November 2024, Vucic said that the idea of changing the course of the Ibar had existed since 1985. “We can divert the course of the Ibar, and they would be left without Gazivode. Then there would be no lake anymore,” Vucic said at the time.

He added that he had always opposed the idea. “I did not want us to use nature for political purposes. After all, we were supplying them with electricity,” he said.

On Sunday, Kosovo’s Minister of Environment, Fitore Pacolli, called Vucic’s statements unacceptable.

“According to the Helsinki Convention, states have an obligation to cooperate for the fair and rational use of transboundary waters, to prevent transboundary damage and to protect aquatic ecosystems. Water resources cannot be used as an instrument of threat, pressure or destabilisation against another state,” Pacolli said.

World.title: Zelensky’s Belgrade Visit Tests Serbia’s EU-Russia Balancing Act
World.content:
Serbia and Ukraine have maintained a more functional relationship since Russia’s full-scale invasion than Serbia’s domestic media environment might suggest. From the beginning of the war, Belgrade has formally supported Ukraine’s territorial integrity while refusing to impose sanctions on the Kremlin.

Serbia has backed UN resolutions affirming Ukrainian sovereignty, accepted Ukrainian refugees and provided financial, humanitarian and energy assistance. Kyiv, meanwhile, has not recognised Kosovo’s independence, enabling both governments to emphasise reciprocal respect for territorial integrity. Political contacts have steadily intensified. This has included meetings between Vucic and Zelensky on the margins of international summits, visits by senior Ukrainian officials such as Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba’s trip to Belgrade in 2024, and Vucic’s two visits to Ukraine in just over a year.

Yet Serbia’s foreign policy abroad and its political communication at home tell different stories. While the government formally describes EU membership as a strategic objective, much of the pro-government media ecosystem continues to cultivate anti-Western, anti-EU and pro-Russian narratives.

A 2026 Belgrade Centre for Security Policy study found that the narrative presenting Ukraine as a proxy in a wider Russia-West war was dominant in the Serbian pro-government press between early 2022 and mid-2025. Echoing Kremlin rhetoric, pro-government media portrayed Zelensky as Ukraine’s illegitimate president, while repeatedly depicting the country as subordinate to NATO and the West. Corruption scandals involving Zelensky’s inner circle have likewise been amplified by tabloids to portray the Ukrainian leadership as compromised.

The ruling party also echoed “colour revolution” rhetoric – that Serbia is being subjected to foreign subversion – through loyal media outlets, to delegitimise and justify the crackdown on mass protests against corruption, growing autocracy and political repression. There have been repeated warnings that the authorities would not allow another “Euromaidan in Belgrade”.

Zelensky’s visit creates a domestic communications challenge for Serbia’s president, particularly with his pro-Russian electoral base. The same media ecosystem that has spent years cultivating suspicion of Ukraine and hostility towards the West must now explain why Zelensky is being formally welcomed in Belgrade.

For tabloids such as Informer, the crucial message is not what the visit changes, but what it does not. Closer ties with Ukraine, and Zelensky’s visit to Belgrade, do not necessarily signal a shift in Serbia’s policy toward Russia, nor do they imply the introduction of sanctions. Vucic has already stated that Serbia defined its sanctions policy years ago and that this position will remain unchanged.

That is also a reason not to read too much into the visit. Just weeks earlier, Vucic was the only leader at a Ukraine-South East Europe summit in Kyiv who refused to sign the joint declaration calling for continued support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. He also did not attend a ceremony honouring Ukrainians killed in Russia’s aggression. At the same time, Serbia is seeking to deepen economic ties with Kyiv to advance its bid for membership in the World Trade Organization, while continuing arms exports, exploring possible security and defence cooperation, and publicly reaffirming its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.

This is not necessarily a contradiction, but rather the essence of Vucic’s foreign policy: cultivating relationships with competing powers while avoiding commitments that would foreclose other options.

Zelensky’s visit therefore demonstrates to Moscow that Serbia is not exclusively Russia’s partner, while signalling to Brussels and Washington that Belgrade wants to remain geopolitically useful. But unless it is followed by sanctions, substantially greater alignment with EU foreign policy or a structural reduction of Serbia’s dependence on Russia, the visit looks less like a Serbian pivot to the West than another attempt by Vucic to continue his balancing act.

Maja Bjelos is a senior researcher at the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: In Solving World War II ‘Puzzle’, Young Greeks Help ‘Heal a Wound’
World.content:
After wading through the archives at Arolsen, municipal registers, the Internet and other documents, the tram was able to return a wristwatch to the family of Vangelis Kerasiotis, who spent time in a forced labour camp in Germany in 1944, aged 19.

Having worked at the camp as an interpreter, Kerasiotis returned to Greece in 1945, where he moved in with a Jewish woman and joined the police. He died at the age of 25.

“The objects are of zero value in terms of their literal value, but they are of enormous value in terms of mental upliftment,” said his niece, Chrysanthi Kerasotou, who received the watch with her sister and mother during an event organised by the Greek government in late June.

Hotzidis, a historian, said that between 50,000 and 60,000 Greek Jews perished in the Nazi camps and at least 10,000 other Greeks were sent to labour camps, including leftists involved in the resistance against the Nazi occupation of Greece.

“We do not know if Kerasiotis was engaged in any political activity,” Hotzidis said. “The relatives did not mention anything, but even if wasn’t, his name was certainly heard somewhere by Greek collaborators of the German battalion security forces and some gendarmes who collaborated with the Germans.”

“It is important to remember, because this way we know not only our recent history, but we can think that it is good that all these events do not happen again,” he said. “So, first we must know them and secondly remember them, ensuring they are never forgotten.”

In Arolsen, Meiwes said that some 2,000 envelopes remain. For some, they known neither the nationality nor the identity of the person whose belonging are inside.

“It is possible that some of these still belong to Greek nationals,” she told BIRN.

The Nazis turned people into numbers, Meiwes said, so it is important “to give them back their names and to tell their stories”.

World.title: A Decade After North Macedonia’s Deadliest Floods, Dangers Remain
World.content:
On August 6, 2016 torrential rain triggered a devastating flash flood in the north-east outskirts of Skopje, killing 22 people and causing more than 30 million euros in damage.

Suburbs of the capital like Singelic and Cento, villages like Stajkovci and Aracinovo, and surrounding areas were among the worst hit, as torrents of water and mud swept through streets and homes within minutes.

“We narrowly escaped death. The water was almost two metres deep. I have never seen this kind of weather,” one Stajkovci resident said at the time. “It was terrible. We had only half a minute to get outside [the house] and save ourselves when the water surged,” said another.

In the aftermath, experts pointed to several factors that had turned an extreme weather event into a disaster. Around 93 litres of rain per square metre fell on the heavily deforested southern slopes of Skopska Crna Gora Mountain in just four hours, allowing water and mud to rush towards the settlements below.

World.title: Albania Could Face Costly Arbitration Battle After Scrapping Vlora Airport Plans
World.content:
An international arbitration dispute is looming after Albania’s Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy announced last week that it has officially started the procedure to terminate the concession contract for Vlora International Airport.

The decision follows a bitter legal tussle between the two consortium partners, Mabco Construction and 2A Group, which began in the autumn of 2025 over a dispute concerning the division of shares between them.

There have also been large confrontations between workers from the two companies over access to the site, and a series of court rulings. The deadlock persisted even after the Supreme Court in May rejected 2A Group's requests for interim measures to secure its lawsuit. That decision was later followed by additional blocking rulings issued by the Court of First Instance Tirana.

World.title: Albanian Court Puts Turkish Activist in Custody After Extradition Demand
World.content:
Protesters rally with pictures of victims of the 2013 Gezi Park protests in Istanbul, April 2022. Photo: EPA-EFE/SEDAT SUNA.

The Tirana Court on Friday ordered a custody remand for Julide Yazici, who is wanted for extradition by Turkey to serve a prison sentence for aiding a terrorist organisation – charges that she claims are motivated by her political activism.

Yazici was arrested on August 4 at Tirana Airport while travelling from France to Albania after it was discovered that she was wanted for extradition to Turkey.

The judge granted the prosecution’s custody request despite Yazici’s lawyer’s arguments that his client “holds political asylum status in France and poses no danger”, and could be placed under house arrest instead.

The lawyer, Artan Shllaku, said that the decision will be appealed.

Shllaku added that Yazici, who teaches at an elementary school in France, had visited Albania a year earlier to see relatives and had encountered no issues.

Yazici is wanted by Turkish authorities to serve the remainder of a four-year prison sentence – three years, five months and 22 days – for providing logistical support to and participating in a terrorist organisation.

According to a decision by the French National Court of Asylum dated November 2020, a document obtained by BIRN, Yazici was involved in political activism in Turkey and participated in the Gezi Park mass protests in 2013 against the administration led by Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

She actively supported the former People’s Democratic Party, HDP, a left-wing political group that supported Turkey’s Kurdish minority, and which later became the DEM Party.

The French court decision granting asylum to Yazici stated that she was arrested in January 2016 “for having allowed a young woman she did not know, who had been introduced to her by a friend, to stay in her student room”.

The French court decision in the document that Yazici had “a well-founded fear … of being persecuted if she returns to her country due to her political activism”.

Yazici is not the first Turkish national to be arrested in Albania for extradition in controversial circumstances in recent years. Teachers and others linked to the movement previously led by the now-deceased cleric Fethullah Gulen, which is classified as a terrorist organisation by the authorities under Erdogan, have also been detained and then deported in line with Ankara’s demands.

World.title: Omiš Returns to its Pirate Past With a Real Spectacle at Sea!
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – Located in the very heart of central Dalmatia, Omiš is closely connected to the world of the pirate, and the 18th of August promises an absolute spectacle at sea.

If you’ve ever been to Dalmatia (and particularly if you’ve sailed along the heavily indented coastline and islands), you may have asked how the country fared back during the days when marauding pirates ruled the Adriatic. Turning the pages of the history book (a long way) back, we find ourselves in an era where piracy wasn’t nearly as frowned upon as it is today. Back then, it was a legitimate business that only the brave dared try their hand (or sword) at.

Along the heavily indented, cove-ridden rocks of the Dalmatian coast, the tradition of piracy goes back even further. It was noted way back during the reign of the various Illyrian tribes that used to live there before the ethnic Croatians arrived.

a hard lesson for venice…

Across the Adriatic Sea, the mighty and somewhat problematic Venetian Empire was very wary of the pirates from Croatia’s Neretva basin. Dominating Adriatic trade, Venice stacked up its enemies and had good reason to keep looking over its proverbial shoulder.

Indeed, back in 887 AD, a battle near Makarska between the Venetians and the so-called Narentine pirates took place, and during which Venetian Duke Pietro Candiano lost his life and his fleet was sunk to the watery depths below. After this event, the Venetians likely paid dearly for the freedom to travel and trade without encountering problems in the Croatian part of the Adriatic.

That relative ease didn’t last long, as the Omiš pirates (or gusari, if you want to truly go local) began disrupting it. That time period coincided with the rising prominence of the Kačić dynasty during the 12th century. This family didn’t have a tree. It was more like a forest. They were dukes and widely known for their ruthlessness and ruled over a large part of southern and central Dalmatia. Although they were officially the subjects of the Hungarian-Croatian king, they enjoyed plenty of autonomy. They opted to use that by organising professional piracy within their dominion.

keeping up with the Kačić family

This fearsome dynasty controlled the majority of the maritime traffic along the eastern Adriatic coast, and both Venetian and Ragusan (Dubrovnik) merchants had to pay up if they wanted to ensure their safe passage through that part of the sea. Just how far they were willing to go in their efforts to fully control that traffic is best explained by the fact that they were accused of attacking the vessels which took the Crusaders to the Palestine, and that even the Pope Honorius III started a war with the pirates, which he lost.

Every peace agreed upon with the Kačić family and Omiš pirates was short-lived, and it took almost two centuries to defeat them and establish safer passage along the Adriatic coast. The Kačić dynasty was eventually defeated and expelled from Omiš after the Venetians finally got the upper hand in 1287. Piracy lingered on, but it eventually weakened. By the time 1444 rolled around, Omiš ended up entirely occupied by the Venetians, and that marked the end of the tradition of piracy once and for all.

Thankfully, you can now freely sail in Dalmatia without any fear of being plundered, pillaged, or forced to pay for your safe passage, but it wasn’t always so peaceful!

Omiš takes us back to its pirate past on august the 18th

Now we’ve delved into the history of just why pirates are so significant to this part of the Dalmatian coast, we can look at what’s to come. After a six year break, Omiš is finally bringing back its beloved Pirate Battle. If you were to ask most people, they’d argue that it’s by far the Adriatic’s most spectacular historical reenactment, and it couldn’t possibly take place in a more apt location. On Tuesday the 18th of August, the Port of Omiš will shed all signs of modernity and totally transform into an authentic thirteenth-century battlefield.

Old vessels will cut across the water, cannons will drown out the summertime cicadas, swords will be drawn and fireworks will light up the blackness of the night sky above the Cetina canyon’s imposing rock faces. This is so much more than a show by the sea, it’s a living, accurate recreation of the moment when the fearless pirates of Omiš outsmarted the powerful and problematic Venice and cemented their rightful place in Dalmatian and indeed wider Croatian legend.

spectators will watch an ancient pirate battle from a modern setting

The last Pirate Battle took place in 2019, just before the coronavirus pandemic struck. An extremely extensive 15 million euro reconstruction of the Port of Omiš began soon after, forcing the event into a temporary pause. Now, the brand-new pier and seafront promenade are finally complete, offering the perfect stage for one of Croatia’s most atmospheric summer spectacles. You’ll be able to watch this ancient battle from a modern waterfront, witnessing heritage and history blend with modern Omiš in perfect harmony.

The newly renovated port and accompanying waterfront can comfortably host 10,000+ spectators, meaning that you’re guaranteed to find a spot from which you can enjoy the re-enactment and the rest of this marvellous event.

Around 150 costumed participants will take part in the upcoming event, with the local KPU Omiški gusari (Omiš Pirates Association) at the helm (no pun intended). They’ll be joined by allied historical groups from across the rest of Croatia: Kumpanija Vela Luka, the Dubrovački trombunjeri, the Klis Uskoks, Društvo Poljičana Sveti Jure – Priko, Bakar Town Guard 1848 and the Požega Town Guard. The event is being entirely organised by the Omiš Tourist Board, with great care paid both to historical accuracy and as a big “welcome back” to a much loved event.

what we can expect on the evening

The programme is set to begin early so that families with children and history lovers can soak up every moment.

18:30 – Activities for children on the waterfront will take place.

19:15 – A grand parade of all of the historical troops through the ancient streets of Omiš will delight all those gathered.

20:15 – The main event will begin, with the Pirate Battle itself in taking place in the ultra-modern, new port.

celebrations across the town

Immediately after that, the celebrations will continue with a performance by Kumpanija Vela Luka, ceremonial cannon fire from the famous Dubrovački trombunjeri (21:10), a dramatic fire show and an incredible fireworks display that will light up the entire harbour and the surrounding tall cliffs which make this town is instantly recognisable (21:40). Once those cannons eventually do fall silent, the celebrations will move to the Croatian Veterans’ Park. Organised by KPU Omiški gusari, the after-party features local food and drink, demonstrations of traditional crafts and a live concert by the popular band Vigor (21:50).

We can say with confidence that this is certainly the perfect way to bring an unforgettable Omiš summer evening to a close.

here’s a look at 2019’s event to get you prepared!

Should you need further information, look no further than here, and make sure to follow along on Instagram for more fantastic images and videos.

World.title: Zagreb Under the Surface – Explore the City Below the City
World.content:
August the 11th, 2026 – Zagreb might not have a metro network, but there’s a world under those tram tracks. Here’s how to explore the city below the city.

One of Zagreb’s most fascinating attractions lies out of sight, far from everything that has transformed the once overlooked Croatian capital into a hit city break. Underneath the streets lie a network of tunnels, shelters and passages, all hidden beneath the historic centre. The most famous and accessible of these is the weird and wonderful Grič Tunnel. Few realise however that this tunnel forms only one bit of a far more expansive underground saga, encompassing the horrors of war to a modern, swanky cultural space.

These odd and fascinating subterranean areas offer a different way to experience the capital. They provide a lot of relief with their much cooler temperatures in summer, as well as a handy shortcut through the heart of the city.

Grič – from protection from allied bombing to a quirky underground exhibition space

The Grič Tunnel is an underground artery stretching for approximately 350 metres deep beneath the historic Grič (Gradec) neighbourhood of Upper Town (or Gornji grad, if you want to go local). It connects the very old Mesnička Street on the west with Radićeva Street on the east, with southern exits leading towards Ilica and Tomićeva Street, including two that open into the Art Park near the funicular.

Construction began in 1943 during WWII, when Zagreb’s authorities at the time ordered the proper construction of a public air-raid shelter under the Upper Town hill in response to the threat of Allied bombing. Croatia, then the so-called Independent State of Croatia, was in a very precarious position politically, and found itself in serious danger from attack. Despite the end of that terrible war finally arriving in 1945, construction actually continued all the way until that year. It was projected and designed both as a protective space and a potential promenade or traffic corridor should it be needed. It fell into more or less total disuse after the end of WWII, serving at times as storage, occasional shelter, or simply remaining closed to the public entirely.

It became useful again as Croatia was fighting for its independence during the 1990s, acting as a shelter for civilians. In 1993, it even hosted the legendary Under City Rave, one of the first major rave parties in all of Croatia and an event that even drew attention from no less than MTV. Decades of neglect followed, with the city eventually deciding to renovate and open the tunnel to the public once again in July 2016. It now operates daily (typically 09:00–21:00) as a free pedestrian passage used daily by locals and visitors alike, as well as an occasional cultural event and/or exhibition space.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

When it isn’t playing host to an art exhibition or an event, the tunnel’s thick concrete walls and dim lighting instantly reveal its original wartime purpose. In fact, even the original wartime signage remains there. The constantly cool temperature makes it a welcome escape from the scorching Croatian summer heat or indeed the tiresome winter rain that plagues Zagreb when the temperatures drop. During the much loved Advent in Zagreb, it is decorated with lights, installations and seasonal programmes, transforming this wartime structure into one of Zagreb’s more unexpected and highly unusual festive venues.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

If you fancy a stroll through this wartime tunnel, the entrances are easy to find. Either head to Mesnička Street, the courtyard at Radićeva 19, Art Park (at which there are two entrance points), and of course – Ilica. Many people choose to combine the tunnel with a loop through Upper Town, emerging near Strossmayer Promenade, Lotrščak Tower or the historic St. Mark’s Square.

this tunnel wasn’t built in isolation…

Julien Duval/TZGZ

While it’s true that the fascinating Grič Tunnel is the only totally public section of Zagreb’s wartime underground, it wasn’t constructed in isolation. Between 1943 and 1945, various other secret tunnels and shelters were excavated under Upper Town, intended both for civilian protection and official use. One parallel passage connects the area around Tkalčićeva Street with the famous Dubravkin put near Tuškanac. Others were connected to government buildings of the period. Most of them are now closed or restricted, their echoes of an uncomfortable past silenced with them.

Sime Modric/TZGZ

If you want to head outside of the city itself and spend some time in nature, then Medvednica is your best bet. While the panoramic views, nature and the chance to see all kinds of wildlife are all lures, there are wartime bunkers and tunnels on the northern slopes towards Medvednica, as well. That goes without mentioning the natural cave systems…

These include those located around the former Villa Rebar area. It does have to be stated that generally speaking, these tunnels aren’t open for casual tourism and some carry local legends of longer connecting systems. Stories of older, pre-20th-century passages, sometimes linked to medieval cellars, church treasuries or strange 19th-century-era freemasonry, circulate. There’s been no proof that this is what they were for, but what would a weird tunnel be, without a weird legend to go with it?

zagreb is a city of layers, both above and below the ground

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

I’ve often said that Zagreb is a bit like an onion. In fact, I used that exact expression when describing the city’s architecture. It spans very old, Austro-Hungarian, socialist, brutalist, and ultra-modern. These styles are all contrasting, yet they somehow blend together effortlessly.

The same can be said about layers of history that form the underground world, deep beneath the plodding of shoes and the noise of tram tracks. Zagreb’s darker periods lie beneath the pavement. WWII ghosts can still be felt, and all the consequences that came with being an Axis country remain within the walls of these tunnels. Whether you fancy a stroll for the sake of it, or intend to visit to see an exhibition or an event, they’re absolutely worth seeing.

Interested in going even deeper, as it were? Look no further!
