World.title: Armenian Catholicos Garegin II attends first hearing in criminal trial
World.content:
Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

A court in Armenia‘s Armavir region has begun hearing the criminal case against the Catholicos of All Armenians and six bishops who serve on the Supreme Spiritual Council. Garegin II attended the hearing in person.

Clergy members and politicians gathered outside the courthouse. Lawmakers from the opposition Armenia Alliance and I Have Honour Alliance left parliament during the afternoon and travelled to Etchmiadzin to show their support for the Catholicos. Dozens of worshippers also gathered outside, periodically chanting “Your Holiness” and singing traditional Armenian church hymns (sharakans).

Prosecutors accuse the Catholicos and the senior clergy of obstructing the enforcement of a court ruling.

Garegin II removed Bishop Gevorg Saroyan, head of the Masyatsotn Diocese, from his post. Saroyan is one of the senior clerics who joined Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s campaign to “reform the Church”. The bishop challenged his dismissal in court. The court ordered his temporary reinstatement as head of the diocese until it reaches a final decision in the case. However, before the court could rule on the merits, the Supreme Spiritual Council, led by the Catholicos, also defrocked him. The council argued that the courts have no jurisdiction over the Church’s internal affairs.

Lawyer Ara Zohrabyan says the Catholicos faces criminal prosecution for carrying out his “ecclesiastical and canonical duties”.

He argues that state interference in the Catholicos’s decisions violates the principle of Church autonomy, the constitutional relationship between the state and the Church, and freedom of religion.

“In this criminal case, the court will examine not only the charges against specific individuals, but also another fundamental question: whether the secular authorities can interfere in the internal life of the Church and criminalise the exercise of the canonical authority of the Catholicos of All Armenians,” the lawyer said.

The trial comes after tensions between the government and the Church steadily escalated.

About a year ago, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He first argued that Garegin II could not lead the Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and had a daughter. He later accused the Catholicos of having links to foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party has also included the removal of the “de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Members of the ruling party accuse the Church of interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy. The parliamentary opposition rejects that claim. Opposition lawmakers argue that it is the government that is unlawfully interfering in the Church’s affairs.

First hearing ends after 30 minutes as judge recuses himself

Shortly after the hearing began, Judge Hakob Manukyan announced that part of the proceedings would take place behind closed doors because they would involve “personal information”. He said the information concerned both himself and the Catholicos’s lawyer.

“A few minutes later, lawyer Ara Zohrabyan told journalists: “The judge has recused himself. He has withdrawn from hearing this case.”

According to Zohrabyan, the judge said he had once granted him his licence to practise law, which could “raise doubts about his impartiality”. Zohrabyan said he did not believe this constituted valid grounds for recusal.

“However, he refused to take part in this disgraceful trial. The very fact that the Catholicos is standing trial is deeply troubling. The case will now go to another judge.”

After the hearing, the Catholicos of All Armenians and his supporters headed to the cathedral to attend a church service and pray together.

Garegin II: “The authorities are trying to bring the Church under their control”

After the service, the Catholicos addressed those gathered outside the cathedral. He said the authorities were taking steps to undermine the Church’s authority, restrict its autonomy and bring it under their control.

“The authorities are persecuting the Church and the clergy. They have arrested and restricted the freedom of a number of clergymen, benefactors and other patriotic individuals through unlawful and fabricated criminal cases,” he said.

The Catholicos dismissed the charges against himself and the six clergymen as groundless.

“We remain steadfast in our faith and determination to defend our rights, which are guaranteed both by our country’s Constitution and by the fundamental principles of international law.”

Opposition declares a “day of shame”

Marianna Gakhramanyan, an MP from the opposition I Have Honour Alliance, said:

“Today is a day of shame. The Catholicos of All Armenians, our spiritual father and the head of our Church, is standing trial in Etchmiadzin. It is shameful and unprecedented. This is an attack not only on the independence of the Armenian Apostolic Church but also on Armenia’s Constitution, which clearly states that the political authorities have no right to interfere in the affairs of the Church and that the Church is separate from the state.”

“Who is defending the Church – us or you?” asks ruling party MP

Commenting on opposition lawmakers who came to support the Catholicos, Civil Contract MP Artur Hovhannisyan said:

“The Church has begun interfering in Armenia’s domestic and foreign policy.”

He also referred to the allegations that the Catholicos had violated his vow of celibacy:

“We are the ones standing with the Church. We are the ones defending the Church. You are defending clergymen who broke their vow of celibacy, who engage in politics and use religion and the Church to protect themselves from the consequences of breaking that vow and taking part in politics. Anyone who has broken the vow of celibacy should leave the Church.”

The ruling Civil Contract party’s election manifesto also outlines plans to reform the Church. Under the proposal, the “de facto head of the Church”, as Pashinyan’s team refers to the Catholicos, should leave office. The plan calls for the election of a locum tenens, the adoption of a new Church charter containing “mechanisms to preserve centuries-old traditions”, and, ultimately, the election of a new Catholicos.

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan told Reuters:

“Pashinyan has come to see the Church as a political threat and as an institution capable of supporting the opposition and various political parties in their efforts to gain power.

“The case against the clergy fits into a broader pattern of selective justice pursued by Pashinyan’s government, under which leading opposition figures have been arrested and some of their property has been confiscated by the state.”

Catholicos of All Armenians appears in court

World.title: Azerbaijan FM in Kyiv: gas for Ukraine, visit to Irpin, Ukrainian drones
World.content:
Azerbaijani FM visits Ukraine

Azerbaijan‘s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov paid an official visit to Ukraine on 6 August.

It was the first visit by an Azerbaijani foreign minister to Kyiv since the start of Russia‘s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Bayramov began his visit with a trip to Irpin, where he viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones and laid a wreath at a memorial to fallen defenders at Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.

He also held meetings with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, President Volodymyr Zelensky, Head of the Presidential Office Andriy Yermak, Defence Intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov and National Security and Defence Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

One of the most notable announcements was Azerbaijan’s stated willingness to supply Ukraine with natural gas if needed.

The two sides also discussed the possible use of Ukraine’s underground gas storage facilities to strengthen regional energy security.

These developments are significant both regionally and internationally, particularly in the context of Azerbaijan’s relations with Russia.

In mid-July, Bayramov met Sergei Lavrov in Moscow and said the “difficult period” in bilateral relations was over and that ties had been fully normalised. A few weeks later, in Kyiv, he reaffirmed Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, while also signalling Baku’s interest in expanding energy cooperation.

The visit illustrates Baku’s multi-vector foreign policy. While maintaining dialogue with Russia, Azerbaijan has continued to provide humanitarian assistance to Ukraine and has expressed its readiness to support the country in the energy sector if required.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

Symbolic and practical significance of the Irpin visit

Irpin was one of the towns where the Russian advance on Kyiv was halted in 2022. Hundreds of civilians were killed during the fighting, and more than 70% of the town’s housing stock was destroyed.

Azerbaijan has contributed to Irpin’s reconstruction.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿@Bayramov_Jeyhun met with @Kyrylo_Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine 🇺🇦 during his official visit to Ukraine.



The sides commended the intensive political dialogue and high-level contacts… pic.twitter.com/ZAf6bdfRkd — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

The minister laid flowers at the bust of academician Zarifa Aliyeva in the park named after her, and visited the Zarifa Aliyeva Linguistic Lyceum and Irpin Central City Polyclinic, both rebuilt with Azerbaijan’s support. He was also briefed on future reconstruction projects, including plans to restore the town’s House of Culture.

In his statement, Zelensky said Bayramov had visited a school, a hospital and a rehabilitation centre supported by Azerbaijan. The visit to Irpin was seen as a demonstration of humanitarian solidarity with Ukraine, as well as Azerbaijan’s willingness to share its experience in rebuilding territories recovered from occupation.

I received Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, @Bayramov_Jeyhun. This is the Minister’s first visit to Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. He began his visit in Irpin, where he visited a school, a hospital, and a rehabilitation center supported by… pic.twitter.com/7HTLIaz3EF — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) August 6, 2026

The visit to a town devastated by Russian forces, together with Bayramov’s review of reconstruction efforts and Azerbaijan’s continued support, was seen as underscoring Baku’s intention to reaffirm its longstanding position despite the “normalisation” of relations with Moscow, particularly its commitment to the principle of territorial integrity.

Following the official welcoming ceremony at the Foreign Ministry, Bayramov and Sybiha viewed an exhibition of Ukrainian-made drones. They then laid a wreath at the Memorial to the Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and observed a moment of silence in their honour.

Meetings and gas supply pledge

During expanded talks with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, the two sides discussed their strategic partnership, trade, energy, transport, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Bayramov reiterated the need for an early end to the fighting and a diplomatic settlement based on international law, while reaffirming Azerbaijan’s support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

He said Azerbaijan’s total humanitarian assistance to Ukraine had exceeded 50 million US dollars. Bayramov also highlighted reconstruction projects in Irpin and rehabilitation programmes for children.

During his meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the discussions focused on Russian attacks, the situation in the Black Sea, the disruption of grain export routes, defence cooperation, and cooperation in the energy, oil and gas, and agricultural sectors.

Zelensky thanked Azerbaijan for its energy and humanitarian assistance, as well as for maintaining constructive dialogue. Bayramov, in turn, spoke about the post-conflict situation in the South Caucasus and reconstruction efforts in the territories regained by Azerbaijan.

As part of his official visit to Ukraine 🇺🇦, FM of Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 @Bayramov_Jeyhun visited the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Kyiv.



The Minister met with the Embassy staff and received a comprehensive briefing on the Mission’s activities. pic.twitter.com/UPqN5Hn9rx — MFA Azerbaijan 🇦🇿 (@AzerbaijanMFA) August 6, 2026

At a joint press conference, particular attention was drawn to Bayramov’s remarks on possible gas supplies: “If the need arises, we will be ready to supply gas to our friendly Ukraine.”

He highlighted SOCAR’s long-standing presence on the Ukrainian market, as well as the importance of Ukraine’s underground gas storage system – the largest in Europe – for regional energy security.

The statement can be seen as signalling Azerbaijan’s willingness to contribute to the diversification of Ukraine’s energy supplies, while also supporting alternative routes for Caspian gas exports to Europe. Against the backdrop of Russia’s strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Ukraine, Baku’s offer also underscores the importance of competition and diversification in the energy sector.

During meetings with Kyrylo Budanov and Ihor Klymenko, the sides also discussed regional and international security, as well as prospects for energy cooperation. They reaffirmed their commitment to the principles of state sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders.

Expert: “Azerbaijan will continue to provide Ukraine with political, economic and humanitarian support”

lkhan Shahinoglu, head of the Atlas Research Centre and a political commentator considered close to the Azerbaijani authorities, wrote that the visit is being closely watched by Russia:

The Kremlin will closely monitor Jeyhun Bayramov’s meetings in Kyiv. Azerbaijan’s partnership with any country is an exclusive sovereign right, and no other state has the right to interfere in that process.

At the same time, Russia, which is waging a war of conquest against Ukraine, closely watches those who cooperate with Kyiv. President Ilham Aliyev‘s response to the same question from Ukrainian journalist Gordon, asked at the Shusha Global Media Forum two years in a row – that ‘Ukraine should not reconcile itself to occupation’ – angered chauvinistic circles in Russia. They believe Azerbaijan should accept the annexation of Crimea and the occupation of Ukrainian territories.

Just as Jeyhun Bayramov visited Moscow some time ago, he has now travelled to Kyiv. Ukraine is Azerbaijan’s partner, and Baku will continue to provide it with political, economic and humanitarian support.”

World.title: Giga Avaliani case: Two more arrested 10 months after Georgian teacher’s murder
World.content:
Two more arrested in Giga Avaliani murder case

Two more suspects have been identified in the high-profile murder case of a 28-year-old teacher in Georgia. On 5 August 2026, two teenage girls – Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili – were arrested.

Giga Avaliani, a mathematics teacher, was killed in October 2025. Five people have already been convicted over his murder, while the trial of a sixth defendant is still under way. With the arrest of the two girls, the total number of suspects in the case has risen to eight – all of them minors.

The arrests of Nia Imnadze and Anastasia Beruashvili, after several convictions had already been secured, mark an unexpected and significant development in the Giga Avaliani case.

Nia Imnadze was one of Giga Avaliani’s former students and the girlfriend of the principal defendant, Aleksandre Gabashvili. Prosecutors accuse her of incitement to commit the crime.

According to local media, Anastasia Beruashvili is a friend of both Nia Imnadze and another convicted defendant, Giorgi Rikadze. She has been charged with failing to report the crime.

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics tutor, was returning home late on 1 October 2025 when he was attacked outside his apartment building. He fell into a coma following the assault and died on 24 October without regaining consciousness. Investigators say the attack was motivated by jealousy and what they describe as “unwanted communication with a girl”. The defendants have given a similar account. According to their version of events, Avaliani sent sexually explicit messages to his student Nia Imnadze, who told her boyfriend, prompting him to confront the teacher. Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, rejects that account. She says Nia had been skipping lessons and that Avaliani informed the girl’s mother, angering the student. According to Kupatadze, the attack was planned afterwards.

The Giga Avaliani case has become one of Georgia’s most high-profile criminal cases in recent years. Much of the public attention surrounding it has been driven by Avaliani’s mother, Eka Kupatadze, who campaigned for what she said should be a thorough and impartial investigation. Her efforts also helped generate significant public pressure over the handling of the case.

From the outset, Kupatadze maintained that Nia Imnadze bore primary responsibility for what had happened and repeatedly called for her arrest. The recent detention of the two girls has therefore raised new questions.

But the key question remains: if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, why were the two girls not arrested earlier? Was their detention the result of new evidence, or did it come only after sustained public pressure and Eka Kupatadze’s campaign?

Detention of two girls

Both girls were arrested late on the night of 5 August, in what appeared to be coordinated operations. News of the arrests first emerged through a video of Nia Imnadze’s detention, which was released by her lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili.

The footage is deeply distressing. It shows a large number of police officers arriving at Nia’s home. Her mother, visibly distressed, pounds on the front door, shouting: “Come in, all of you!”, “Maniacs!”, “Murderers!”, “Do you know that Niako is innocent?!”

The girl’s father, meanwhile, tells the police: “You are going to make me do something the whole of Georgia will be talking about. If you treat my child so unjustly, I will do it.”

Police officers try to calm the distraught parents.

“Why are you taking my child? On what grounds? What does the court order say?!” the mother asks.

“The lawyer has reviewed the court order,” one of the officers replies.

“Giorgi, on what grounds are they arresting her?” the mother asks the lawyer.

“On the basis of a court order containing only formal wording, nothing specific,” the lawyer replies.

Nia sits in the hallway on a sofa, curled up with her face buried in her hands. The video is being filmed by her lawyer, who occasionally strokes her hair.

Shortly after the video was released, reports began circulating on social media that the second girl, Anastasia Beruashvili, had also been detained. No footage of her arrest was made public, but the Ministry of Internal Affairs later confirmed that she had been taken into custody.

During her arrest, Nia Imnadze became unwell and was taken to hospital, where she spent the night. On 6 August, she was transferred to a pre-trial detention centre. Anastasia Beruashvili was also taken there.

Minors charged in Giga Avaliani's murder case in Georgia – read more Five people have already been convicted in connection with Giga Avaliani’s murder: Aleksandre Gabashvili – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. He was the principal defendant in the case and was found guilty of organising a group assault and intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm as part of a group, resulting in the victim’s death. Giorgi Rikadze – sentenced to 10 years and five months’ imprisonment. A friend of Aleksandre Gabashvili, he was convicted on the same charges. Demetere Chikovani – sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was convicted of attempted intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm in the Avaliani case, as well as organising group violence in connection with the case and four other incidents. Ani Naskidashvili – sentenced to five years and three months’ imprisonment. She was found guilty of failing to report a particularly serious crime. Another minor – sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He was convicted of giving false testimony. The nature of the false statements has not been disclosed. His case was heard behind closed doors, lawyers involved in the proceedings are bound by a non-disclosure order, and the teenager’s parents have declined to speak to the media. According to TV Pirveli, the boy is named Luka Klatkin. Giorgi Malania – arrested in July 2026 and charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. Malania is the son of a former senior Interior Ministry official, who served as deputy interior minister between 2016 and 2019. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered.

Eka Kupatadze’s reaction

“Georgia has won another battle against the killers of a healthy, innocent and talented young man – Giga Avaliani!” Eka Kupatadze said in response to the girls’ arrests.

Giga Avaliani’s family has always maintained that those who carried out the attack were not the only people involved. They have consistently called on investigators to identify and prosecute all those who may have played a role in the crime.

The family has paid particular attention to the alleged role of the two girls. Eka Kupatadze has repeatedly said that they knew the attack was being planned.

Until recently, however, prosecutors had taken no apparent action against additional suspects, prompting repeated criticism of the investigation from Avaliani’s family.

Kupatadze even appealed for help to Ekaterine Khvedelidze, the wife of Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling party and widely regarded as Georgia’s “informal ruler”. Khvedelidze replied to her letter, expressing sympathy and support for the mother who had lost her son.

“As far as I am aware, the investigation has not yet been completed. I am confident that the relevant state authorities will see it through to the end and that all the circumstances will be thoroughly examined, so that no question surrounding the terrible tragedy that has befallen you remains unanswered,” Ekaterine Khvedelidze wrote in her reply.

Formal charges

On the evening of 6 August, both girls were formally charged.

Nia Imnadze at the time of her arrest

Nia Imnadze has been charged with incitement to intentionally inflict grievous bodily harm committed by a group. The offence carries a maximum sentence of 13 years’ imprisonment.

Anastasia Beruashvili has been charged with failing to report a particularly serious crime, an offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment.

Under Georgian law, sentences imposed on minors are reduced by one quarter.

“The investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs under the supervision of the Prosecutor’s Office established that, in September 2025, Nia Imnadze began taking mathematics lessons with Giga Avaliani. The accused, Nia Imnadze, told her friends Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Malania that her teacher, Giga Avaliani, had allegedly shown her excessive attention. By doing so, the accused incited Aleksandre Gabashvili to attack Giga Avaliani together with his accomplices,” the Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement.

According to the statement, Aleksandre Gabashvili, together with Giorgi Rikadze, Giorgi Malania and Demetere Chikovani, “decided to act on that incitement.”

What defence says

The defence has denied all the charges.

According to Nia Imnadze’s lawyer, Giorgi Lekishvili, there is no evidence in the case to support the allegation that she incited the attack.

The lawyer also rejected reports that prosecutors had obtained data and messages from Meta, and that the arrests followed an examination of those materials.

“Criminal proceedings cannot be based on suspicion. They must be based on lawfully obtained evidence, and no other standard can override that principle,” Lekishvili told reporters.

Ketevan Vardanashvili, the lawyer representing Anastasia Beruashvili, made similar arguments. She said Anastasia had not witnessed any crime and that she and Nia Imnadze had seen each other only once, for a few minutes.

“They had no friendship and no contact,” the lawyer said.

As for Anastasia’s relationship with the convicted defendant Giorgi Rikadze, Vardanashvili said that “even if she was his girlfriend, that does not mean she had any knowledge of the crime.”

Complaint or incitement?

The arrests of the two girls have sparked intense debate on social media. Many commentators agree that everyone responsible for Giga Avaliani’s death should be held accountable and that justice should be served. Many have also expressed sympathy for Eka Kupatadze.

At the same time, some have questioned the actions of the law enforcement authorities. They have asked whether prosecutors have sufficiently strong evidence against the two girls, particularly Nia Imnadze, who faces a lengthy prison sentence if convicted.

The Prosecutor’s Office statement says only that Nia Imnadze told her friends that Giga Avaliani had allegedly shown her excessive attention. It does not explain whether she knew an attack was being planned or whether she urged her boyfriend to take any specific action.

“Does complaining to friends amount to incitement?” some social media users have asked.

Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Live: No change to interest rates expected as RBA board meets
World.content:
The Reserve Bank is expected to keep interest rates on hold when its monetary policy board wraps up its meeting today.

After three rate hikes earlier this year, financial markets are pointing to the cash rate remaining steady at 4.35 per cent.

The central bank will also release its updated economic forecasts, including the inflation, growth and unemployment outlooks.

Follow the RBA decision, plus the day's financial news and insights, from our specialist business reporters in our live blog.

World.title: High school student juggles classes and McDonald's job while running for parliament
World.content:
Eighteen-year-old Hera Sheppard is expecting her schedule to be jam-packed over the next few months.

In between the demands of high school studies and a part-time job at McDonald's, the year 11 Warrnambool College student will be squeezing in a political campaign.

Ms Sheppard has thrown her hat in the ring ahead of Victoria's state election, making her one of the youngest candidates endorsed to contest a seat.

"I'm not going to have any free time. I'll be campaigning every minute that I'm not at work or school," she said.

" It's quite the sacrifice, but it's something that I'm willing to give up to try and campaign for a better world. "

Ms Sheppard has been pre-selected by the Victorian Socialists as the candidate for the South West Coast seat.

She will go up against incumbent Liberal member Roma Britnell, who has held the seat since a 2015 by-election.

The electorate is a Liberal stronghold and has been held by the party since its creation in 2002.

It largely spans rural communities, including the regional centre of Warrnambool and the smaller towns of Portland, Port Fairy, Heywood, Terang and Koroit.

Ms Sheppard said she aimed to represent the next generation of workers on issues including housing, workers' rights and public transport.

She is also advocating for a six-carriage train for Warrnambool's V/Line service with better travel times.

Hera Sheppard will campaign for improving public transport in south-west Victoria. (ABC News: Violette Storm)

Ms Sheppard said she spent most of her life living in public housing, and issues around public housing waitlists and supply were close to her heart.

"I think we need to be able to have public housing available for whoever needs them," she said.

If elected, Ms Sheppard would be the youngest-ever MP to make it to an Australian parliament.

In 2010, Queensland MP Wyatt Roy was elected to the House of Representatives aged 20, and in 2025, 21-year-old Charlotte Walker became the country's youngest senator in South Australia.

In Victoria, former premier Jacinta Allan was the state's youngest female MP, elected at 25 years old in 1999.

Victorians will go to the polls in November.

World.title: 'A lot of nerves': How it feels to pilot a Eurofighter Typhoon over Darwin
World.content:
Over the past three weeks, dozens of high-powered fighter jets have dominated the skies above Northern Australia as part of the country's largest international aviation war games, Exercise Pitch Black.

With the ability to reach top speeds of more than 2,400 kilometres per hour, the Eurofighter Typhoon is the fastest jet in the training exercise, capable of climbing double the height of Mount Everest.

For Spanish Air and Space Force Captain Jaime Molina Cegarra, the privilege of flying such a plane comes with "a lot of nerves".

One of the Spanish Air and Space Force's Eurofighter Typhoon jets in Darwin for Exercise Pitch Black. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We learn through our training how to calm those nerves, so they're always there, but you concentrate and you focus and you push on," he said.

"You keep your mind busy, but take everything one step at a time [and] try not to rush it … and practice makes perfect.

" So, just breathe in, breathe out and move on to the next thing. "

Jaime Molina Cegarra, right, travelled over from Spain to take part in Exercise Pitch Black. (ABC News)

Captain Cegarra has a prior connection to Australia — more than a decade ago, he spent three years studying at St Edmunds College in Canberra, making the country his second home.

"It was a great time when I was living here and I really hold Australia close to my heart," he said.

After joining the Spanish air force in 2015, Captain Cegarra said he spent six years learning to battle extreme acceleration G-forces of up to nine times his own body weight while training to become a combat fighter pilot.

Pitch Black draws in aviation enthusiasts Dozens of people are out in Darwin this month to photograph planes taking part in Exercise Pitch Black.

"We can go up to nine Gs but that's just because it's the human limit for us," he said.

"The jet can go even higher, but you practice that and you train and you go to do this special manoeuvre [where] you strain your body to keep the blood from flowing down to your legs.

"With nine Gs it can go up to nine times your weight. So imagine your head could weigh between five to 10 kilos, so multiply that [to] just imagine the force on your neck when you're pulling those G [forces]."

In just 30 seconds, Eurofighters can travel the speed of sound before climbing to a maximum height of 55,000 feet.

Exercise Pitch Black invites military personnel from all over the world, including Spain, to participate in the aviation war games. (ABC News)

Despite flying over crocodile-inhabited waters in the Northern Territory, Captain Cegarra said Darwin's sheer size and lack of traffic made the area's airspace a prime training ground.

"It's very easy going out and coming back, and then in the fighting airspace you don't really have to worry about different altitudes or airliners coming in and out, which is a real big problem in Europe, given the air space is so saturated," he said.

"Out in the desert there are no cultural lights as we call it, no city lights, nothing — so you're just flying in a big, black void.

"You've just got to keep your instruments in mind to make sure you're not flying upside down when you think you're flying straight and level."

Spain is one of 21 nations participating in this year's Exercise Pitch Black. (Supplied: RAAF/Maddy Butcher)

Back home, Captain Cegarra performs heart-stopping aerobatic manoeuvres as a part of the Spanish Air and Space Force's flying demonstration team.

Loading TikTok content

Despite enjoying the Mindil Beach flyover last month, he said he would like to see the NT air display incorporate more thrilling stunts in the future.

"It's really fun flying low and very fast, upside down, doing rolls, loops, all the good stuff," Captain Cegarra said.

"I was enjoying it myself a lot from down at the beach, especially the flare dispenses, that was really cool.

"We don't get to do that [kind of demonstration in Spain] and it's always nice to see a sunset show, and the flares were just the cherry on top."

World.title: Gridlock ahead: Perth's industrial hub faces a decade of disruption
World.content:
It is 6am and truck driver Carolus Broers is standing outside a fuel depot in Perth's south with a service-station coffee in hand.

It is here in Kwinana where the city's petrol passes through before being delivered to pumps across the metropolitan area.

Carolus jumps in his tanker and hits the road bound for his first stop — a service station in Ascot, less than 50 kilometres away.

Carolus Broers prepares his truck for a trip across Perth. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

Within minutes he is stationary.

The truck crawls onto the Kwinana Freeway, where traffic has already ground to a halt. It is not peak hour. It is barely 7am.

It doesn't take long for traffic to grind to a halt. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

For the next 45 minutes, the truck struggles to reach 20km/h.

For hundreds of truck drivers moving fuel, fertiliser and waste in and out of Kwinana, this is the daily reality.

And it's about to get worse.

Traffic banked up on the Kwinana Freeway near Anketell Road in Perth's south. (ABC News)

Kwinana is on the cusp of its biggest transformation in decades. The region will become home to AUKUS submarine support facilities and a defence manufacturing precinct, while nearby Westport will become the state's future container port.

Supporting that vision will require billions of dollars in new infrastructure, including a $1.1 billion upgrade of Anketell Road and a $700 million widening of the Kwinana Freeway. Construction is expected to begin early next year.

The state government has been touting its $700 million upgrade of the Kwinana Freeway. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

'Unrecognisable'

The Kwinana Industry Council's David Harrison said the region will be "completely unrecognisable" in a few years.

David Harrison says it's critical Kwinana is able to function as efficiently as possible. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"We are gearing up for the largest infrastructure transformation in Kwinana's history," he said.

"This is off the charts. We have never seen anything like it and we have never done anything like it.

"We're looking at probably a decade or more of infrastructure upgrades. It's not going to be quick or easy."

The government is also spending hundreds of millions of dollars upgrading Anketell Road to be the main gateway to Perth's new container port. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

The challenge, he said, is keeping Kwinana moving while it is rebuilt. The region is the industrial heart of the state.

"The fuel for your cars comes out of Kwinana. The fertiliser to grow our food comes out of Kwinana. Even the oxygen going into our public hospitals comes out of Kwinana," Mr Harrison said.

Kwinana is set for an overhaul with the arrival of the AUKUS submarine project. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"These roads are the arteries of industry. They have to continue to function."

Meanwhile the US Navy expects up to 2,300 Americans to call Perth's southern suburbs home by 2030.

Defence Minister Richard Marles said it was part of a rotational force to support the AUKUS nuclear submarine based at HMAS Stirling.

Federal politicians are known to frequent HMAS Stirling for announcements when travelling west. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"It's 1,200 personnel, there are civilians, contractors and families, which make up the larger number," he told reporters on Friday.

The premier said more than six-billion dollars of construction work will take place ahead of the American influx, beginning next year.

Planning ahead

Waste company Veolia runs around 200 trucks a day collecting kerbside rubbish before taking it to Kwinana's landfill and waste-to-energy facilities.

WA Municipal Manager Rebecca Goodwin said the company was already planning for heavier congestion by rostering extra drivers and trucks.

Rebecca Goodwin says her company is already planning for the disruption. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

"The impact is large. It is something we are planning for," she said.

" We expect we will need at least another two trucks operating in that southern corridor … just to make sure we can get everybody's bins collected on time. "

Those extra trucks come at a cost, one Veolia hopes it will not have to pass on to councils and ratepayers.

Fuel distributor Atlas Fuels faces the same problem.

Operations executive Tina Hopkins said longer journeys meant more trucks, more drivers and higher operating costs.

Tina Hopkins says her company will be impacted by the delays. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"We have to have extra trucks and extra drivers to manage the deliveries we need to do," she said.

The state government has warned commuters to expect average delays of about 15 minutes while freeway upgrades are underway.

Test of patience

For freight operators, however, those delays quickly multiply across dozens of vehicles and hundreds of deliveries.

By the time Carolus pulls into the Ascot service station, he's been behind the wheel for an hour and 45 minutes.

Carolus Broers says the traffic is a serious issue. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

They're already more than half an hour behind schedule and the major roadworks have not even begun.

It's a glimpse of what lies ahead as Kwinana embarks on a once-in-a-generation rebuild.

It marks the start of years of construction to support WA's industrial future, and a daily test of patience for the people who keep it running.

Carolus Broers stuck in traffic while driving along the Kwinana Freeway. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

World.title: Student's visa plea after helping Bondi terror attack victims
World.content:
An international student who helped victims during the Bondi Beach terror attack is appealing for the federal government's help to stay in the country.

Abdullah Ashraf, a law student from Pakistan, had his student visa lapse while on compassionate leave from his studies in the aftermath of the attack.

The December 14 attack claimed the lives of 15 people when two gunmen opened fire on a Jewish community event marking the start of Hanukkah.

Mr Ashraf, who was driving a rideshare car at the time, said an instinct kicked-in when he heard gunshots near the beach.

"It was in the back of my head that, if there's a bullet out there [with] my name on it, it would find me … but if I could help someone else, if I could save a life, I think that's a good bargain," he said.

Abdullah Ashraf says his student visa lapsed while on compassionate leave from his studies. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Attending to the injured

Mr Ashraf said he helped an injured police officer, before caring for a young mother after getting her children to safety.

"The kids were standing there; I made sure that they were behind the car, so even if there were bullets flying around, at least they're safe," he said

"I attended to the mother and made sure she was conscious. I started putting pressure on her wounds and kept talking to her, trying to tell her she was going to be okay."

Mr Ashraf said it made him "very happy" she survived.

"I'm sure she has a long road ahead in terms of recovering mentally, and the trauma, but the two kids won't grow up without a mother," he said.

Loading...

Once she was with paramedics, Mr Ashraf then tried to help 27-year-old French man, Dan Elkayam, and held his hand as he died.

"His pulse was very weak," he said.

"I did look in his eyes, but I couldn't [see] his wound or where it was, and he just passed away."

Trauma takes its toll on Ashraf's studies

In the months after the incident, the trauma weighed heavily on Mr Ashraf.

"It takes time to deal with trauma, everyone does it in their own way," he said.

" Initially you don't feel a lot, but after a little while you start thinking about it, when you're alone at night. "

After trying to push through with his studies, he was granted compassionate leave from the University of New South Wales on his doctor's recommendation.

"Considering what I'm studying, the load is quite intense and it needs a lot of time and consistent effort, and I just didn't have it in me at the time," he said.

Mr Ashraf says he would think about the December 14 attack when he was "alone at night". (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

In that period, his student visa lapsed. Mr Ashraf has applied for a new one, but said he was also struggling with uncertainty.

"It is very uncertain and causes a lot of anxiety sometimes not knowing how it's going to turn out," he said.

"I don't know how the department might look at it or how the case officer might look at it.

"If my visa gets rejected, that puts me in a very difficult situation."

The Home Affairs minister's office has been contacted for comment.

'I would love to stay here'

In recent years, the federal government has rewarded people on temporary visas who have shown extraordinary acts of bravery with permanent residency.

Bondi lifeguard still processing terror attack Much of Jackson 'Jacko' Doolan's memory from December 14 is a blur, but there is one moment that remains crystal clear.

After the Bondi Westfield stabbing attack in 2024, security guard Muhammad Taha and French national Damien Guerot, nicknamed "bollard man", were both granted permanent visas.

Israeli national Geffen Bitton and Indian man Rahemath Pasha were also granted permanent residency for their acts of bravery during the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.

When asked if he would like to stay in Australia long term, Mr Ashraf said that would be "life-changing".

"I absolutely love this country and I would love to stay here and continue my journey," he said.

Mr Ashraf said his dream would be to continue working with the Aboriginal Legal Service, an organisation he had been volunteering with during his studies.

"I have no idea how hard their life has been or what their generational story is, but what I do like to think is even if I've helped one of them, it has made a positive impact on everyone in their life and probably a lot of people who come after them," he said.

World.title: Live: Teal MP urges Albanese to 'pick up phone' and apologise for melon gaffe
World.content:
Anthony Albanese will hold talks today in Canberra with the President of Vietnam To Lam, as the two countries prepare to strike a host of new agreements.

To Lam has emerged as perhaps the most powerful leader in Vietnam for decades, and is rapidly putting his own stamp on both domestic and foreign policy in the south-east Asian nation.

Like Australia, Vietnam is trying to manage both an increasingly forceful China, as well as an unpredictable – and sometimes vindictive - Trump Administration.

Australia and Vietnam have drawn closer in recent years, and the economic relationship has boomed.

Expect both leaders to sign new pacts on multiple topics, like digital technology, vocational training and economic resilience.

It will be fascinating to see what the economic resilience pact covers, with both countries grappling with the economic implications of the War in Iran and its shock to global supply chains.

And while both countries already do plenty of business in hydrocarbons (like coal and crude oil) they’ve also identified clean energy, critical minerals and the green transition as growth areas in the economic relationship.

The visit won’t be totally without controversy, however.

To Lam is a former public security minister in Vietnam, and protesters from parts of Australia’s Vietnamese community fiercely opposed to the communist government have flagged they will show up to voice their anger.

World.title: Yarning circles raise concerns about repetition of Stolen Generations
World.content:
Some carers say Stolen Generations history is repeating itself with the number of children in South Australia under the Department for Child Protection (DCP).

A series of yarning circles to collect feedback from carers has heard staffing issues and delays in medical assessments were hindering progress for Aboriginal children in state care.

South Australia has the second highest rate of children in out-of-home care (OOHC) in the nation and almost 40 per cent, or 1,785, of those children are Aboriginal.

The Aboriginal-led organisation KWY has created a four-year research project called Wilto Willo (meaning "spring star" in Kaurna language) to investigate community-led solutions to reduce the over-representation of Aboriginal children in care.

Yarning circle participants made weavings to place at local DCP offices. (Supplied: KWY Adelaide)

About 200 carers have provided feedback through yarning circles at Port Lincoln, Port Augusta and Adelaide.

KWY research and development senior manager Rebecca Cort said the next phase would focus on yarning circle peer-led solutions.

"We have a really big problem in Australia of over-representation [of Aboriginal children in care] and it's growing," Ms Cort said.

"We know that it's growing since last year, so the problem despite all the policy, despite the investment, despite the agreement on closing the gap, the numbers are still worsening."

Rebecca Cort is the senior manager of research and development at KWY Adelaide. (Supplied: KWY Adelaide)

One of the key focus areas was the need to tackle child protection earlier.

"Australia nationally spends about $15 billion a year in child protection and family support — 84.1 per cent of that investment is looking … at intervening after harm has occurred for children and families," Ms Cort said.

Residential care

Children in SA are almost four times more likely to live in residential care than children nationally, with 772 children, or 17.2 per cent, of all OOHC placements in the outmoded type of care.

This is out of step nationally according to 2026 monitoring of the Productivity Commission's Report on Government Services by SA's Guardian for Children and Young People.

"[It] raises serious questions about whether the system is adequately prioritising children's rights to safe family-based care in their community," the report stated.

The rate of Aboriginal children in care in South Australia was 88.6 per 1,000 Aboriginal children in the total care population, compared with 62.4 nationally.

The report stated South Australia continued to fail Aboriginal children at scale despite incremental improvements.

Evelyn Walker says staffing issues have left children without case workers for six months. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Port Lincoln carer Evelyn Walker said there were several issues raised at the local yarning circles about the Department for Child Protection.

These included a large turnover of staff, a fly-in fly-out workforce, staff shortages, a lack of communication and delays in accessing assessments, she said.

Ms Walker said the lack of a permanent and stable workforce left some children and care families without a support worker for six months, and some children had not accessed a psychologist or been assessed to ensure they were on the right medications.

She said some staff did not understand or adhere to Aboriginal placement principles.

"Some children being in non-First Nations placements didn't have connection with their families and even with their culture and going out on country — that's all part of wellbeing," Ms Walker said.

Yarning circle sessions heard concerns about children losing touch with their culture. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"We have had some children that appear to have lost their identity of who they are.

"They don't know their cultural background, they don't know their family connections, they don't know story to country, haven't been on country."

Part of Ms Walker's childhood was spent growing up in another family.

"I can say from my experience when I reconnected back with family, it was very overwhelming … however, it was the best thing for my wellbeing," she said.

Department for Child Protection chief executive Jackie Bray said DCP sought to improve outcomes for Aboriginal children by drawing on the advice of Aboriginal colleagues and community members.

Jackie Bray is the chief executive of SA's Department for Child Protection. (ABC News)

"We have a strong focus on embedding family-led decision-making in our everyday practice, through measures including increasing the use of family group conferencing, where extended family members come together to make decisions about the safe care of children," Ms Bray said.

"Laws which take effect next year mandate the implementation of the Aboriginal child placement principle, which acknowledges connection to country, culture and community as fundamental for the safety, wellbeing and identity of Indigenous children."

Ms Bray said the department had vacancies in Port Lincoln and was actively recruiting to fill them.

"A small number of staff are currently based outside Port Lincoln and regularly travel to the Eyre Peninsula for their roles," she said.

"In many regional areas, fly-in fly-out arrangements are an established workforce model that helps address skill shortages and support the delivery of essential services."

Aboriginal children put in non-Indigenous placements are at risk of losing their sense of identity. (ABC News: James Dunlevie)

Ms Bray said the department offered incentives for staff to move to country locations, including accommodation or subsidised housing, return flights and reimbursement of relocation and education expenses.

She said DCP worked to support children and young people to access health care, with specialist consultants and support teams working alongside staff and carers to connect children with supports tailored to their individual needs.

Children 'criminalised'

Ms Cort said research showed children in care were more likely to end up in the judicial system.

"What we're hearing about the criminalisation of children … confirmed by lived experience, that when children are in out-of-home care, it's more likely that the police will be contacted for small behavioural problems that would normally be privately managed in a home, for example, where police wouldn't intervene," she said.

Generations of families are impacted by a child being put into care, Ms Cort says. (ABC News: James Dunlevie)

"And that intervention starts a pathway that leads to criminalisation, leads to youth justice, and that's confirmed in the research."

She said the placement of a child into care impacted entire generations of families.

"We've also heard of families really grieving the loss of culture that their children experience," Ms Cort said.

Ms Walker said the history of the Stolen Generations was "repeating itself".

"DCP [and] the welfare is more advanced, but it's still the same thing that's happening.

" Our children's identities are being lost, they're disconnected from family, being connected to culture and country. "

Yarning circles have been held at Port Augusta, Port Lincoln and Adelaide. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Yarning circle facilitator Tamara Noel said the carers spoke about feeling unsupported.

"They really wanted DCP and other organisations in the area to come and listen … to hear what their experiences are and to learn from them, to sit with community," Ms Noel said.

Ms Cort said if the solutions could be taken seriously, there was "certainly a light at the end of the tunnel".

World.title: Major football bodies pen letter seeking Infantino exit over 'deception'
World.content:
UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC believe FIFA President Gianni Infantino's recent plan to sell an interest in the World Cup was a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions world soccer's governing body serves.

In an "open letter to the football family", the governing bodies also said that "when trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

UEFA runs football in Europe, CONCACAF does the same for North, Central America and the Caribbean, while the AFC governs the sport in Asia.

FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan FIFA has reiterated its support for embattled president Gianni Infantino, while apologising to its member associations for the aborted bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

The letter was co-signed by UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, AFC President Salman Bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani and three general secretaries.

"Football is the world's greatest shared passion. It belongs to no individual and no institution. It belongs to the players, the fans, the clubs, the member associations and every institution entrusted with safeguarding its future," the open letter said.

"It is in that spirit, as confederations representing its members, that we speak collectively today."

Infantino is facing a revolt after his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him," the letter said.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Australia's Socceroos also fall under the AFC, which has spoken out against Infantino. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Ziyu Julian Zhu)

UEFA previously issued a threat to boycott the World Cup and other FIFA competitions despite the governing body abandoning and apologising for its failed plan.

Norway's football federation called for Infantino to step down, while the English Football Association has also withdrawn its support for his re-election next March.

"Football's strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now," the letter said. "For leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."

Last Wednesday, FIFA said it had apologised for errors made over the failed plan but that senior staff at a crisis meeting in Morocco "reaffirmed their full support" for his presidency.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, the nature of the meeting was also met with criticism.

"FIFA's own letter also confirms that only one elected official was present at the leadership meeting in Morocco," the open letter said.

"No FIFA Council members or Member Associations were invited to participate. Only the management committee, composed of FIFA-employed senior staff, was present."

FIFA was also urged to go further than just acknowledging mistakes were made.

"It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgement," the letter said.

"There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgement — not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve."

In a statement Saturday, FIFA defended Infantino against what it called a "concerted and ongoing effort" to undermine his leadership of the organisation.

That statement followed a report by British newspaper The Daily Telegraph raising questions about an exit package paid by UEFA to a female staffer who worked with Infantino when he was general secretary of European soccer's ruling body.

UEFA confirmed a "departure payment" was made to the employee and said it was "in line" with regulations at the time.

Infantino worked at UEFA for 16 years before being elected FIFA president.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Albanese tells Labor caucus he expects gambling bill to pass with Coalition support; At least 110 killed in Colombia after 7.4 magnitude earthquake
World.content:
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has dismissed claims Labor is not focused on bringing down inflation through lowering spending, as the Reserve Bank is set to meet today to decide whether to raise, lower or hold interest rates steady.

Appearing on Nine’s Today, Gallagher was asked: “Leading economists are now accusing you of spending too much time fiddling with taxes rather than reducing government spending. How do you respond to that accusation?”

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher. Alex Ellinghausen

Gallagher said: “Well, I don’t accept that at all. I mean, in every budget, we have reduced, we have found savings either to return to budget so that we have lower debt, or to you know reallocate across the budget”.

The minister said the budget was under “enormous pressure” because of the cost of social services and defence, saying the government found “more savings than we spent” in the last budget.

“We really do make a huge effort to look at where we can trim spending. But we also need to be honest, and accept that there is a lot of pressure on the Commonwealth budget to do more and to provide more support to people, and we have to try to find the right balance with that,” Gallagher said.

World.title: At least 111 people killed, many trapped as powerful earthquake hits Colombia
World.content:
Updated WorldSouth AmericaEarthquakes At least 111 people killed, many trapped as powerful earthquake hits Colombia Updated August 11, 2026 — 6:56am ,first published 2:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bogota, Colombia: A powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble. Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and about 1600 buildings damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. He declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. “We aren’t going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination,” he said. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4800 people in the Choco region about 400 kilometres west of Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.



The quake ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo, Cali and Manizales. In the country’s third-largest city, Cali, search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. A vehicle is crushed by debris after the earthquake struck Cali, Colombia, on Monday. AP Photo/Juan Diaz Residents and rescue workers in Cali search through the rubble. AP Photo/Santiago Saldarriaga The desperate scene brought memories of the searches still ongoing in neighbouring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes.



Colombia’s Geological Service said Monday’s quake was the strongest recorded in Colombia “in the 21st century”, and that it was followed by 21 less powerful aftershocks. While Colombia typically registers thousands of small quakes every month, Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the strong magnitude, inland epicentre near soft river valleys and movement of the plates may have contributed to more intense damage. View post on X “This one was far below the (earth’s) crust, and in theory, it shouldn’t cause as much shaking. At this magnitude, it did actually cause a lot of shaking,” she said. “A magnitude 7.4 is about 32 times as powerful as a magnitude 6.4.” Colombia’s Pacific region around the quake’s epicentre lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of the poorest regions in the country. Nestled in the dense jungle, much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose a problem for authorities in assessing the wider toll.



Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. “My entire house shook. I’ve never lived through such a powerful earthquake,” he said. “We’re thanking God we’re alive.” The rescue effort in Cali. AP Photo/Santiago Saldarriaga Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, as well as 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died.



Authorities said flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage. The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5000 people. A rescue worker searches for survivors. Santiago Saldarriaga Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of region’s capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake’s epicentre, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport, and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira. In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming.



In the city, people were shown running through rubble and plumes of dust. Pereira’s mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that more people were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings.” In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Police look at a building damaged after an earthquake struck Colombia. AP Photo/Vladimir Encima In Cali, a city of 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed. Small earthquakes, known as “temblores”, are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1100 people.



Colombia’s newly inaugurated president said Monday that he had personally taken charge of the government’s response to the emergency. “You are not alone. The state is present and taking action,” he said. Patients evacuated from a hospital in Cali. Santiago Saldarriaga Response to the earthquake presents the first major challenge to de la Espriella, a Trump ally who was sworn in as president over the weekend. Messages of support rolled in from leaders across the Americas, including Mexico, Brazil, Ecuador, El Salvador and the United States.



“The Trump administration is closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote in a post on X. A number of countries offered aid, and the UN deputy spokesman, Farhan Haq, said “we stand ready to help as needed”. World.title: ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street slips; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip on RBA day, Wall Street slips; Oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty Stan Choe Updated August 11, 2026 — 6:51am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market edged down from its all-time high on Monday, while oil prices rose on uncertainty about when the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and get the global flow of crude going again. The S&P 500 slipped 0.1 per cent from its record set on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 60 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.3 per cent. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a steady session. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent at the open. The ASX slid 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision at 2.30pm AEST, with money markets and economists in near-unanimous agreement that the central bank’s monetary policy board will hold the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent when it wraps up its latest two-day meeting. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.56¢. Reporting season is starting to heat up, with Southern Cross Media Group and Life360 among companies due up today.



Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Momentum slowed for Wall Street stocks following a rally powered by soaring profits for big US companies. Reports are on track to show earnings per share leaped 50 per cent in the spring from a year earlier for companies in the S&P 500, according to FactSet. That would be the best growth since five years ago, when the economy was roaring out of the chasm created by COVID. Berkshire Hathaway is one of the latest companies to deliver a stronger profit for the last quarter than analysts expected, and the company built by legendary investor Warren Buffett said over the weekend that it’s also invested some of its massive pile of cash into stocks under its new CEO, Greg Abel. Berkshire Hathaway has been famous for buying stocks at what it considers low prices, and criticism has been high that US stocks generally look too expensive. But when they report strong profits, it helps them look less pricey. Berkshire Hathaway’s stock rose 1.5 per cent.



MarineMax jumped 46.1 per cent after the retailer, marina operator and superyacht services provider said it agreed to sell itself for about $US1.5 billion in cash to a portfolio company of Blackstone. Varex Imaging leaped 48.8 per cent after Teledyne Technologies said it would buy the maker of X-ray imaging components for $US18.90 per share in cash. But Intel helped offset such gains and fell 4.1 per cent after saying it may sell $US15 billion of its stock. Such a move would dilute the ownership stakes of shareholders, and Intel said it would likely use the cash for investments to take advantage of the huge spending underway on artificial-intelligence technology. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 4.53 points to 7,753.11. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 60.95 to 53,975.98, and the Nasdaq composite sank 85.26 to 26,605.36. In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 5 per cent to $US87.72. It had swung between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach an agreement that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Middle East again to deliver crude worldwide.



But hopes are turning toward caution again, and the price of Brent is back to where it was earlier this month, as well as in mid-July, mid-June and in the first week of the war in March. Higher oil prices push inflation upward, and the main event for Wall Street this week will likely be Wednesday’s update on how bad inflation was last month. Economists expect it to show inflation slowed to 3.4 per cent from 3.5 per cent in June. A slowdown would mean less pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Related Article Opinion

Retail How one David Jones supplier got paid when the others didn’t Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



A report on Friday showing unexpectedly weak hiring across the United States lowered Wall Street’s expectations for an upcoming hike to interest rates. But traders still see a nearly 52 per cent chance the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.70 per cent from 4.65 per cent late Friday. That’s up from 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, and the climb has already sent rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans significantly higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe after rising in much of Asia. Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 2.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves.
