World.title: Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job
World.content:
CultureBooksTake 7 Thomas Keneally told Matt Nable to keep writing, so he quit his job Kylie Northover August 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Nable is quite the Renaissance man, having begun his career as a professional NRL player for Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles and South Sydney Rabbitohs, before becoming a national amateur boxing champion. After retiring from sport in his 20s, he began writing a novel about the sporting world, and sought the advice of playwright and author Thomas Keneally, who mentored him. The Final Winter eventually became a screenplay for his debut film, in which he also starred – launching him as both writer and actor. These days he’s also a director and a bestselling author. With the recent release of his latest novel, Mire, Nable says if it wasn’t for Keneally, he wouldn’t be enjoying the multifaceted career he has today. “That conversation,” he says, “changed my life.” Renaissance man: Matt Nable’s career spans professional sports, acting, directing and writing. Sally Flegg Worst habit?

I have a few. But probably being a noisy eater. At least that’s what my wife and daughter tell me. It really annoys them. And an internal habit that drives me crazy is that I can fixate on something, and it plays on a loop in my head – really frustrating when you’re trying to move forward and be productive. Over the years, I have gotten better at shutting down that noise and letting go. But every now and then, it still bites me. Greatest fear?

Losing one of my children. Beyond that, I can’t see anything to be afraid of that matters. There’s fear around certain things that I would consider irrational fears; I don’t like spiders or snakes, sharks I have a healthy fear of, but none of those keep me up at night. Losing a child does. I think all parents feel that way. I used to fear death. That’s completely gone. I don’t quite know why that it is, but I’m not afraid of dying. I was a horribly affected Catholic boy, to a point I was in some constant manner of guilt. It was exhausting. I was going to hell for everything. When I turned, and I turned hard, I had no fear of where I’d go when I died. So maybe that’s how I got to where I am now.



Nable (right) with his brother Aaron, who died from MND in 2024. The line that has stayed with you? “The people that matter, are the people that believe you matter … and tomorrow is never promised.” My brother passed away with MND in March 2024. And when he was diagnosed, and because there is no cure, he had that quote tattooed on his arm. It was a stark reminder that we are all just here without any idea of what’s coming and how long we have left. I now have the same tattoo. In February last year I did a psilocybin retreat, which for me was profound – confronting but enlightening. One of the great understandings I got from the experience was the people who matter are the people who believe you matter. And that’s where my attention, my time and my love need to be directed. Biggest regret?



Not being more present when my kids were smaller. I’m envious of parents when I see them with their small kids. It just went so fast. I yearn for those moments now, I cherish the memories. I look at photos all the time … I was far too self-involved back then. If I could run into my younger self, I’d give him a good clip behind the ear, and tell him to pay attention to what’s going on right before him. Nable’s latest novel, Mire is out now. Tell us about your turning point I had written a manuscript and had given it to Thomas Keneally. He’s a mad Manly fan, and somehow remembered me when I’d played there. He read it, and told me that I should continue writing. I did. And 12 months later he read my next effort. It took a while for him to get back to me, but he called one day, and he said, “Son, this is what you should be doing, and I wouldn’t say that if I didn’t believe it because it would be immoral of me.” I literally quit the job I was doing a week later. If not for Tommy and what he’d said, I’m not doing any of this. Not writing, not acting … I don’t know where I’d be. The artwork or song you wish was yours?



I have great respect and a love of songwriters who are able to tell vivid stories in short pieces of language. John Mellencamp, Billy Joel – they have the ability to give enormous texture through words mixed with the music. You can taste and smell where they’re talking about, and you can feel the people in the centre of the composition. I’d love to be able to do that. I started playing guitar in 2002, and I really am not very good. I got to a level and just kind of stayed there. So, I tried to write a few songs – and it was just awful. I quickly packed that up and got back in my own lane. Related Article Take 7 ‘My opinion didn’t count’: Tina Arena discusses ill-fated marriage to Ralph Carr in new documentary If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? The future is kind of scary to me. I’m not technological, so I fear I’d be redundant somewhere in the not-too-distant future. Perhaps to when I was a young boy, with my family bouncing around army barracks. As I said, I lost my youngest brother in 2024. We were all together back then. They were much simpler times, and we were all so happy. I’ve written about those memories to some degree in every novel that’s been published. There are moments while writing that are of real joy, and sometimes sadness. And then [I’d go] to a time when all my children were younger. Mire (Hachette) by Matt Nable is out now.

World.title: Rocket Lab reports record quarter amid Iridium takeover bid
World.content:
Rocket Lab has announced record revenue of US$234 million for its second quarter, up 62 percent from the same period last year.

Despite the record revenue, Rocket Lab remained loss-making, posting a second-quarter net loss of US$49 million, compared with a loss of US$66 million a year earlier.

The US-listed space company says its order backlog has reached a record of just under US$2.4 billion dollars.

Rocket Lab founder and chief executive Sir Peter Beck said: "Q2 was another fantastic quarter for Rocket Lab, highlighted by record results and massive momentum that has continued well after the close."

The company has recently signed a series of military contracts and is in the process of acquiring satellite communications operator Iridium, as it seeks to diversify its business from launches and rocket manufacturing into communication services.

Its shares fell by about by 3 percent to around US$78 in after-hours trading.

Looking ahead, Rocket Lab expects revenue in the current quarter to rise further to between US$250 million and US$265m, which would represent another record result if achieved.

The company said it expected growth in both its launch and space systems divisions.

The company said work on its medium-lift Neutron rocket remained on track, with production of the first-stage tank aligned with plans to deliver the rocket to the launch pad in the final quarter of this year.

World.title: Former inmate says Mt Eden Prison should become crime museum
World.content:
Former inmate calling for old Mount Eden Prison to be preserved Morning Report Download MP3 4m

When 23-year-old Greg Newbold shuffled under the imposing rocky archway, it felt like he was stepping into the past.

"I was really shocked when I first went in there," he said. "I mean, I was from Auckland and I'd driven past the prison many, many times, but it looked like a medieval dungeon.

"I said, 'What's this?', and [my co-offender] said, 'This is the remand wing'. I said, 'What? You mean, this is where we stay?'

"He said, 'Yep'."

The now-author and retired sociology professor was arrested for dealing heroin in 1975, and remanded at the old Mt Eden Prison for five months, before he was moved to Paraparaumu to serve his sentence.

He remembered the awful conditions.

A general view of the Mount Eden prison 1900. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"It had high windows, which had no glass in them, because the glass had been smashed, and it just had bars," Newbold recalled.

"In the winter time, pigeon feathers would fly in, because the pigeons used to roost there, and you'd quite often get lice in your blankets.

"There was no plumbing in the prison either. You had to piss in a piss pot."

Constructed as a timber stockade in 1856, the prison's stony exterior was built up over the next 60 years, using volcanic rock mined by the prisoners from Mt Eden itself.

The damp and rugged cells held inmates until 2011, when the last prisoners were moved next door to the new Mt Eden Corrections Facility.

Since then, historian Mark Derby said it had fallen into disrepair.

"When I last saw the prison, it was in an obviously decaying state," Derby recalled from researching his 2020 book Rock College.

"It has been closed now for quite a few years. Nothing's been done to it, it's been sitting empty.

"Clearly, some decision has to be made as soon as possible about this."

Despite some bad memories, Newbold said it should become a museum.

"Oh, it's a museum, it's unbelievable," he said. "There's so much history in that institution and it's a relic of a past era.

"It should never, ever be pulled down."

Mt Eden Prison entry 1900. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"They could do it relatively cheaply and they could make money out of it, because people would love to see inside that place."

The prison was a treasure trove of historical misadventures, Newbold said, including a rumoured explosive escape attempt.

"In 1931, the inmates at Mt Eden, who worked in the quarry, they used to get gelignite and bring it in underneath their fingernails, and then scrape the gelignite out," he recounted.

"Finally, they had enough gelignite to create a big blast and they blasted a hole right through the f**king prison wall - right through the wall - and two guys escaped."

Derby suspected that particular escapade had been exaggerated over the decades, but said prison breaks were common.

"It was very easy to escape, but not at all easy to remain at large once you're outside the walls," he said.

"Guys used to do it more or less for a break in routine, knowing that they'd be stuck in solitary for a few weeks on bread and water, once they got back."

The prison's colourful history also contained much darker shades.

Derby recalled the 'Lock Hospital', a short-lived wing of the prison that kept people with contagious diseases against their will in the late 19th century.

Mt Eden Prison corridor with celldoors. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"Most of the patients at the Lock Hospital were sex workers," he said. "The youngest I found on record was 13.

"She would have been regarded as the one at fault - the malefactor - not the clients who were responsible for her medical condition."

Derby said many of the people held at Mt Eden Prison wouldn't be considered criminals today.

"Male homosexuals held for consensual sex as adults were in there," he said. "Alcoholics were held there for no other reason than they were a nuisance on the streets.

"We have a lot to learn about the past and it can give us plenty of pointers for the future, I think."

Derby said that uncomfortable history was precisely why the building should be preserved and opened for public viewing.

He said many former inmates he had interviewed felt the same way.

"Sometimes, I would ask them, 'What do you think should happen to it?' They all said that they didn't want to see it demolished, that even though they thought it was a terrible place where terrible things had happened, that wasn't a sufficient reason to see it knocked down.

"It would be a marvellous base to construct a museum from."

A Department of Corrections spokesperson shot down the idea.

"The old prison sits within the confines of the new, fully operational prison, which would pose challenges for use such as a public museum," they said.

World.title: Bougainville president warns of going against peace process
World.content:
Bougainville's President Ishmael Toroama says if Papua New Guinea's national parliament refuses to back the 2019 referendum result it will undermine the peace process.

Toroama made the comment while addressing last week's meeting in Port Moresby of the Joint Supervisory Body co-chaired by PNG's prime minister, James Marape.

As a result of the meeting, after months of uncertainty, both governments have decided that the referendum results will finally be tabled for deliberation by the national parliament on 27 August.

The historic, non-binding referendum saw 97.7 per cent of respondents in the autonomous PNG region vote in favour of independence.

The referendum was provided for by the Bougainville Peace Agreement, a long term commitment which was forged in 2001 as a settlement after the Bougainville civil war in the 1990s.

Toroama told the JSB last week that Bougainville entered the talks determined to uphold joint agreements and he called on PNG to honour the Joint Consultations report and the Melanesian Framework.

"We are compelled by legal, political and moral responsibilities to respect, accept and adhere to the report and implement the framework," Toroama said.

"These are compliance documents. They reference nothing but the truth."

"They hold us accountable to our own signatures, Prime Minister," Toroama said.

Toroama went on to say he wanted to address the "elephant in the room", the national government's recently formalised position on what it calls a "non-affirming decision".

"I have read the text, and I must tell you frankly: it is a masterpiece of bureaucratic evasion and historical revisionism," he said.

"The PNG government's position argues that the national parliament has an "unfettered discretion" to simply say "no" to the 97.7% referendum vote, and that a rejection would merely reset Bougainville to the existing autonomy framework."

Toroama added that this was a "dangerous legal fiction".

"Firstly, the national government position suggests that if Parliament rejects our independence vote, Bougainville will retain its autonomy status and focus on "milestones" like fiscal self-reliance and drawing down of Section 290 powers," he said.

"The national government is treating our constitutional right to self-determination as if it were a performance review or some corporate evaluation subject to external yardsticks or the shifting political tides of the national parliament.

"Bougainville is moving away from the Autonomy space, let me make that clear," Toroama said.

He also criticised proposals that Bougainville could revisit its political status after meeting further conditions.

"This insults the intelligence of our people. By doing this, the National Government is asking us to trade a constitutional, internationally witnessed referendum result for an ambiguous promise of future political charity," he said.

"We do not need a 'clear pathway to revisit the question', the question has been asked, answered, and sealed in ink and blood.

Voter's finger gets inked during polling for Bougainville's independence referendum RNZ / Johnny Blades

He argued that rejecting the referendum outcome would contradict the Bougainville Peace Agreement.

"The agreement was built on the promise that the choice of the people would be negotiated in good faith toward a definitive conclusion," he said.

"It was never intended to be an endless loop of consultations where Waigani holds a permanent veto."

"Any attempt by the national parliament to vote down the referendum result, freezes us in a dead autonomy framework, or demand constitutional amendments just to kick the can down the road, is a rejection of the peace process itself. It's unacceptable," he said.

Toroama also challenged recent parliamentary decisions on voting thresholds and sessional orders, saying they were introduced without the joint consultation required under previous agreements.

"Bougainville had no part in those decisions as required by law. Those were unilateral decisions made by the national government and the speaker of the national parliament," he said.

"Bypassing mandatory consultation was, and is, actually, stepping away from the very spirit of our partnership."

He called on PNG's lawmakers to study the Joint Consultations report, describing it as a blue-print for Bougainville's transition to self-governance and eventual sovereignty.

Toroama said Bougainville's final position on independence had been endorsed by the Autonomous Bougainville Government, its House of Representatives and national MPs through a series of consultations culminating in the July 2026 Kuri Resolution.

"This position has been systematically refined through extensive consultation at Bougainville's highest political levels," he said.

Toroama also defended the autonomous PNG region's record on weapons disposal, noting it had been overseen and certified by the United Nations.

He said the overwhelming referendum vote for independence remained beyond dispute.

"During those 40 days, not a single objection, dispute, or challenge was raised against the result by any party or citizen, including the national government and the international community."

"The 97.7% vote for independence is a sealed, certified, and immutable historical fact," he said.

World.title: Labour leader Chris Hipkins defends his performance after drop in recent poll
World.content:
The Labour leader is defending his performance following a drop in support in a recent poll, saying his party is doing "significantly better" than the last election.

According to a Taxpayers' Union Curia poll released on Friday, Labour had dropped 3.7 points to 27.8 percent since the last poll in July.

Chris Hipkins dismissed the poll as being funded by a "right-wing lobby group" that wanted to keep the current government in office.

It comes as the prime minister's grip on his leadership is again being questioned following a week of communication gaffes and a fresh report his MPs are unhappy.

Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 7m

On Morning Report, it was put to Hipkins the same poll in March showing National's support had dropped was impactful on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Hipkins said Labour considered all the polls, but RNZ's Reid Research poll also showed a drop in support for Labour between March and July.

He maintained that Labour was doing "significantly better" than the last election, despite acknowledging the party had been annihilated in 2023.

"The fact that we, within three years, are back in a position where people are talking about the fact that we could be forming government after the next election is a very good sign for Labour."

Both the recent TPU-Curia poll and RNZ Reid Research poll still had the current coalition able to form a government.

Asked why he wasn't doing better, Hipkins said the election campaign was just getting underway.

"My job in the next few months is to get out there and campaign on the policies that Labour's put out there around tackling the cost of living, around supporting small business, and we've got plenty more policy to come."

He said Labour was putting out policies that would "make a difference to New Zealanders" such as capping public transport fares, and making it free to go to the doctor.

Hipkins said people were currently "disaffected and disillusioned with politics".

"I totally get why people are pretty despondent, particularly when they see politicians arguing about things that don't matter to them, or that actually are the wrong things to argue about."

He referenced racist arguments and politicians arguing about whether English should be an official language, saying "people get pretty frustrated with politics" as a result.

"That's a a pretty common vibe at the moment."

Hipkins maintained he would lead the Labour Party into the next election, and voters could make the decision about whether he was doing a good enough job for the party.

He also said he was "absolutely committed" to leading Labour into government after the next election, without specifying if he would lead Labour into opposition if the party did not win.

Labour has a policy announcement in Rotorua later on Tuesday, and Hipkins didn't say if it was planned ahead of Luxon's comments to small business owners at a Rotorua Business Chamber event.

Last Monday Luxon apologised to leaders from the Rotorua Business Chamber after he criticised them for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

Hipkins said on Tuesday "treating people like adults is generally a good approach to take when you're a politician".

New Zealand First ruled out

It also comes as Hipkins finally and officially ruled out working with New Zealand First in any government he leads.

Asked what led him to shift from previously saying it was "highly unlikely" his party would work with New Zealand First again, to a formal rule out, Hipkins mentioned racist remarks by Winston Peters and Shane Jones had caused "a lot of upset in our community."

"We've heard direct feedback from Chinese New Zealanders, from Indian New Zealanders, that they are now being subjected to more emboldened racism out in the community, and that racism is being emboldened by the actions of parties like New Zealand First.

"That's not who we are as a country, we're a better country than that."

World.title: Former Silver Fern captain Ana Noovao dies aged 58
World.content:
Former Silver Ferns captain Ana Noovao has died aged 58.

The midcourter played for New Zealand between 1989 and 1992, picking up 23 test caps.

She debuted against Australia in 1989.

Noovao was a member of the Silver Ferns squad that lost the 1991 World Cup final by one goal to Australia.

She was elevated to Silver Ferns captain in 1992 following the retirement of Waimarama Taumaunu.

World.title: Uni students skipping meals and classes to keep on top of bills
World.content:
Student questioning whether to continue due to cost-of-living Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A Wellington student is doubting that pursuing a degree is a smart move as she skips meals because she can't afford to eat.

A student association survey of 1238 students at Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University Wellington found many were skipping meals and missing classes as they worked to pay rent and bills on top of their studies.

Thirty-three percent of the students who responded to the survey said they had skipped a meal in the previous week because they couldn't afford to eat.

Pyper-Alex Adams is in her third year at Victoria University - studying Psychological Sciences.

She said a part-time job and a casual position on top of her full-time studies helped keep her rent paid, but she often skimped on meals - especially when shifts were sparse.

"If I get offered shifts that's great but I don't have any shifts this week, I don't have any shifts next week. I've actually had to apply to the student hardship grant to help with my power bill this month because I don't know if I'm going to be able to pay it without any shifts from my second job," Adams said.

She said she was starting to question whether a tertiary qualification was really a smart move.

"It makes me just want to drop out of university. I am barely able to afford rent. We're cold all the time because we're only using the heat pump during free power. I'm skipping meals.

"I'm going to university to try and get a degree. To maybe have a job someday - if I can get one in this country - but I'm seeing people my age that are doing so much better without the degree - which is the thing that we're all told in high school to do, right?" Adams said.

300 level student Pyper-Alex Adams. RNZ / Bill Hickman

Third-year maths and statistics student Cam Dickson was trying to be creative to find his way around the high cost of living.

"You know people talk about chicken and rice? We're not doing chicken and rice, we're doing beans and rice. I'm moving away from fresh fruit and vegetables because they're not super accessible right now. Going heavy on the carbs - on the cans - on the box stuff," Dickson said.

Dickson is one of the nearly 38 percent of students surveyed who said they had missed classes because they couldn't afford public transport costs.

"I don't have public transport in the wiggle room. I've got no way to own a car, to pay for the fuel. I'm very constrained to where my feet can get me and sometimes that's not university," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'.

Cam Dickson said many students' experience of the slogan might be different to what the advertisers imagined.

"It means to be cold a lot of the time. Sometimes it means to be hungry. Sometimes it means to be damp. Sometimes it means to just kind of struggle to get by and I wouldn't really recommend anyone that experience," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'. RNZ / Bill Hickman

The situation appeared to become more acute for students in their later stages of study.

Seventy-eight percent of third year students said they had considered heading overseas for better job opportunities - eight percent higher than respondents from across the entire survey population.

President of the Victoria University Students Association and Masters student, Aidan Donoghue, said the intense competition for work was changing how students approached their degrees.

"It's so competitive that you must be a straight A student. You must have X amount of internships. You must have all these extra curricular activities at this point just to put your name out there," Donoghue said

He had a message for people who saw today's student poverty as the same rite of passage experienced by previous generations.

"Students aren't just complaining. It's just as expensive as it was then but twenty years of inflation on top. Plus stagnant wage growth, plus competitive working environment. All the bad things of university that you have experienced have gotten worse over decades of compounding interest," Donoghue said.

World.title: Where have all the ATMs gone?
World.content:
Why is it harder to find an ATM? Morning Report Download MP3 2m

If you have looked for somewhere to get cash out recently, you might have noticed a change - many bank-owned ATMs have vanished.

Sometimes they been replaced with non-bank options, which can cost $2.50 per withdrawal, and sometimes they have been removed completely.

The country's largest bank ANZ said it has reduced its ATM numbers by 85 in the past two years. In all but 10 cases, the contract for the site was given to another provider.

Westpac said its number had dropped by 54 over the same period.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

The Reserve Bank said the number of bank branches around the country was down by 40 percent and the number of bank-owned ATMs had dropped 32 percent over the past decade. Between 2012 and 2017, total ATM numbers fell by 14.7 percent per million people.

Consumer NZ said it was concerned.

"While cash use is declining, it is still used by many people. The Reserve Bank's latest cash-use data, from September 2025, found that 40.3 percent of people said they used cash for everyday things and only 2.5 percent said they never use cash."

New Zealand Banking Association chief executive Roger Beaumont said banks were responding to customer demand.

"The main reason there are fewer ATMs is that fewer customers are using them. Around 1.5 percent of all customer transactions are made at an ATM, and that's slowly reducing every year.

"In some cases, landlords making changes to tenancy agreements, or seismic risk, may lead to banks removing or relocating ATMs."

Claire Matthews - a banking expert at Massey University - said there was a cost associated with ATMs and a risk due to the cash being held. There had to be enough use being made of them to make them worthwhile for banks, she said.

"People use less cash and are more likely to get cash with eftpos transactions if they do want it, so there is less use of cash. I'm struggling to remember when I used an ATM."

University of Auckland senior lecturer in economics Chanelle Duley said the drop in ATM numbers was part of a broader "retreat" from physical banking infrastructure.

Fincap the financial mentor network said cash was important for many of the people mentors dealt with. Some people used cash to help them budget.

It said that it had heard from mentors in urban and rural areas that some people found it hard to access cash.

"In rural areas the cost of significant travel to access cash can compound financial hardship. In urban areas, we have heard concerns around hardship or exclusion for clients who have a disability and/or, limited time amongst their other obligations to queue or travel for the limited local available services which do not charge for cash withdrawal."

It is something that the Reserve Bank has its eye on.

It has been consulting on plans to propose minimum standards for cash services in New Zealand and will release its findings late next month.

Its proposal was to put a floor under the number and location of places where bank customers could withdraw, deposit or swap cash.

It wants 95 percent of people living in urban areas to have walking-distance access to a free cash point.

It said meeting the standard would cost banks about $100 million a year but that was only 1 percent of their combined annual profit.

A spokesperson said it was analysing the 6000 submissions it had received and was not in a position to comment further at this stage.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's grip on leadership questioned again
World.content:
Political update with Craig McCulloch Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Christopher Luxon's grip on his leadership is again being questioned following a week of communication gaffes and a fresh report his MPs are unhappy.

The Prime Minister last week endured days of mishaps and missteps and started this week inadvertently talking about three taxes the National Party may introduce if back in government.

He and his deputy, Nicola Willis, had called a press conference on Sunday to put pressure on Labour to sign up to its Budget responsibility rules, yet by his Monday morning media round Luxon was instead explaining that a fuel excise tax, bed tax, and bank tax would be on the table under a future National-led government.

On Monday night the NZ Herald reported National MPs had spent the day on the phones with one confirming they had fielded "several" phone calls about a potential leadership change.

"There's going to be change in the top job. It's just a question of who is going to be it", the NZ Herald reported the MP to have said.

RNZ spoke to about ten MPs on Monday night and received a mixture of responses.

Some said they wouldn't comment, while another said they couldn't comment, and others denied there were any leadership murmurings or that they knew about them.

One MP said the direct quotes in the reporting suggested there must be some truth to it, and at least one MP said it was nonsense.

RNZ understands the caucus will have a meeting online on Tuesday night, as Parliament is in recess this week.

On Saturday it was put to Luxon whether the confidence vote he called on his leadership back in April had resulted in a caucus split of 27 votes to 22.

He responded, "I have the support of my caucus - I'm very confident in my leadership."

It was speculation about whether Luxon was up to the job and had the backing of his caucus to stay on as leader that prompted him to test his support with a vote.

At the time when Luxon said that had put the rumour to bed and he had his caucus behind him.

Just four months later MPs appear to be musing about the prospect of changing leaders again.

While some spoken to by RNZ on Monday night said they supported Luxon, it wasn't unanimous.

There has been agitating since late last year from some MPs concerned Luxon's lack of personal popularity was also dragging the party vote down, and some MPs would lose their seats in Parliament if he didn't improve.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll in July had National down 2.1 points to 28.7 percent, its fourth consecutive decline in the Reid Research series and its weakest result since Luxon became leader in November 2021.

While Luxon's confidence vote win looked to have given him some reprieve, his performance in recent weeks has done little to convince concerned MPs they'll be safe come November 7.

Last Monday Luxon apologised to leaders from the Rotorua Business Chamber after he criticised them for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

He also faced questions about his foreign minister Winston Peters, and why he wasn't doing anything to reprimand him after labelling his comments about another MP, "racist".

Luxon then had to justify his use of a New Zealand Defence Force plane flying him home from a National Party fundraising dinner, and on the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

On Thursday he was using talkback radio to make a captain's call to hold a referendum on MMP, which blindsided his own caucus.

World.title: Big Tex leaves big impact on and off the field
World.content:
Taylor Walker's legacy is littered with athletic greatness and career-defining goals but his impact off the field and in the community makes him a true champion.

Nineteen years ago, a boy from Broken Hill with tips in his hair and a room littered with Crows posters crossed the border to pursue a dream.

The man affectionately known as Tex, after Chuck Norris' iconic character, was a 75-kilogram prospect who'd only ever wanted to be a footballer.

"When I arrived here as a skinny kid from Broken Hill, I never imagined where this journey would take me," Walker said on Monday.

"Football has given me so much but more than anything it's given me people."

Walker — who yesterday announced he would be retiring at season's end — was the final pick in the 2007 draft, but had to wait as Melbourne and Fremantle passed their final selections before the Adelaide Crows took a punt on an injured prospect who had been injured riding his motocross bike shortly after making the NSW Under-16 squad.

Walker joined the Crows as a "skinny kid from Broken Hill". (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

What followed was a rollercoaster journey of growth, leadership and legacy.

"His stats tell a story … but that is just part of his story," Crows CEO Tim Silvers said on Monday.

"He's been a great person, a wonderful leader, and he's led through the ups and downs of our footy club. He's led with strength, resilience, passion and determination.

" We're really proud of what he's done, the human he's become and the family man he is. "

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks echoed those sentiments, saying Walker's legacy at West Lakes is the greatest of any Crow in club history.

"I don't think there's been anyone bigger, when you talk about the impact he's had — not just on football, but on this state and our supporter base," Nicks said.

An emerging talent

It was a perfect storm that landed Walker at West Lakes. The AFL was eager to expand its growth areas in New South Wales and launched a scholarship program requiring clubs to take two players from the state.

Junior scout Mark Ross was sent to the region and caught a glimpse of a young man who would become Adelaide's all-time leading goalkicker.

Thankfully for recruiting boss Hamish Ogilvie, his injury meant no-one else got to see his potential ahead the draft.

Walker takes a mark in front of Port Adelaide's Paul Stewart during a 2011 Showdown. (AAP Image: Ben Macmahon)

It wasn't all smooth sailing for the soon-to-be seven-time leading goalkicker. After kicking over 50 goals in the SANFL for Norwood, Walker was given a debut against Collingwood in the first round of 2009, recording five touches and a goal in a thrilling four-point win.

But his 14-game debut season ended in the reserves and numerous omissions in 2010 as the young forward clashed with coach Neil Craig over his defensive pressure.

Premiership Crow and former Adelaide board member Rod Jameson remembers his treatment being unique for key forwards at the time.

"Neil Craig made it hard for him. They sent him back to work on his defensive game which was rarely heard of then," Jameson said.

" He'd go back and still kick numerous goals. We all knew there was talent there but it was the timing and consistency. "

There were rumours of a move to expansion club GWS and an omission after being caught on live TV drinking a beer at the SANFL — but the appointment of Brenton Sanderson as Adelaide's head coach in 2012 proved a turning point.

Walker watches from the player's bench after injuring his knee in 2013. (Joe Castro: AAP Image)

A 63-goal season led to a runner-up finish in the Coleman Medal and it felt like South Australia's next big thing had arrived, but an ACL injury early in 2013 was a devastating blow.

"I always tried to look at it glass half full … you've always got a choice to make. You can sit and sulk and look at the negatives or get on with life and do something about it," Walker said.

"You go through challenges in your career that make you want to get better."

Securing the captaincy

Walker's optimism and determination saw him return early in the 2014 season and inspired his teammates to appoint him captain the following year.

His first season at the helm was one of the most difficult any leader could have faced, with the tragic death of senior coach Phil Walsh.

But Walker was able to unite a shattered playing group and guide them into three consecutive finals series that culminated in the club's first grand final in 20 years and back-to-back AFLPA best captain awards.

The Crows got close to a premiership in 2017, but Richmond proved too good on the day. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Jameson recalls Walker's maturity and guidance in the club's darkest period being an inspiration to a devastated community.

"At heart he's a larrikin … [but] he says and does things that the group is able to follow, and it's a special trait," he said.

"The passing of Walshy and the grand final hardship … it wasn't easy but that's how you learn.

"He's just a ripping bloke. It's what good clubs are made of — they're the building blocks you want in the club. To build connections and catchers, he's gone about it his way and it's been an incredible career."

Walker himself believed the experience gave him perspective and pride.

"One of Walshy's favourite sayings was just get the job done," Walker said.

"If he was looking down he would've been incredibly proud of what we were able to do in that time.

" Life is hard, it's challenging. Things happen that you can't control. Don't take it too seriously. Have fun along the way because it's so short. "

Challenges on and off the field

Entering 2020, the winds of change had struck West Lakes, with coach Don Pyke stepping aside for Matthew Nicks, and Walker handing over the captaincy to Rory Sloane.

Walker faced concerns over his own future, battling a knee injury and engulfed in a racism scandal that saw him suspended for six matches for delivering a slur to North Adelaide's Robbie Young.

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and … I learned that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people," he said on Monday.

"I'm a better person for that mistake I made. I wish it never happened but also I feel like I'm better for it."

Walker shakes hands with North Adelaide's Robbie Young in the aftermath of the 2021 incident. (Adelaide Football Club)

A refreshed strength and conditioning program not only wound back the clock but saw Walker soar to career highs, with a 76-goal season in 2023 and his first All-Australian blazer.

Firmly in the premiership window after a minor premiership in 2025, Walker was hell-bent on helping the club break its near three-decade long drought but as the injuries rose and the weekly recovery got harder, the decision arrived at 3am last Tuesday.

"The closer I've gotten to the end it's probably become more evident it might be this year but I've treated it like my last year for the past six years," Walker said.

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club to retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership medallion around my neck.

"I might go out with a bang."

Walker celebrates a Showdown victory in 2018. (Getty Images: AFL Media/James Elsby)

Leaving a legacy

Walker's influence and impact will forever be etched into South Australian footy folklore, with a club record 706 goals and counting, and over 300 games that will see him finish third all-time.

"He's up there with the greats of the club. His impact, his longevity and his leadership," Jameson said.

"When you reflect on the stats and what he's been able to accomplish — he puts himself up in the elite category."

"Everyone sees the goals and big moments but those who have worked closely with Tex know the care he has for his teammates, our coaches and staff, and the club," Nicks said.

"He's someone who led through actions as much as words. He was prepared to stand up when things were going well and, importantly, he stood tall when they weren't."

Taylor Walker and Crows coach Matthew Nicks in 2020. (AAP: David Mariuz)

A clash with the ladder-leading Fremantle Dockers awaits Friday night as the Crows fight for a top-four finish, but when it's all said and done Walker will finish thankful for the opportunity to represent his childhood club.

"I've had three loves in my life — my family, my friends and footy," he said.

"I want to go back [to Broken Hill] and win a premiership there. Coaching is on the radar but I want to take a deep breath.

World.title: Greyhound badly injured in race supporting Tasmanian industry
World.content:
On a Sunday night in the regional New South Wales town of Temora, tragedy struck on the greyhound track.

It was race two, August 9, a 330-metre dash to the finish for seven greyhounds.

The race was named "We Stand With Tasmania Pathways".

WARNING: This story contains images that may cause distress for some readers.

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby bolted from the box and collided with another dog at the first turn.

She was flung into the side metal barrier and struggled to get back up.

A stewards' report from the night said it was likely she broke her shoulder blade and injured her "tricep".

The greyhound has been stood down from racing for 60 days and the race replay video has been deleted from the state's racing website.

On a prominent betting site, the race replay has also been edited to exclude the fall.

It is one of several races called "We Stand With Tasmania" that have resulted in falls and injuries.

Loading...

On December 22, 2025, during race three at Maitland in NSW, Hey Pat fell and sustained a serious foreleg fracture.

The greyhound is now listed as deceased.

Two greyhounds fell on October 20 last year during race one in Nowra, NSW.

And during race five in Warragul, Victoria, on October 23, Collinda Blinder fell and tumbled after the first turn.

Printed caps in support of Tasmania's greyhound industry have been spotted track-side. (Supplied)

The race where Manila Shelby was injured has been uploaded to Greyhound Racing SA's website.

In Tasmania, when a dog is injured on the track, a video of the race is never uploaded.

The Tasmanian industry's peak body Tasracing said this decision is made out of respect to the industry, as well as the greyhound trainer and animal involved.

Tasmanian Greens animal rights spokesperson Cassy O'Connor said the race was "horrible viewing" and "characteristic of the dangerous conditions greyhounds are forced to race in".

"This is happening in our name as Tasmanians," Ms O'Connor said.

"Manila Shelby isn't the first greyhound to be injured in mainland races under the 'Stand With Tasmania' banner, and sadly, she won't be the last.

"But we have the power to stop greyhounds being put in harm's way in this state."

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby sustained injuries during a race in Temora, New South Wales, on August 9, 2026. (Supplied: Greyhound Racing NSW)

The greyhound races authorities don't want you to see If you watched greyhound race videos on Tasracing's website, you would likely never know that dozens of dogs were injured or killed during events last year.

The state government has committed to cutting funding to the industry from 2029, which coincides with the end of the current funding deal for the code.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said in August last year "it was time to make a call on the future of the sport", and he "continues to be concerned about animal welfare".

"It's time to draw a line in the sand and ensure an orderly exit from greyhound racing in Tasmania," Mr Rockliff said at the time.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with a greyhound (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Legislation to phase out the industry passed the Tasmanian parliament's lower house in December 2025, but was pulled from the upper house after the state government feared it didn't have the numbers to pass.

"Greyhound racing is out of step with community expectations. It does not prioritise animal welfare," Tasmanian Liberal MP Marcus Vermey said.

Tasmanian Labor continues to support the industry.

Greyhound Racing NSW has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Former championship winning team cut from A-Leagues
World.content:
Western United has had its A-Leagues participation agreement terminated, effectively ending any flicker of hope of the troubled club making a return.

United has essentially been an A-Leagues club in name only for more than a year amid varied financial woes, which included not paying players and staff.

The club was placed into hibernation by the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) in September 2025, with A-League Men and Women players having to scramble to continue their careers elsewhere.

Ownership West Melbourne Group avoided a wind-up order from the Australian Tax Office in January by settling a $15.5 million tax debt.

Football Australia declined to reinstate the Tarneit-based club's licence in May and United again won't participate in either the ALM or ALW.

West Melbourne Group have another wind-up hearing in the Federal Court on Tuesday and on Monday the APL officially terminated their participation agreement in the A-League competitions.

Western United won the A-League Men's grand final in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"Since the club was placed into conditional hibernation in September 2025, the APL has been in close consultation with Western United as they've worked through financial, governance and legal matters to try and rebuild the club," APL chair Stephen Conroy said in a statement.

"The APL board has since taken the decision to terminate Western United's club participation agreement.

"The club was in breach of a number of its obligations under that agreement, including its obligation to comply with the Football Australia National Club Licensing Regulations.

"It's been a difficult period for everyone connected to Western United — and we want to acknowledge the management, staff, players and especially the fans — who have given so much to the club and will no doubt be hurt by this news."

Sadness after Western United licence removal Western United fans have expressed their disappointment and sadness after the team was stripped of its A-League licence late last week.

AAP understands United still owes some of its former players and staff money.

United was granted a licence in 2018, off the back of grand promises to build its own stadium, entered the A-League Men ahead of the 2019-20 season and won the ALM championship in 2021-22.

A women's team followed in 2022-23 and reached the grand final in their first season.

United has consistently been defiant and adamant it will return to the A-Leagues.

When put into hibernation, the club claimed it wasn't a "step back".

Western United finally opened their small Ironbark Fields ground in 2024. It saw just one season of A-League football. (Getty Images: MB Media/Santanu Banik)

After the tax debt was paid in January, the club declared its ambition to seal a "strong return to the A-Leagues".

Despite the latest development, the club on Monday broadcast plans to return in a year's time under new ownership.

"Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership," United said in a statement on Monday.

"This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start.

"The objective must now be to preserve Western United's identity in Melbourne's west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027-28 season.

"This should not be the end of Western United. It should be the reset that allows the club to rebuild and return stronger."

AAP

World.title: Injury could rule Socceroos defender out of Asian Cup
World.content:
Socceroos defender Cameron Burgess's Asian Cup hopes appear in jeopardy following a possible Achilles injury while playing for Swansea City.

The towering central defender played every minute of the gruelling English Championship campaign last season.

That made for 4,140 minutes, plus stoppage time, across all 46 league matches.

But there are fears Burgess's season is over after he limped off late in Swansea's 1-0 League Cup loss to Birmingham City.

In the 87th minute he challenged for a header, landed awkwardly and grabbed at his right lower leg, prompting his Birmingham opponents to check on him.

The 30-year-old, who has 29 Socceroos caps, headed to hospital for scans.

Cameron Burgess played against Türkiye and the USA for the Socceroos at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

"It doesn't look good, but I prefer to wait for the assessment we will do," Swansea head coach Vítor Matos said.

"It could be related to the Achilles, but let's see."

If Burgess has ruptured his Achilles, he faces a significant stint on the sidelines, ending his Asian Cup hopes.

Losing Burgess ahead of tournament, to be held in Saudi Arabia early next year, is a significant blow to Australia's defensive stocks.

Burgess lost his starting spot to teen sensation Lucas Herrington during the World Cup, with coach Tony Popovic preferring a back three involving the teenager, Harry Souttar and Alessandro Circati.

But as a left-footer, Burgess is always a valuable part of Popovic's squad.

Souttar spent more than a year on the sidelines after his own Achilles tear, while wing-back Lewis Miller is on the comeback trail from the same injury, which ruled him out of World Cup contention.

Star wing-back Jordan Bos is sidelined until about October after having surgery on the left knee injured in Australia's round-of-32 loss to Egypt.

The Socceroos are next in action for friendlies against Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and Brisbane four days later.

AAP

World.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
World.content:
Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

AAP

World.title: Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal
World.content:
Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's "please explain" as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Also on Monday, Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended Hocking.

Pressure has been mounting on Geelong and the AFL since it emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who had a history of concussion.

Drummond apologises AFL chair Craig Drummond issues a statement apologising for his part in the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion contract saga.

"We acknowledge this has been a challenging time for Jake, our club and Geelong supporters," Cats president Grant McCabe said in a statement on Monday.

"The board has met this morning to discuss our response to the AFL's letter. That will be submitted by end of day Tuesday, 11 August.

"This will provide the club with the chance to detail the actions it took in navigating this complex matter. We welcome this opportunity.

"The club remains committed to providing our players with the highest standard of care and support."

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

On the weekend Hocking defended the club in a radio interview and argued there was not a lot they would do differently.

"As a leader it's really important to take ownership and just lead through this. It's not easy to do, but I wouldn't change too much — we are a really good football club," he said.

"I know there are people out there who say culturally we are maybe not as strong as we have been, but we do so much right and occasionally there might be one or two per cent we don't get right.

"In this case that will be proven, I would suggest, that will be proven with the 'please explain'. We don't get everything right."

Drummond also released a statement in which he apologised over the deal. He added he would not be involved in the AFL's assessment and deliberation of the Kolodjashnij situation.

On Monday, Dangerfield told Fox Footy that Hocking was one of the most "placid" people he had met and gave him his full support.

"He's a man of the highest integrity … we're lucky to have him," Dangerfield said.

But he acknowledged mistakes had been made.

"Clearly there were some parts that we buggered up as a club. We can be better," he said.

AAP

World.title: WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul
World.content:
DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky has been ejected after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever.

Minutes after the eviction on Saturday (local time), Carrington posted on social media the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever.

Cunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break lay-up in the first quarter when Carrington, who is black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.

Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90–86 Indiana win was "absolutely" intentional.

"Clearly I think it was unnecessary," Cunningham said.

"I've never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff."

DiJonai Carrington had little to complain about, most suggested. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.

"It was a hard foul," White said.

"I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call."

Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

"I popped up," Cunningham said.

"I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it, because she wants attention."

Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after popping up after the foul. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Melissa Tamez)

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was wind-up, impact and follow-through on the foul.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had not seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he did not believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.

"I haven't looked at that play since, so I really don't know if it was justified or not," he said.

"But, that's what I thought in the moment."

Marsh was then asked about Carrington's social media post.

"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," he said.

"So yeah, we'll handle that."

But Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.

"I think the league is taking care of that," she said.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

In the third quarter, Fever star Caitlin Clark was assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds.

WNBA champs rubbish claims of Clark jealousy The outsized spotlight on Caitlin Clark has prompted some to suggest others in the WNBA are jealous of her, but two champions of the league say that is nonsense.

The technical was Clark's eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana's next game if not rescinded by the league.

"She said I ran into her," Clark said in a post-game television interview.

"I've already watched it on the tape, so we'll let the league decide. But it wasn't intentional or anything, so I'm hoping it's getting rescinded,"

A few hours after the game, Clark got her way. The WNBA rescinded the technical foul.

Cunningham has frequently come to Clark's defence after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season.

World.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
World.content:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

Bluesky has added a new feature that lets you hide reposts from a specific person in your feeds. The tool might be helpful if you want to stop seeing reposts from that one person who clogs up your feed with reposts of things you don’t care about. If you follow me, I may be that person, I’m sorry. I try not to be.

You can hide reposts from individual users by going to their profile, clicking the three dots button, and selecting the option to “Hide reposts in feeds.” (X offers a similar toggle.)

Bluesky also says that it’s launching a beta feature that will automatically add post numbers to threads. For long threads, it could be a useful way to get a sense of how much there might be to read, and it means you won’t have to manually add the numbers yourself. (Meta’s Threads already adds post counts to threads.) You can turn the feature on from Bluesky’s settings.

Tech.title: Costco’s great Switch 2 console bundle includes over $100 in free stuff
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The cost of the Nintendo Switch 2 is going up by $50 on September 1st, 2026, resulting in a $499.99 price tag for just the console. We’re just weeks away, but Costco is offering a fantastic $499.99 bundle for its members that includes a Nintendo Switch 2, a 256GB microSD Express card (usually $59), and a one year subscription to Nintendo Switch Online’s Expansion Pack tier, which normally costs $49.99 per year. That’s over $100 in value, and a great way to kickstart your Switch 2 experience.

The Switch 2 has 256GB of internal storage, so a microSD card is likely something you’ll need eventually for storing more games without having to constantly manage your library. With first-party Nintendo games typically running between 10 and 25GB, and larger third-party games reaching 50GB, a 256GB card should store anywhere from 5-20 additional games.

The Switch Online subscription includes a variety of features like cloud saving, online play, plus classic NES, SNES, and Game Boy titles. The Expansion Pack adds games from the GameCube, Game Boy Advance, N64, and Virtual Boy, and includes features for modern games, notably the Switch 2 upgrade packs for The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

Tech.title: What to expect from Google’s 2026 Pixel hardware launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s that time of year: On Wednesday, Google is set to host its annual Made by Google hardware launch event for Pixel gadgets. Google itself has already teased new slab-style and foldable Pixel smartphones, but leaks also indicate that the company could announce updated watches, a new color for familiar earbuds, and perhaps a brand new AirTag-like item tracker.

However, unusually, Google’s event is taking place in the evening: It kicks off on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT instead of in the early afternoon or mid-morning, like many other tech events. And this time it has a celebrity host in Trevor Noah.

Even more strange: As noted by 9to5Google, the Google Store homepage has a Pixel 11 preorder countdown that will end at 10AM ET on Wednesday — which is many hours earlier than the launch event itself. That could mean that all of the details about Google’s new devices will be officially revealed long before the company hosts the formal launch event.

Here’s what we expect to see Google announce this week. If you want to watch the event live, you can catch it on YouTube.

The Pixel 11 lineup

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Image: Evan Blass

Google has already hinted at its new phones while promoting the event, including shadowy glimpses of updated Pro and foldable phones. But the new smartphones could be largely iterative updates.

Google is expected to announce four new smartphones: the Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Based on leaked images, they should look largely the same as the Pixel 10 lineup, though it appears they’ll have camera bars that are black all the way across and colors that might rule.

Perhaps the most notable visual difference will be a rainbow glowy light on the camera bar, which Google has already shown off for the Pixel 11 Pro. The company hasn’t yet specified what it’ll do or what it’s called. But code in Google’s contacts app spotted by 9to5Google indicates that it will be called “HiLight” and, at least for that contacts app, HiLight can be customized with different colors to indicate when certain people call you. Presumably, the light will work in some way with other apps as well. Based on a translation of a leaked Pixel 11 Pro Fold image, HiLight will also light up when you talk with Google’s Gemini AI.

A tease from Google showing the new light. Image: Google

Inside the phones, it seems likely that they’ll be powered by a new Tensor G6 chip. It’s rumored that the new chip will use TSMC’s 2nm process, which is expected to bring performance and power efficiency gains. If it does launch with a 2nm chip, the Pixel 11 series will be the first smartphones on the market to do so, and potentially by a hair; Apple’s chip for its next Pro phones that presumably launch in September is also expected to use the 2nm process.

Google is rumored to raise the starting storage of the base Pixel 11 and the base Pixel 11 Pro to 256GB, up from the 128GB floor with the Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro. However, early Pixel 11 Pro listings have stated that the Pixel 11 Pro will have 12GB of RAM. If accurate, that would be down from the 16GB of RAM found in the Pixel 10 Pro lineup.

And expect the whole Pixel lineup to have a higher starting price, as a Google VP recently told 9to5Google that the Pixel family will get pricing “adjustments” due to the memory crisis.

The Pixel Watch 5

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel Watch 5. Image: OnLeaks and The Tide Chart

We already know that Google has manufactured at least one device called the Pixel Watch 5 thanks to, uh, Borderlands creator Randy Pitchford. In a May post that included two images, Pitchford said that a friend found the watch underwater while scuba diving. But recently, Google briefly teased the watch for an August 12th launch, so we should see more soon.

Leaked renders of the Pixel Watch 5 indicate that it may come in colors including black, polished silver, yellow gold, and a brass-y color, though the overall design looks quite similar to the Pixel Watch 4. Specs obtained by MyMobiles say that the new watch comes in 41 and 45mm screen sizes with battery life rated at 30 and 40 hours, respectively, matching the Pixel Watch 4. MyMobiles says that the Pixel Watch 5 will get 64GB of storage, which is double the 32GB of storage available previously.

On the software side, marketing materials obtained by MyMobiles suggest that Gemini Intelligence — which Google revealed earlier this year for Android phones — will be a big feature for the Pixel Watch 5 this year. One apparent marketing slide calls Gemini Intelligence a “personal, proactive assistant” that can proactively surface helpful information for you. A feature called “Proactive Suggestions” will also be able to help you reply to messages by recommending “context-aware replies” based on a conversation. The marketing materials also promise that the new watch will have Google’s “most accurate sleep tracking yet.”

However, like with the Pixel phones, expect higher prices. MyMobiles reports that the 41mm Wi-Fi model may start at $399, up from the Pixel Watch 4’s $349.99, while the 45mm Wi-Fi model could start at $429, up from $399.99.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 in a new color

A leaked marketing render of new Pixel Buds. Image: Evan Blass

Google first launched the Pixel Buds Pro 2 in 2024, but two years on, it seems as if the company is just going to launch a new color instead of refreshing the product.

An apparent marketing image leaked by Evan Blass shows new earbuds in a nice olive green color that matches other renders that Blass and others have surfaced of the Pixel 11 lineup. But the headphones themselves otherwise look just like the Buds Pro 2 — and they have apparently already appeared on a Google Play rewards page with the name “Pixel Buds Pro 2.”

I guess there’s always next year for the Buds Pro 3.

The Pixel Tag item tracker

An image apparently showing off the Google Pixel Tag. Image: 9to5Google

Google may also launch something brand new: Pixel Tag, an AirTag-like item tracker. Based on an image 9to5Google recently obtained, it has an oval shape, meaning it could look a little bit different than Apple’s circular AirTag.

Presumably, the Pixel Tag will play nicely with Android’s Find Hub network. A machine translation of a now-removed online listing said the tracker will connect with the “Find My Device” network, which was the name of the network before Google changed it to Find Hub. But detailed specs and an expected price haven’t leaked just yet.

Don’t expect Googlebook laptops or smart glasses

Some leaks for new Googlebook laptops have also cropped up recently, but when it first announced the Googlebooks, Google said they would be launching in the fall. Google is also working on smart glasses and Android XR glasses, but those are scheduled for the fall, too.

Sure, Google could throw curveballs. But that hardware will probably get full reveals at a later date.

Tech.title: YouTube is making it harder to earn money on YouTube
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Starting February 1st, 2027, creators who want to monetize their channel through YouTube’s Partner Program (YPP) will need at least 1,000 subscribers and either 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. That’s a sizeable jump from YouTube’s current requirement of 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 watch hours in the past year, or 1,000 subscribers with 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days. Creators will also need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over 90 days to earn money from the Shorts Creators Pool, though falling below this threshold won’t result in removal from YPP.

Additionally, YouTube says creators will benefit from an expansion of its cheaper Premium Lite subscription, which is coming to all countries where it offers Premium. YouTube splits up subscription revenue to creators based on watch time and views, with 55 percent dedicated to long-form videos and 45 percent for Shorts. “With these additional subscribers, creators can expect higher earnings: when a user signs up for Premium, partners, on average, earn more than when the user was watching ads,” YouTube says.

The requirements are changing as YouTube ramps up efforts to become more like a premium TV service alongside Netflix, HBO Max, and Disney Plus, rather than just an online platform for videos. This year, YouTube struck deals to broadcast shows from big names like Trevor Noah, and broadly rolled out a feature that allows creators to organize their videos into seasons.

Separately, there are some new requirements for creators to keep earning money from ads and subscriptions through the YPP, though. That includes maintaining either 1,000 watch hours over the past year, 1 million Shorts views, or two long-form videos or five Shorts uploaded every 90 days. YouTube’s existing policies say it will remove creators from the YPP if they haven’t uploaded a video or published content to the Posts tab for at least six months. Creators already in the program will need to accept the new terms by January 31st, 2027, to keep making money from their content.

Tech.title: Four takeaways from Mark Zuckerberg’s massive AI manifesto
Tech.content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a lot to say about the idealized future he now envisions for humanity co-existing with artificial intelligence — his latest essay spans more than 6,500 words on the matter. The lengthy manifesto Zuckerberg published on Monday, titled “The Future is for Everyone,” broadly lays out his beliefs about how the technology should be developed, expanded, and regulated, and how Meta is positioning itself to enable those goals.

Some points echo a similar (albeit, much shorter) public letter that Zuckerberg put out last year, heralding the importance of public access to superintelligent AI — a term for artificial general intelligence (AGI) models capable of surpassing human intelligence, which AI companies are racing to develop. Both were published with similar intentions: to pitch the supposed personal, societal, and economic benefits of superintelligent AI, and to grandstand Meta as a responsible steward to deliver that future.

Here are some of the main takeaways from Zuckerberg’s latest essay:

Sway the public on data centers

“Sustainable infrastructure development means that communities must benefit significantly from each project,” Zuckerberg said, detailing how Meta plans to resolve the ongoing PR crisis surrounding AI data center projects. This includes pledges to build energy-generating infrastructure “wherever we invest” that could potentially give low-cost energy back to the communities, and a commitment to “restore more water than we use in the watersheds where we operate by 2030.” Meta is also launching a Future Is For Everyone Fund to support local communities, and Zuckerberg says the company is providing free training and “guaranteed high-paying jobs” for skilled tradespeople in areas where Meta is building data centers.

Open AI for everyone

Meta is planning to focus its efforts on “delivering personal superintelligence to billions of people and small businesses,” arguing that doing so will empower everyone to become more entrepreneurial. Part of this involves offering the technology “for free or as affordably as possible,” and leaning into releasing more open source AI models that anyone can download. Doing so “will bring an abundance of personal agency, expression of ideas, deepening of relationships, economic and financial prosperity, improved health, and inventions we cannot imagine today,” according to Zuckerberg. He also says this will have an impact on “some aspects of the way we work,” but waves off concerns that AI will result in fewer jobs overall.

Less government oversight

Zuckerberg voices the importance of the US leading the open source AI ecosystem, citing concerns that competing models released by foreign labs “hold several advantages” because they face fewer training data restrictions. He pitches that the US needs to rethink policies around distillation and data use, arguing that while “some have tried to frame distillation as harmful,” the US will not be able to keep up if it keeps restricting AI models from learning from other models.

“I do not believe restricting access to foreign open source models is an effective solution,” said Zuckerberg. We should note here that these concerns are likely being voiced in response to the release of open-weight models from Chinese AI companies like Alibaba and Moonshot, which isn’t the same thing as being open-source, and the models Meta has released so far aren’t truly open-source either. He also espouses that access to personal superintelligence is essential for individuals to maintain their freedom, and should only be subject to restrictions “when truly required.”

But also, more government oversight

In cases where cybersecurity is involved, Zuckerberg proposes that frontier AI labs should work with the US government to help with bolstering critical infrastructure, and believes open-source AI models will improve system security over time — especially “once superintelligence enables most of the world’s code to be verifiably secure.” That plan includes pushing AI developers to share the training information of new models “for government use and review” intermediately instead of waiting until training has completed, which aligns with the Trump administration’s AI testing framework.

“This way the government will have early access to the most powerful models and an army of capable engineers to identify and patch security issues,” Zuckerberg said. “Labs should also work with law enforcement to help identify bad actors attempting to misuse their systems.”
